This is information only: the reinforcement does not change. An element that is not cracked (EN 1992-2 Annex LL (107), with the transverse shears) gets no such note.

docs.title: EN 1992-1-1:2023
docs.text:
Annex G.4 replaces Wood–Armer: the element moments mx, my and mxy give the capacities needed in the bottom and top layers, with Tables G.2 and G.3 (the optimum reinforcement). The preference ec2_slab_method chooses:

Method Does auto (default) Tables G.2 and G.3, and the sandwich model where they do not apply optimum only the tables sandwich only the sandwich model

The tables do not apply where |mxy| ≥ 0.07·d²·fcd. The sandwich model (G.4(1) to (3)) takes two layers of thickness 2·cover, designs each as a membrane with Table G.1, and checks the strut against ν·fcd (ν from ec2_nu_mode). A face with no tension gets no reinforcement. Each row says which method produced it (wood-armer in 2004, optimum or sandwich in 2023), whether a sandwich layer crushes, and carries the warnings of the check: a strip over-reinforced (x/d > 0.45), no solution (the area is then not a number), the limit |mxy| ≥ 0.07·d²·fcd forced in optimum mode.

docs.title: Out-of-plane shear
docs.text: Both editions verify the out-of-plane shear, from the transverse shears vx and vy: the row has the principal shear v_Ed [kN/m], a shear_mode (none, no shear reinforcement, stirrups or strut crushing) and the required shear reinforcement. A crushed shear strut is reported as crushing. In 2023 the shear follows §8.2 (G.4(4)), and the chord force of the truss is added to the sandwich layers; in 2004 it follows the inner layer of EN 1992-2 Annex LL (109) to (111) from the Wood–Armer bars, and the chord force is only noted in the row.

docs.title: Which elements
docs.text: The design covers the triangles and the quads of the model that have a Concrete section: in a plane model the membrane ones (including CST and Allman triangles, and Q4 and QM6 quads), in a plate model the plate-bending ones (DKT and MITC3 triangles, DKT4 and MITC4 quads).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The rows are in the Shell reinf. tab of the Design panel (Concrete ▸ Shell reinf.), one per element and combination: the forces or moments, the required areas in cm²/m (in each direction, and split into bottom and top), the concrete stress σc against ν·fcd, the strut (OK or CRUSHING), and ★ on the governing combination of each element.

On the canvas, the Shell reinf. (As) view draws the envelope of the design combinations over each element, with a component selector: As,x, As,y and the concrete stress σc for a wall; for a slab, the reinforcement of each face. Hover an element to see the values and the combination that drives each one.

For the step-by-step calculation of an element, see Design reports.

docs.title: Concrete: beams and columns
docs.text:
The reinforced-concrete design of bars to EN 1992-1-1 (EC2). Slabs and walls are on Concrete: slabs and walls, and punching on Concrete: punching. Before you start, see Materials and sections for design and Design codes and preferences.

Menu item What it does Design ▸ Concrete members (ULS) the reinforcement of every concrete bar: flexure, shear and, in a grillage, torsion; then the bars of each beam Design ▸ Crack width the crack-width check (SLS), from the reinforcement of the previous design Design ▸ Suggest column reinforcement (ULS) the lightest symmetric layout of bars for each column Design ▸ Beam definitions which bars form one continuous beam Design ▸ Beam bars detailing… the window where you refine the bars of each beam

docs.title: Beams and grillage members
docs.text:
Concrete members (ULS) designs every bar whose section is of type Concrete. Each bar is checked at its critical sections: both ends, and the points of extreme bending moment and shear along the span, for every selected ULS combination. The section that needs the most steel is marked governing (★).

A bar that is a column is not designed here: it goes to the column check (see Columns). Envelope combinations (an envelope, a seismic one) are designed by their maximum and minimum bands, each as a case of its own.

docs.title: Method, EN 1992-1-1:2004
docs.text:
Flexure. Rectangular sections are designed for the dimensionless moment μ = M_Ed / (b·d²·fcd), giving the tension steel As; when μ exceeds the singly-reinforced limit, compression steel is added. The effective depth is d = h − cover. Minimum and maximum steel ratios follow EC2 §9.2.1.

Shear. The concrete resistance VRd,c (EC2 §6.2.2) is checked first. When the shear exceeds it, the variable-angle truss model (§6.2.3) is used: the strut angle is swept from cot θ = 2.5 (θ ≈ 21.8°) down to cot θ = 1.0 (θ = 45°), choosing the flattest strut the concrete can carry so that the stirrup demand Asw/s is minimised, while respecting the strut-crushing limit VRd,max. If the section crushes even at θ = 45°, it is reported as inadequate in shear at the crushing limit.

All the partial factors come from Code preferences: fcd = αcc·fck/γc and fyd = fyk/γs.

docs.title: Method, EN 1992-1-1:2023
docs.text:
With the 2023 edition selected:

  • fcd = ηcc·ktc·fck/γc (Eq. 5.3), and αcc is not used. ktc is a preference.
  • Shear follows §8.2 (γv, ddg, τRdc,min, a compression field with ν = 0.5, the minimum stirrups of Eq. 12.4); the axial force and the shear span enter VRd,c.
  • Torsion follows §8.3 (ν from Annex G), and the combined shear and torsion Eq. 8.86.

Each result row says which edition produced it. The crack width and the anchorage and lap lengths keep the 2004 rules in both editions.

docs.title: Grillage members
docs.text: In a plate model a bar is a grillage member: it bends out of its plane and carries St-Venant torsion, and the N slot of its end forces is the torsion T. The flexure and the shear are designed with N = 0, and the torsion to EC2 §6.3, combined with the shear (Eq. 6.29).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The Design panel lists, under Concrete ▸ Reinforcement, one row per critical section and combination:

Column Meaning Element, Combination, Location which member, combination and section Reason why the section was checked (end, M⁺ or M⁻ peak, V peak) M_Ed, N_Ed, V_Ed design action effects at that section As,bot / As,top [cm²] required tension-face and compression-face steel Asw/s [cm²/m] required shear reinforcement (stirrup area per metre) cot θ strut inclination used by the variable-angle truss Strut the concrete strut crushing limit VRd,max Gov. ★ marks the governing section of each element

On the canvas, the reinforcement envelopes are drawn along each member: the required longitudinal steel (As) and the shear reinforcement (Asw), enveloped over the selected combinations, station by station.

docs.title: Beam bars
docs.text:
Right after the design, Concrete members (ULS) turns the required areas of each beam into bars, in the Beam bars tab: for each span, zone by zone, the bars of the bottom and top faces, the continuous ("through") bars, and the stirrups with their anchorage and lap lengths. The parameters are the EC2 · beam bars group of Code preferences.

What a beam is. A beam is a continuous chain of spans: spans that meet collinearly at a support or at a column are joined into one beam (columns are ignored at the joint; a change of section, or a hinge, ends the beam). Beams are numbered B1, B2, … from bottom to top and from left to right. Beams the program finds are automatic. Design ▸ Beam definitions opens a panel where you select bars, tag them as one beam and give it a name, to correct what the detection would do. These tags are design data only: they do not change the analysis, so they can be edited on a locked model. Re-run the design to apply them.

Zones. Each span is divided into zones, in one of two ways: at the cutoff points of the envelope (the required steel is quantised into a number of steps, and a zone boundary is placed wherever the envelope changes step; zones shorter than a minimum are merged), or at fixed fractions of the span. The requirement of a zone is the envelope of the steel required in it. The bars of each zone are chosen with the minimum steel As,min, uniform diameters, and the through bars present in every zone.

Beam bars detailing… opens a separate window to refine the proposal, with the tabs Bars, Stirrups, Lengths and Parameters. You can split and merge zones, edit the bars and the stirrups with undo and redo, and the window checks each zone live against what is required. Zones you edit are manual and are kept when the design is re-run (flagged if they no longer comply); the others follow the new proposal. The decisions are stored with the model.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
A bar is a column when its section is marked Physical column by default, or the bar itself is (a bar can override the section in Design ▸ Buckling lengths…, see Buckling lengths). Collinear bars are grouped into one physical member, and each is checked, over the selected combinations, for:

  • slenderness and second-order effects (EC2 §5.8), by the nominal curvature method (§5.8.8, the default) or the nominal stiffness method (§5.8.7), as the section says;
  • the N–M interaction of the section (§6.1), for the layout of bars the section gives: a number of bars for a circular section, or a number on each pair of faces for a rectangular one.

The columns are rectangular or circular. xdfem2D is a 2D program, so each element has one in-plane bending moment, which is taken as the moment about the major axis; the moment about the other axis is zero, and the minimum-eccentricity rule of EC2 is still applied to it in the biaxial check. The checks are eurocodepy's (the 2023 edition uses the 2023 fcd and keeps the 2004 slenderness and N–M rules).

The Columns tab lists, per member and combination, the slenderness (λy, λz), whether it is slender, the method, the moment resistances and the check. The canvas can colour the columns by their N–M utilisation.

Design ▸ Suggest column reinforcement (ULS) does the reverse: instead of checking the layout you gave, it finds the lightest symmetric layout of bars (number and diameter) that satisfies EC2 for the governing combination of each column, in the Suggested rebar tab. A column for which no layout in the search range works is listed with the error, not dropped.

docs.title: Crack width
docs.text:
Design ▸ Crack width checks the crack width (EN 1992-1-1 §7.3.4, always with the 2004 rules) of each concrete bar, with the reinforcement of the previous design, station by station (with an As,min floor), for the combinations ticked under SLS in Design combinations. It needs Concrete members (ULS) to have run first. Combined bending and axial force are accounted for. The limit w_max and the SLS combination type come from the preferences, and the main bar diameter from the section. The Crack width tab lists, per element and combination, the two ends and the governing station, whether the section is cracked, wk, the limit and the check; the canvas can draw the crack width along the member.

The crack width is the only serviceability check: there is no check of deflections.

docs.title: The design report
docs.text: For any of these checks, Design ▸ Design report… produces the step-by-step calculation: see Design reports.

docs.title: Concrete: punching
docs.text: The punching-shear check of a slab at its columns, to EN 1992-1-1 §6.4 (2004) or §8.4 (2023), for plate models only. A column punches a slab locally, and the finite-element model does not know the size or the shape of a column, so the check runs over a list of punching columns that you define. It is Design ▸ Punching…, which is listed for every model but only works on a slab: in a plane model it says so.

docs.title: Defining the columns
docs.text:
Design ▸ Punching… opens the Punching panel in the left dock (a tab of its own), with the list of punching columns and these actions:

Button What it does Add… pick a supported node on the canvas; a dialog opens already filled with it Edit…, Delete change or remove the selected column Calculate run the check for every column and fill the Punching table of the Design panel Draw draw the control perimeters on the canvas Clear remove that drawing Show columns on canvas mark the column nodes

A punching column has:

Data Meaning Node the slab node the column reaction acts on Shape and size rectangular (bx × by) or circular (bx is the diameter) Position center, edgex, edgey or corner: the control perimeter differs at a free edge or a corner dx, dy the distance from the column to the slab edge (for an edge or corner column) Force the design punching force [kN]. Left empty, it is the support reaction Rz at the node, for each combination β min the smallest load-eccentricity factor to use. When a support transfers no moment the computed β falls to its floor; EC2 §6.4.3(6) allows the simplified 1.15 (interior), 1.4 (edge) and 1.5 (corner). The design uses the larger of the computed β and this value; 1.0 keeps the computed value

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
For each column and each combination the design computes:

  • the design punching stress τEd, with the eccentricity factor β from the moments transferred at the node (the reactions Mx and My);
  • the concrete resistance τRd,c and its minimum, from the reinforcement ratio ρl, the effective depth and the concrete strength;
  • the utilisation τEd/τRd,c, and whether punching reinforcement is needed;
  • the strut limit τRd,max, and whether the strut crushes.

ρl is taken from the bottom bars that the slab design gave near the column (the mean of the elements that touch the node, at most 0.02). Run Concrete areas (ULS) first for a ρl that reflects your slab; without it the check uses 0.005.

When the force is taken from the reaction, envelope combinations are skipped: they carry no single reaction. Give the force on the column to check them.

The formulae are eurocodepy's. The 2023 edition takes γv, dmax and η_sys from the preferences (see Design codes and preferences), or from the data of the edition and the national annex when they are left empty (Table 4.3).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The Punching tab (in the Design panel, under Concrete) has one row per column and combination:

Column Meaning Column, Node, Combination, Position which column, where, for what N_Ed the punching force [kN] β the eccentricity factor d, u1 the effective depth and the length of the basic control perimeter τEd, τRd,c, τRd,max the stress, the concrete resistance, the strut limit [MPa] τEd/τRd,c the ratio of the stress to the concrete resistance u_out,ef the perimeter outside which no punching reinforcement is needed Verdict OK, REINF NEEDED or CRUSHING (in red)

The step-by-step calculation is in the design report, under Punching.

docs.title: Materials and sections for design
docs.text: A design reads two things from the model: the material of each section, which carries the strengths, and the section itself, which carries the shape, the type and the data of the design (cover, bars, orientation, service class). This page says what each design needs.

docs.title: The type decides what is designed
docs.text: A section has a type: Concrete, Steel, Timber or Other. A design runs only for the elements whose section has the type it designs: Concrete members for concrete bars, Steel members for steel bars, and so on. A section of type Other, and a material of type Other, are analysed but never designed. The type of a section follows the Material type of its material, which you set in the Material dialog.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
In Structure ▸ Materials, picking a class in the Material dialog fills the elastic modulus, the unit weight, the thermal expansion, the Poisson ratio and all the strengths the design reads, from the eurocodepy database. The classes available are:

Material Classes Concrete C20/25, C25/30, C30/37, C35/45, C40/50, C45/55, C50/60, C55/67, C60/75, C70/85, C80/95, C90/105 Reinforcement A500EL, A500ER, A400NR, A500NR, A400NRSD, A500NRSD, B400A/B/C, B450A/B/C, B500A/B/C, B550A/B/C, B600A/B/C, B700A/B/C Steel S235, S275, S355, S450 and S460, and the variants the database has: S235JR, S275JR, S355JR, S450J0, S275N, S355N, S420N, S460N, the NL, M, ML, W, Q, QL and QL1 grades Timber solid C16, C18, C24, C30, D24, D30, D40, D50, D60, D70; glulam GL20h to GL32h and GL20c to GL32c; CL24; LVL32P, 35P, 48P, 50P, 80P, 22C, 25C, 32C, 36C, 70C, 75C

What the design stores, in the material's design properties:

Material Stored Read by Concrete class_conc and fck, class_reinf and fyk all the concrete designs Steel class, fy, fu the steel design Timber class (the EN 338 grade) and its strengths the timber design

The numeric fck and fyk are used when they are present. When a concrete material carries only its class names, the strengths are looked up from the class. A concrete material needs both a concrete and a reinforcement strength to be designed: a section whose material lacks either is skipped. You can also type the strengths yourself for a class that is not in the list.

A material made from the generic reference catalogue of the dialog (structural steel, plain concrete, sawn timber, stone, …) has the type Other and no design properties: it is for the analysis only.

docs.title: Concrete
docs.text:
Data Where Used for Shape and size Structure ▸ Sections beams: a rectangle b × h. Columns: a rectangle or a circle Cover [m] section dialog the mechanical cover to the bar, so d = h − cover Stirrup angle [°] section dialog the inclination of the stirrups in the shear design Bar diameter φ [mm] section dialog the main bar diameter of the crack-width check Physical column by default section dialog bars using this section are columns (EC2 §5.8). A bar can override this in Design ▸ Buckling lengths… φ_ef (creep), N. bars (circular), N_y / N_z bars (rectangular), 2nd-order method section dialog the column design. Nominal curvature (§5.8.8, the default) or nominal stiffness (§5.8.7)

For slabs and walls (the area sections, called Panel in a plane model and Slab in a plate model) the cover is given per face and direction (top and bottom, x and y) and the thickness is the section's; see Concrete: slabs and walls.

docs.title: Steel
docs.text: The shapes designed are I, rectangular hollow (RHS and SHS) and circular hollow (CHS). Choose a catalogue profile (for example IPE300) to fill the shape, the area and the inertias, and the grade comes from the material. The angle θ turns the profile in the plane of the frame: 0° puts the major axis in the plane, 90° the minor axis, and the in-plane actions are resolved onto the principal axes with it (My = M·cosθ, Mz = M·sinθ).

docs.title: Timber
docs.text: The shapes designed are the rectangle, a generic section with its area and inertia given, and the circle. The service class (SC1 to SC4; SC4 only in EN 1995-1-1:2025) drives kmod and kdef. The load-duration class of each load case (instantaneous, short, medium, long, permanent) is set on the load case, or left automatic; combined with the service class it gives kmod. A bar with a beam tag is designed as a tagged timber beam: see Timber.

docs.title: What is left out of a design
docs.text: A design does not stop at an element it cannot design: it skips it, so a missing result can mean a missing property. The concrete design of bars skips a bar whose material has no fck or no fyk, and a bar whose section is defined by an area and inertia given by hand instead of a real b × h. If no bar has a section of type Concrete at all, the menu item says so. For slabs and walls, when nothing could be designed, the message names the sections whose material lacks usable strengths. If a member you expected is missing from the results, look at its material and its section first.

docs.title: Design reports
docs.text:
Design ▸ Design report… opens a Design report side panel (a tab in the left dock, like the Punching and Buckling workbenches) that produces a full, step-by-step calculation report — every partial result, the code clause, the symbolic expression and the numeric substitution — for the checks the engine actually ran. The panel is read-only with respect to the model, so it can be used on a locked model.

Controls:

  • Material — lists only the design kinds present in the model: Steel members (EC3), Timber members (EC5), Concrete members (EC2) (bars / grillage), Concrete areas (EC2) (membrane / slab triangles) and Punching (EC2).
  • Scope — Whole model or Current selection (defaults to the current canvas selection). Selecting a row in the summary table highlights that member / element / column / triangle on the canvas.
  • Detail — Envelope (governing) gives one report per member (the governing case across the chosen combinations); Per combination gives one report per member and combination.
  • Combinations — a multi-select; nothing selected means all available.
  • Format — HTML (self-contained, with MathJax equations and a linked table of contents), PDF (composed pages with typeset equations and the section figure), Word (.docx, equations as images, or native editable OMML when pandoc is installed) and Markdown (with a sibling assets folder for the figures).

Preview renders the HTML and opens it; Export… saves in the chosen format. Each report embeds a small cross-section drawing (rectangle for concrete/timber, and the I / RHS / SHS / CHS outline for steel profiles).

docs.title: Report tools (pandoc and Ollama)
docs.text: Editable Word equations use pandoc, and the local AI assistant uses Ollama — both optional external tools. Preferences → Dependencies shows whether each is installed, explains what it unlocks, and offers the per-OS install command (copy or run). Without them the app still works: Word equations fall back to images, and the assistant uses the remote providers you configure.

docs.title: Steel (EC3)
docs.text: The design of steel bars to EN 1993-1-1:2005, with Design ▸ Steel members (ULS). Before you start, see Materials and sections for design (the section must be of type Steel and a supported shape), Design codes and preferences for the parameters, and Buckling lengths for the K factors the stability checks use.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
For every steel bar, for each selected ULS combination:

  • the cross-section resistance (§6.2): N, My, Mz, Vy, Vz and T, reported as three ratios: bending (the N + M interaction), shear and torsion;
  • the member stability (§6.3.3): flexural buckling and lateral-torsional buckling together, computed once per physical member (a chain of collinear bars, found automatically) and shared by its bars.

The governing ratio of each bar is its combined ratio. The forces of each bar are enveloped over its critical points and over the combinations, which is conservative. The axial force is tension-positive, so the design compression is −N.

The shapes designed are I, rectangular hollow (RHS, SHS) and circular hollow (CHS), normally from a catalogue profile. The in-plane actions are resolved onto the principal axes of the profile with its angle θ (see Materials and sections for design). A section of any other shape is not designed.

docs.title: In a plate model
docs.text: A grillage member has no axial force: the N slot of its end forces is the St-Venant torsion T, and it carries bending out of the plane and shear. Only lateral-torsional buckling is then relevant.

docs.title: Choices that change the result
docs.text:
These are in Design ▸ Code preferences ▸ EC3 · Steel:

Choice Meaning Interaction factors kij (§6.3.3) Annex B (method 2, the default) or Annex A (method 1) Class 4 effective properties on: a Class 4 section is checked with its effective properties LTB rolled/welded method (§6.3.2.3) on: the more favourable method for rolled and welded sections γM0, γM1, γM2 the partial factors (1.0, 1.0, 1.25) Cmy, Cmz, CmLT, C1 the default equivalent-moment and LTB-moment factors K_y, K_z, K_LT the default buckling-length factors, overridden per member in Buckling lengths

Two rules of the design: hollow sections are not susceptible to lateral-torsional buckling, and the shear area of RHS and SHS sections is the one of the standard. A member can also be marked as not susceptible to lateral-torsional buckling in the Buckling panel.

The model is 2D

The out-of-plane bracing is invisible to a planar model. The buckling length out of the plane is the in-plane one unless you set K_z for the member (see Buckling lengths).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The Design panel lists, under Steel, one row per physical member and combination:

Column Meaning Member, Elements, Section, Profile, L the member, its bars, its section and profile, its length Combination, Class the combination, and the cross-section class N_Ed, My_Ed, Mz_Ed the design actions χy, χz, χLT the reduction factors of buckling about each axis and of lateral-torsional buckling 6.61, 6.62 the utilisation of the two interaction expressions of §6.3.3 Check the governing ratio and its verdict

On the canvas, the Steel design view colours each bar by its utilisation, with a selector for the check shown: combined, bending, shear, torsion or buckling (§6.3).

The step-by-step calculation of a member is in the design report.

docs.title: Timber (EC5)
docs.text: The design of timber bars to EN 1995-1-1 (2004 or 2025), with Design ▸ Timber members (ULS). Before you start, see Materials and sections for design (the section must be of type Timber, with a grade, and a service class), Design codes and preferences for the parameters, and Buckling lengths.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
For every timber bar, for each selected ULS combination, the grouped cross-section and member verification of EN 1995-1-1 (from eurocodepy):

  • bending and axial force (N + My + Mz), including the compression stability factor kc and the lateral-torsional factor km;
  • shear (Vy, Vz) and their interaction;
  • torsion (T) and the shear and torsion interaction.

The buckling lengths are obtained as for steel: collinear bars form a physical member, and its length is multiplied by the member's K factors (or the global defaults) to give l_0y, l_0z and l_0m. The forces are enveloped over each bar's critical points and over the combinations, and the sign of the axial force is kept, so both the tension and the compression points are checked (the rules differ).

The resistances depend on the material, the service class and the duration of the load: the grade of the material (solid, glulam, LVL, CLT or panels) picks the partial factor γM from Code preferences, the service class of the section and the load-duration class of each load case give kmod and kdef. Both editions are implemented, chosen in Code preferences.

In a plate model a grillage member has no axial force (its N slot is the torsion T) and the design checks bending, shear and torsion.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The Design panel lists, under Timber, one row per physical member:

Column Meaning Member, Elements, Section, Grade, L the member, its bars, its section, its grade and length SC, Duration the service class and the load-duration class N_Ed, My_Ed, Mz_Ed, Vy_Ed, Vz_Ed the design actions k_cy, k_cz, k_m the stability factors N+M, Shear, Torsion the utilisation of each check Type, Taper, Apex M, Apex t90, Apex t90+V for tagged beams: see below Governing sections, Check where it governs, and the verdict

On the canvas, the Timber design view colours each bar by its ratio.

docs.title: Special timber beams (pitched, tapered, curved)
docs.text:
Design → Timber → Special timber beams opens the Beams panel in timber mode. Select the bars of a beam (they need not be collinear — a ridge or an arc is fine), press Assign to beam, and the design treats them as one member — or press Detect beams automatically… to have the chains of timber bars proposed (up to 45° from the horizontal, a ridge or an arc included; posts and columns are never proposed) and accept them. The list follows the beams: grouped, bottom to top and left to right, and along each beam from its left end. Draw the beam with the depth you want in each bar; nothing is generated, the design reads it:

  • the depth along the beam (a taper or a step), and which edge is inclined to the grain;
  • the ridge (apex) and, for an arc, its radius.

The panel shows what was read and lets you override what cannot be read: the spacing of the lateral restraints, the lamination thickness, the inner radius, the type, the inclined edge and the depth change. These parameters are design-only, so the analysis results are kept; re-run Timber Members (ULS) to apply them. The table gains the Type, Taper (§6.4.2) and Apex (§6.4.3: bending, tension perpendicular to the grain, and its interaction with shear) columns. Use enough bars along a taper: a warning appears when the depth jumps between neighbouring bars by more than the Code-preferences limit.

Below the table the elevation draws the beam as modelled, coloured by the utilisation at each position, with curves of N+M, shear, tapered edge and apex along its length. The calculation report of the member adds the geometry read from the bars and, step by step, each EN 1995-1-1 §6.4 check at the point where it governs. The apex clause (§6.4.3) applies to glued laminated timber and LVL only; for other products a warning is shown. Both code editions are implemented (EN 1995-1-1:2004 §6.4 and EN 1995-1-1:2025 §8.3.3–§8.3.4, chosen in Code preferences); the 2025 edition also notes when reinforcement against tension perpendicular to the grain is advised (optional). If you tick Apex reinforced for the beam, the unreinforced checks of the tension perpendicular to the grain and its interaction with shear do not apply (§8.3.4.2(1)); the result gives the force the reinforcement must carry (per metre of beam, and per element if you give the spacing a1). If you also give the bonded-on plane reinforcement (width, thickness, tensile and bond-line design strengths, and optionally the reinforced length and the number per element), its resistance is verified element by element (Eqs. 8.48–8.51). For screws and rods (fully threaded screws, rods with wood screw thread, bonded-in rods) give the diameter, inner diameter, steel strength; the partial factors γ_R = 1.30 and γ_M2 = 1.25 (Table 4.4) are used unless you give others: the resistance follows §11.2.2 with the reinforced length as withdrawal length. The spacing limits of §8.3.4.2(4) and the limits of Table 11.2 are reported as warnings.

Bars that carry a beam tag are designed as tagged beams: the member is the whole tagged chain, and the buckling length is that of the span between supports, hinges and joining bars; a lateral spacing you set on the beam replaces K_LT·L.

The step-by-step calculation of a member is in the design report.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
xdfem2D designs members and slabs to the Eurocodes, from the results of an analysis and the load combinations you choose. It is a design aid, not a substitute for engineering judgement: read Licenses & Disclaimer, which applies to every result the program produces, and the limits at the end of this page.

Material Code Designs Concrete EN 1992-1-1 (EC2), 2004 or 2023 beams and grillage members (flexure, shear, torsion), the bars of each beam, columns, crack width, walls and slabs, punching Steel EN 1993-1-1 (EC3) bars: cross-section resistance and member stability Timber EN 1995-1-1 (EC5), 2004 or 2025 bars, including pitched, tapered and curved beams

The formulae are those of eurocodepy, a required dependency; xdfem2D gathers the actions, calls the checks and shows the results.

docs.title: The Design menu
docs.text:
Everything is in the Design menu, next to Analysis.

Menu item Page Code preferences, Design combinations Design codes and preferences Buckling lengths… Buckling lengths Design report… Design reports Concrete ▸ Concrete members (ULS), Crack width, Suggest column reinforcement (ULS), Beam definitions, Beam bars detailing… Concrete: beams and columns Concrete ▸ Concrete areas (ULS) Concrete: slabs and walls Concrete ▸ Punching… Concrete: punching Steel ▸ Steel members (ULS) Steel (EC3) Timber ▸ Timber members (ULS), Special timber beams Timber (EC5)

What a section needs in order to be designed (its type, its material and class, its cover, its profile) is on Materials and sections for design.

docs.title: Designing a model
docs.text:
1. Model it with the right materials and sections. Set the type of each section and give its material a class, so that the strengths exist (Materials and sections for design).
  2. Analyse it (F5). The design reads the results of the analysis.
  3. Choose the combinations in Design ▸ Design combinations: the ULS tab for the designs, the SLS tab for the crack width. Generate the EN 1990 combinations with Analysis ▸ Auto Comb. (EN1990)… or define your own (Design codes and preferences).
  4. Check the code preferences in Design ▸ Code preferences: the edition, the partial factors and the parameters of each code.
  5. Run the design from its menu item. Each item designs for the combinations you chose, and shows its results.

A design needs the elements to have the right properties, and skips an element it cannot design (see What is left out). If a member you expected is missing, look there first.

docs.title: Where the results are
docs.text:
• The Design panel has one tab per material: Concrete, with the sub-tabs Reinforcement, Shell reinf., Crack width, Columns, Beam bars, Suggested rebar and Punching; then Steel and Timber. Selecting a row in a table highlights that member on the canvas.
  • The canvas has design views, which colour the model by what was designed: the reinforcement envelopes, the shell reinforcement, the crack width, the utilisation of columns, steel and timber members. They are in the View list once there is something to show.
  • Design ▸ Design report… produces the step-by-step calculation of any check (Design reports).

The results are stored with the model, in the .x2d, together with the design code they were produced with (see File Formats). They are discarded when the code preferences change or a new analysis replaces the results, because the ratios no longer apply.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The model is 2D: each element has one in-plane bending moment. Concrete columns are checked for that moment about the major axis, with the minimum eccentricity of EC2 applied to the other; the out-of-plane bracing of steel and timber members is given by K_z (Buckling lengths).
  • Beams are designed as rectangular sections. Columns are rectangular or circular.
  • The only serviceability check is the crack width; there is no check of deflections.
  • With the 2023 edition of EC2, the crack width, the anchorage and lap lengths and the slenderness and N–M rules of columns keep the 2004 rules (Design codes and preferences).
  • Envelope combinations cannot be used for the design of slabs and walls, and the reaction-based punching force needs plain combinations too.
  • Punching is for plate models, and for the columns you define.
  • A national annex is chosen in a script, not in the dialog.

docs.title: Domains (plane vs plate)
docs.text:
Every xdfem2D model lives in one of two domains. The choice is made in New model, and it is fixed as soon as the model has geometry — because every support, load and result changes meaning between them, nodes, bars and areas cannot be switched from one to the other. While the model is still empty (no nodes, bars, areas or objects) the domain can be changed: see below.

Domain What it is Elements DOFs per node Typical use Plane a frame or wall in its own plane frame bars, membrane triangles and quads ux, uy, θz frames, trusses, walls Plate a slab or grillage bending out of plane grillage beams, plate-bending triangles and quads w, θx, θy slabs, beam grillages

Both domains carry three degrees of freedom per node — the solver machinery is shared — but the three slots mean different things, so the same storage reads as ux, uy, θz in a plane model and w, θx, θy in a plate one.

docs.title: Choosing the domain
docs.text: New model shows the two domains as clickable icon cards — a portal frame with a shear wall for Frame / Wall (in-plane), and a supported slab field for Slab / Grillage (out-of-plane). It opens on the domain of the model that is open. Click a card to select it (the border highlights); a double-click selects and confirms in one gesture. A coloured domain badge in the toolbar (blue Plane / green Plate) then shows which one is active, and the window title carries the document name.

docs.title: Changing the domain of an empty model
docs.text: Click the coloured domain badge in the toolbar while the model has no geometry; the same two cards as in New model open, on the other domain (clicking the badge is asking to change it; pick the same one to leave it as it is). What does not depend on the domain (materials, beam sections, load cases) stays; the support definitions and area sections, which do, are removed and named in the status bar. Undo brings them back. Once the first node, bar or area exists the badge stops being a button, and its tooltip says the domain is fixed; use File ▸ New to work in the other domain. In a script, model.set_domain('plate') does the same and raises an error if the model has geometry.

docs.title: Where each domain is described
docs.text: The table of what each domain has — elements, supports, springs, loads, analyses and results side by side — is in Modelling the structure. Each domain has its own page, with the same layout: Plane models (frames and walls) and Plate models (slabs and grillages). The topic pages, Loads, Analysis, Results and Design, cover both.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text: Import and export live in the File menu — Import… brings a model in from another tool, Export… writes the model out to a CAD/analysis format, and the report/table/drawing commands below produce deliverables.

docs.title: Drawing
docs.text: File → Print Graphics… (Ctrl+E) saves the current canvas as PNG, SVG, or PDF, with options for resolution (PNG), transparency, tight bounding box, and grid visibility.

docs.title: Report — Write Report…
docs.text:
File → Write Report… (Ctrl+Shift+W) is the main report command. A single dialog lets you choose the format and the content:

  • Format — PDF (paginated A4, each case/combination on a new page, with title, timestamp and page number), Word (.docx, editable — needs python-docx), or Excel (.xlsx — needs openpyxl).
  • Content — any mix of: project info; the structure and loads drawings; the model tables; the result tables; the result views (deformed, diagrams, stress, …) for the cases you tick; and the design views. Result content requires a solved model.

docs.title: Tables to Excel — Write Tables to Excel…
docs.text:
File → Write Tables to Excel… (Ctrl+Shift+T) is the one-click shortcut: the model tables — plus the result tables if the model has been solved — go straight into a single .xlsx workbook, with no dialog. Headers are bold with frozen panes and auto-fit columns; sheets with no data are omitted.

Model sheets:

Sheet Contents Materials E, γ, α, unit mass Sections material, b, h, area, inertia Nodes ID, X, Y Elements ID, node i/j, section, hinges Supports node, support, UX/UY/TZ Node / Element springs stiffnesses Load cases ID, action type, self-weight factor Point / Distributed / Temperature loads, Settlements, Nodal masses per load case Analysis cases ID, type, coefficients, modal/spectrum/stored-K Combinations ID, type, analysis-case coefficients Spectral functions ID, description, damping, (T, Sa) points

Result sheets (when solved):

Sheet Columns Displacements Case type, Case, Node, ux, uy, rz Reactions Case type, Case, Node, Rx, Ry, Mz (with a bold Σ row per case) Constraint forces Case type, Case, Node, Fx, Fy, Mz (only if the model has constraints) Element forces Case type, Case, Element, End (i/j), N, V, M Span extremes Case, Element, |N|max, |V|max, M⁺, M⁻ Reaction sums Case type, Case, ΣRx, ΣRy, ΣMz Modal Case, Mode, ω, f, T, Meff_X%, Meff_Y%, Cum X%, Cum Y%

docs.title: CAD and other tools
docs.text:
File → Export… writes the model to one of several interchange formats; the chosen file filter drives the target:

Format Extension Direction SAP2000 text .s2k export and import DXF drawing .dxf export and import IFC (openBIM) .ifc export and import Autodesk Robot text .str export Python build script .py export (see Python script)

DXF exports the geometry as a drawing and imports a drawing back into a model (lines become bars); it is the bridge to general CAD. Robot export writes the Autodesk Robot Structural Analysis text format. Import… reads SAP2000 .s2k, DXF, or IFC. The Python export has a section of its own, below.

docs.title: Python script (.py)
docs.text:
File ▸ Export… with the file type Python script (*.py) writes the whole model as a commented Python script that rebuilds it with the public xdfem2d API: materials, sections, nodes, elements, geometry objects, supports, loads, analysis cases and combinations, and also the variants, support sets, variant combinations and construction sequences. It is a script and not another file format: it is readable, it diffs, and it is the obvious starting point for "this model, but with the span at 7 m". Nothing runs it for you; you read it first, and run it when you decide to.

  • A variant that has its own loads and cases is written as a nested helper function.
  • A construction sequence is written with its list of operations exactly as authored, and the state of each phase (its active elements, applied cases and case factors) is re-resolved by resolve_phase_state when the script runs, so the round trip is exact.

The Script editor (File ▸ Script editor…, Ctrl+Shift+E) is a separate window: you write and run Python against the open model in it, and it is where Open shows the Python of an Assistant reply. Exporting does not need it.

docs.title: SAP2000 (.s2k)
docs.text:
xdfem2D can export to and import from the SAP2000 text interchange format (.s2k). The 2-D model is mapped to a planar SAP model in the X–Z plane (xdfem2D X → SAP X, xdfem2D Y → SAP Z), with the out-of-plane DOFs deactivated. This is a best-effort exchange — open the file in SAP2000 and verify a simple case (especially moment/temperature sign conventions).

What is exchanged:

xdfem2D SAP2000 Load case Load pattern (SAP auto-creates its Linear Static case) Linear analysis case Linear Static case NonLinear analysis case (unilateral springs) Nonlinear Static case (no P-Delta) Geometric Nonlinear (P-Delta) Nonlinear Static case (P-Delta) Modal / Spectrum / Mass Modal / Response-Spectrum case + Mass Source Combination (LinearSum) Linear-Add combination Node spring Joint spring (uncoupled, bilateral only) Element (Winkler) spring Frame line spring; tension-/compression-only mode maps to the SAP "SimpleType" Concrete materials EC2 (Eurocode 2-2004) design data: concrete strength, rebar material, per-frame design procedure, section cover, and design preferences (γc, γs, αcc)

Unilateral node springs

SAP joint springs are linear/bilateral, so a node spring's tension-/compression-only mode is not exported. Use a compression-/tension-only element spring (or a nonlinear link in SAP) to model unilateral support along a member. Element-spring modes round-trip both ways.

Concrete design under Eurocode 2

When the model carries concrete materials, the export sets the concrete frame design code to Eurocode 2-2004 and marks the load combinations for concrete design, so SAP runs the RC design under EC2. Importing a .s2k reads the concrete strength, safety factors and per-frame design flag back into xdfem2D.

docs.title: IFC (.ifc)
docs.text:
xdfem2D can export to and import from IFC — the openBIM ISO 16739 exchange format — using the structural-analysis view (IfcStructuralAnalysisModel). This is the branch of IFC meant for finite-element exchange, so it mirrors the xdfem2D model closely; it is not the physical/architectural model (IfcBeam, IfcSlab, …). IFC support needs the optional ifcopenshell package — install the engine with the ifc extra (pip install "xdfem2d[ifc]"); the desktop app already includes it.

Values use the same unit convention SAP2000 itself writes — kN, m, tonne, °C (force in kilonewtons, mass in tonnes, temperature in degrees Celsius) — with every unit, including the derived ones for elastic modulus, mass density, thermal expansion and line/area force, declared in the file so importers resolve the material and load units without warnings. Only nodes attached to a member are written (an isolated node is not a valid structural point connection).

The 2-D model is placed in 3-D space by domain, following the SAP2000 convention: a plane model lies in the global X–Z plane (Y = 0) and a plate model in the X–Y plane (Z = 0). On import the plane is detected from the geometry and the domain inferred (X–Z → plane, X–Y → plate).

What is exchanged:

xdfem2D IFC (structural analysis) Model IfcStructuralAnalysisModel Node IfcStructuralPointConnection Bar element IfcStructuralCurveMember (+ IfcProfileDef for the section) Triangle / quad IfcStructuralSurfaceMember (thickness carried) Material IfcMaterial + Pset_MaterialMechanical (E, ν, density) Support IfcBoundaryNodeCondition on the point connection Load case IfcStructuralLoadCase Nodal load IfcStructuralPointAction Bar distributed load IfcStructuralLinearAction Area (slab) pressure IfcStructuralPlanarAction

Domain choice on import

If the geometry does not identify a plane (for example a single line of nodes), the importer asks whether to read the file as a plane or a plate model, just like the SAP2000 import. A genuinely three-dimensional IFC model (nodes varying out of a single plane) cannot be imported as a 2-D model and is reported rather than silently flattened.

Best-effort exchange

A trapezoidal bar load is exported at its mean intensity, and the FE mesh of a slab is exchanged as its surface members (re-meshed on import). Open the file in an IFC viewer and verify a simple case before relying on it.

Physical-model files

Many BIM tools export only the physical model (IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcSlab, …) with no structural-analysis model. When you import such a file, xdfem2D offers to bring in the geometry only — beam/column centre-lines as drawing polylines and slab/wall outlines as polygon regions — with no supports, loads, materials or sections. It is a drafting aid to trace over, not an analysis import.

docs.title: .x2d — native format (recommended)
docs.text:
A .x2d file is a ZIP archive. Variants and construction sequences are kept apart from the model, so that structure.json stays small and easy to read and compare. It contains:

Entry Contents structure.json the model: nodes, elements, materials, sections, supports, springs, constraints, loads, load cases, analysis cases, combinations, spectral functions, nodal masses, geometry objects, cuts, punching columns, beams. Key by key on JSON data structure variants.json the support sets, the variants (each may carry a complete model of its own) and the variant combinations sequences.json the construction sequences, with their phases and operations beam_detail.json the decisions of the beam-bars detailing, when there are any results.json analysis results, when present, with any design results and the design code they were produced with (which takes precedence over the preference default on reopen) object_mesh.json the mesh that the geometry objects had when the results were computed, so reopening maps the results onto exactly that mesh stiffness_<id>.npy stored tangent stiffness matrices from P-Delta runs snapshots.json the named snapshots, when there are any: name, date/time and the model of each (no results) view.json display options, selection, and Scenes (with per-scene zoom)

This is the default for Save / Open and preserves everything, including the view state.

docs.title: .json — structure only
docs.text: A plain JSON export of the model (no results, no view state). Useful for interchange and version control. Its contents, key by key, are on JSON data structure.

docs.title: Migration of combinations
docs.text: When an older model that stored load-case factors directly in combinations is opened, xdfem2D folds each such factor into a Linear analysis case and rewrites the combination to reference that analysis case. This keeps the three-tier model consistent and is applied automatically on load and before solving.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: All files use the program's units throughout: kN · m · kNm (and t for mass).

docs.title: Geometry objects (parametric)
docs.text:
Instead of placing every node and element by hand, you can define the structure with parametric geometry objects that the program discretises into concrete nodes and elements at solve time. The editable model is left untouched; the analysis runs on the compiled mesh (Analysis ▸ Generate mesh, F6, builds it earlier so you can inspect it).

Objects are node-driven: each one refers to real nodes of the model, and stores no coordinates of its own, so moving a node reshapes every object that uses it.

Object Becomes Defined by Meshing control Segment bar elements its two end nodes Divisions (equal parts), or Max chord Arc bar elements (straight chords) a start node, a node on the arc and an end node (in the GUI you click the three points; the engine also accepts centre, radius and angles) Divisions (8 by default), or Max chord Multisegment bar elements a chain of nodes, open or closed Divisions (one count for all, or one per span), or Max chord Rectangle triangle or quad mesh two opposite corner nodes (an axis-aligned rectangle) Target size [m]: the edge length wanted Polygon triangle or quad mesh a closed polygon of nodes Target size [m]

Create objects from Structure ▸ Objects (Add segment…, arc…, multisegment…, rectangle…, polygon…) and edit them in Manage objects…. A curve also carries its own loads, in the Loads tab of its editor.

docs.title: How a surface is meshed
docs.text:
A surface has two meshers, and the outline decides which one runs.

  • Structured — for a convex outline with four vertices: every rectangle, and a polygon that is a convex quadrilateral. A mapped grid, with the diagonals alternating by quadrant, so the mesh is symmetric about both mid-planes. With a quad section (Mesh as: Quads) each well-shaped cell is kept as one quad; a cell that would be poorly shaped is split into two triangles, so the result can be a mix of both.
  • Delaunay — for every other outline, in triangles only. The boundary is refined to the target size, an interior grid of points is added, nodes that already exist are kept, and triangles whose centroid falls outside the polygon are discarded. It uses SciPy's Delaunay, with a built-in implementation if SciPy is missing. The triangulation is not constrained: a strongly re-entrant outline (a deep notch) can be bridged by a triangle, so look at the generated mesh of a concave polygon before relying on it.

Quads therefore need a convex outline with four vertices. For any other polygon (a circular sector, a ring, an L) the editor switches Quads off, says why under the box, and meshes it as triangles. Model check reports two cases that are not errors but are worth reading:

  • Lost quad elements: the object asked for a quad section and got no quad at all. The fix is Mesh as: Triangles.
  • Mixed formulation: the object got some quads and some fallback triangles. They are displacement-compatible, but the moments or stresses recovered on the two kinds of element are not directly comparable across their boundary.

docs.title: Where objects meet
docs.text: When the model is analysed, bars that coincide are merged, and a node that lies on the span of another object splits that span there (a T-junction), so the parts act together. Crossings are different: two objects that cross are only joined at the crossing when one of them has Intersect with crossing members on. It is off by default; a crossing connects if either of the two objects has it on.

docs.title: The edges of a meshed surface
docs.text:
Supports and springs assigned to the corner nodes of a meshed edge carry to the nodes the mesher creates along that edge. This is how you fix a whole wall base with two assignments instead of forty. The rectangle's editor controls it:

Control Options Edge supports Common restraints (min) (the default): the degrees of freedom restrained at both corners. Only if identical: only when both corners restrain the same ones. None. Edge springs Linear variation (the default): the corner springs kx, ky, kt interpolated along the edge. None. Per-edge override A support for each of the four edges (bottom, right, top, left), instead of deriving it from the corners. Set one and all four must be set.

The per-edge override exists because the corner rule cannot express a pattern such as clamped / simply supported / clamped / simply supported around a slab: a corner shared by a clamped edge and a simple one would clamp both.

docs.title: Turning an object into ordinary elements
docs.text: To change the result by hand, bake the object first: Edit ▸ Line to bar turns a segment, arc or multisegment into its bar elements, and Edit ▸ Surface to mesh turns a rectangle or polygon into its triangles and/or quads. The object is deleted and the elements are yours to edit one by one.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This walkthrough builds a portal frame, loads it, analyses it, reads the results and designs it, in about fifteen minutes. At each step it says what you should see, so that you can tell whether you did it right. The frame is a reinforced-concrete portal, 6 m wide and 4 m high, with fixed bases and 20 kN/m of live load on the beam.

The window and its parts are on The Interface; open it beside this page if you want to find a button.

Plane or plate

Every model is either plane (frames and walls) or plate (slabs and grillages), chosen once in New model. A template chooses it for you. This walkthrough is a plane model; see Domains for the choice.

docs.title: 1. Start from a template
docs.text:
Choose File ▸ New from Template… (Ctrl+T). Set Category to Beams & Frames and Type to Portal, enter a span of 6 and a height of 4, leave the rest as it is (the beam is 0.30 × 0.50 m, the columns 0.50 × 0.30 m, concrete C30/37), and press OK.

You should see the frame drawn and fitted to the canvas, with a fixed support at each base. The template also made, for you:

  • a load case SW, the self-weight (self-weight factor 1.0), and a Linear analysis case with the same name that applies it;
  • two combinations, ULS-1.35G and SLS-G, of the self-weight alone.

docs.title: 2. Look around
docs.text: The panel at the left opens on AI. Press Tables, then the Geometry tab: the four nodes (N0_0, N1_0 at the bases, N0_1, N1_1 at the top), and under Bars the two columns (C0_0, C1_0) and the beam (B0_1). Click a bar on the canvas to select it (the status bar counts what is selected), and double-click it to open its editor. The mouse wheel zooms, and the Pan button, or the middle button, moves the view.

docs.title: 3. Add a live load case
docs.text:
A load belongs to a load case, and a load case is only a definition: it is solved by an analysis case (see Analysis). The self-weight has its own. Add one for the live load:

  1. Loads ▸ Load Cases… opens the table of load cases. Press Add.
  2. Name Q, Action type Q – Live, Self-weight factor 0. Press OK.

The load case Q appears, and so does a Linear analysis case Q: adding a load case always creates the matching analysis case.

docs.title: 4. Load the beam
docs.text:
Loads ▸ Distributed loads ▸ Add…, and fill in:

Field Value Element B0_1 (the beam) Load case Q Fy transverse start / end (kN/m) -20 and -20 (negative is downward) Coord system global

Press OK. Switch the View selector (second row, top left) to Loads, and pick the case Q: you should see 20 kN/m of downward arrows on the beam.

docs.title: 5. Make the combination
docs.text:
The design needs a combination of the cases. Analysis ▸ Auto Comb. (EN1990)… (Ctrl+Shift+C) makes them from the action type of each case, which is why Q had to be Live. The dialog shows the EN 1990 factors of each analysis case: leave them, keep ULS ticked, and press OK.

You should see a new combination, ULS: +1.35_SW+1.50_Q, in Tables ▸ Loads ▸ Cases ▸ Combinations: 1.35 times the self-weight plus 1.5 times the live load.

docs.title: 6. Run the analysis
docs.text: Press F5 (or Run analysis in the tool bar). You should see the Case selector appear beside View, and the padlock close: with results, the model is locked, so that it cannot change under its own results. Unlock with Ctrl+L to edit again; that discards the results.

docs.title: 7. Read the results
docs.text:
Set View to Reactions (Ctrl+5) and the case to Q. A check you can do by hand: the live load is 20 × 6 = 120 kN, so each base takes half, 60.00 kN vertically. The horizontal reactions are equal and opposite, about 11.65 kN, and each base takes a moment of about 15.50 kNm.

Now set the case to ULS: +1.35_SW+1.50_Q and View to Force diagrams (Ctrl+6), with Diagram set to Bending moment. You should read:

Where Bending moment middle of the beam about 103.25 kNm (sagging) top of each column, at the beam ends about 54.53 kNm (hogging) base of each column about 27.18 kNm

The vertical reaction under the ULS combination is 125.44 kN per base: 1.35 × 26.25 + 1.5 × 60.00, the self-weight of 26.25 kN (half of the 52.5 kN of the frame) and the live load of 60 kN, each with its factor.

Other things to try: Deformed shape (Ctrl+4), Shear and Axial in the Diagram selector, and Tables ▸ Results, which has the full numeric report. What each view shows is on Results.

docs.title: 8. Design it
docs.text: Design ▸ Concrete members (ULS) designs the beam and the columns in reinforced concrete (EN 1992-1-1) for the ULS combinations (Design ▸ Design combinations says which: by default, those whose name starts with ULS). Then open Tables ▸ Design ▸ Concrete ▸ Reinforcement: for each member, at each critical section, the required steel As,bot, As,top and the stirrups Asw/s, with ★ on the governing section. The Reinforcement (As) view draws them on the canvas. See Design.

docs.title: 9. Save and export
docs.text:
• File ▸ Save (Ctrl+S) writes a .x2d file: the model, its results, the design and the view.
  • File ▸ Write Report… (Ctrl+Shift+W) makes a PDF, Word or Excel report; Write Tables to Excel… (Ctrl+Shift+T) is the one-click spreadsheet.

See Exporting and File Formats.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Understand the model: Domains, then Modelling the Structure, and Plane models or Plate models.
  • Do it faster: the Assistant builds and edits the model from a sentence (add a 20 kN load at midspan), and the Agent does a job of several steps on its own.
  • Do it in code: Scripting with the engine builds this same frame in ten lines of Python.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
xdfem2D comes in two parts, and you install the one you need:

  • The application, with the window, for macOS, Windows and Linux. It is a ready-to-run program: you do not need Python.
  • The engine, the calculation library for Python, for scripts and other programs: Scripting with the engine.

docs.title: The application
docs.text:
1. Download the file for your system from the Releases page of the project. Each release has these files (<version> is the number of the release):

    System File What it is macOS xdfem2D-<version>-macOS.dmg a disk image with the application, for Macs with Apple silicon (M1 or later); there is no version for Intel Macs Windows xdfem2D-<version>-windows.exe an installer (NSIS) Linux xdfem2D_<version>_<arch>.deb a package for Debian and Ubuntu (<arch> is amd64 or arm64) Linux xdfem2d-<version>-linux.zip the application in a folder, for any distribution: unpack and run

  2. Install it:

    System What to do Where it ends up macOS Open the .dmg and drag xdfem2D onto the Applications folder /Applications/xdfem2D.app Windows Run the installer. It asks for administrator permission, installs the program, puts a shortcut on the desktop and lists it under Apps so that it can be uninstalled C:\Program Files\xdfem2D\xdfem2D.exe Linux, .deb sudo apt install ./xdfem2D_<version>_<arch>.deb: it installs the program, a command and an entry in the applications menu /opt/xdfem2D, and the command xdfem2D (/usr/bin/xdfem2D) Linux, .zip Unzip it anywhere and run xdfem2D from the folder; there is nothing to install the folder you unzipped it to

  3. Start it. The first time, xdfem2D shows a notice that you must accept. It is the same notice the MCP server needs accepted before it will start.

If macOS stops it

The application carries an ad-hoc signature, not one from an Apple developer certificate, so macOS may ask you to confirm the first time: right-click the app ▸ Open, or allow it in System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security. It happens once.

Opening files. A .x2d file opens in xdfem2D when you double-click it. A solved example to try is examples/example_2level_2bay_full.x2d, in the repository.

How long a version works. Each version of the application is valid until a date: Help ▸ Expiration Date shows it. When it passes, download the current version.

Where it keeps its settings. In the folder .xdfem2d of your home folder (~/.xdfem2d): the preferences, the recent files and the history of the Assistant. Deleting it resets the application to its defaults. Your models are the .x2d files you saved.

docs.title: Optional tools
docs.text:
Nothing below is needed to model, analyse and design. Each one adds something:

Tool Adds See Ollama the Assistant, with a model that runs on your computer The AI Assistant Claude Code, Ollama's cloud models, OpenCode the Agent tab The Agent tab pandoc editable equations in the Word design reports (without it they are pictures) Design reports

Preferences ▸ Dependencies shows which of these are installed, what each unlocks, and the command to install it on your system.

docs.title: Updating and uninstalling
docs.text: To update, install the new version over the old one; your preferences and models are untouched. To uninstall: on macOS, drag the application to the bin; on Windows, uninstall it from Settings ▸ Apps; on Linux, sudo apt remove xdfem2d for the .deb, or delete the folder for the .zip. Delete ~/.xdfem2d as well if you also want the settings gone.

docs.title: The engine for Python
docs.text:
pip install xdfem2d

It needs Python 3.12 or newer, and installs numpy, scipy and eurocodepy with it. It has no interface, and needs none. A first script, the conventions and the reference of every call are on Scripting with the engine. The engine is free software under the LGPLv3; the application is freeware, under its own terms (Licenses & Disclaimer).

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Getting Started: a frame, built from a template, solved and read in a few minutes.
  • The Interface: the windows and the controls.
  • Help ▸ Documentation (F1) opens this documentation inside the application, without internet.

docs.title: The Interface
docs.text:
This is the main window, with a portal frame open (the one built in Getting Started), its bending moments drawn, and its parts numbered:

Part What it is 1 Menu bar every command of the program: Menus 2 File New, Open, Save, Run analysis (F5), and Lock (Ctrl+L) 3 Domain badge Plane (blue) or Plate (green): what kind of model this is. See Domains 4 Variants and Sequences the buttons that open their panels, and the selectors of the variant and of the phase to show 5 Zoom pan, zoom to a window, zoom in, zoom out, fit 6 Scene the working subset of the model to show: Scenes 7 View and case what the canvas draws, and the case or combination it draws it for 8 Left panel the AI panel and the Tables of the model: The left panel 9 Canvas the drawing of the model, where you pick and edit 10 Canvas tool bar the tools to add, edit and transform, and to undo 11 Display panel what is drawn, and how: Display panel 12 Status bar the last message, and how many items are selected

docs.title: The tool bars
docs.text:
Across the top, from the left:

Group Contents File New, Open, Save, Run analysis, Lock / Unlock Domain badge the kind of model. Click it while the model is empty to change it (Domains) Variants a button that opens the Variants panel, and the selector of the model to show (the base model, or a variant) Sequences a button that opens the Construction Sequences panel, and the selector of the phase to show Zoom Pan, Zoom window, Zoom in, Zoom out, Fit to structure Scene the selector of the scene

The second row is the View selector, which lists only the modes that have something to draw for the model, so entries come and go as you analyse and design. After an analysis the Case selector appears beside it, then the controls the view needs: the Diagram (bending moment, shear force, axial force or torsion) and the Scale of the force diagrams, the phase of a construction sequence, and Cumulative Δu for its displacements. What each view shows is on Results.

The tool bar of the canvas, vertical, beside the canvas, in four groups:

Group Contents Add Add node, Add bar, Add triangle, Add quad, Add support. Each is a mode: click it, then click on the canvas (Esc leaves the mode) Edit / Delete edit the selected nodes, bars, area elements, lines or areas; clear the selection; delete it Transform Move, Array, Rotate, Scale, Mirror, on the selection, the scene or the whole model History Undo, Redo, Save snapshot, Manage snapshots

The groups of this tool bar, Scene, Variants and Sequences can be shown or hidden from View ▸ Toolbar… or in Preferences. The groups of the top row that matter most (File, Zoom, View and case) are always there.

docs.title: History and snapshots
docs.text:
The History group has Undo and Redo, and two snapshot buttons:

  • Save snapshot asks for a name and stores the model (without results) with the date and time.
  • Manage snapshots lists them, with Restore, Rename… and Delete (double-click restores).

A snapshot never changes: to keep later edits, save another one. Restoring asks first, discards the results and can be undone with Undo. Snapshots are saved in the .x2d file and come back when it is opened (.json files do not keep them), and creating, renaming or deleting one marks the model as modified. New, Open, Import and New from Template start with the snapshots of the file, or none.

docs.title: The left panel
docs.text: The panel at the left of the window is a stack of tabs. It starts with two, AI and Tables, and the commands that need more room open more tabs beside them, as the rest of this section describes. It opens on AI; press Tables to see the model. Hide or show the whole panel with View ▸ Tables panel (F9) and View ▸ AI panel (F10).

docs.title: AI
docs.text: AI has two tabs of its own, the Assistant and the Agent. Both are optional: nothing is turned on until you send a message.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Tables holds the tables of the model: where you add, edit and delete what it is made of, and where its results are listed. It has six tabs, and most have sub-tabs, down to three levels:

  • Properties
    • Project
    • Materials
    • Bar sections
    • Panel sections
  • Geometry
    • Nodes
    • Bars
    • Panels
    • Objects
      • Segments
      • Arcs
      • Multisegments
      • Rectangles
      • Polygons
    • Supports
    • Springs
      • Node Springs
      • Element Springs
    • Constraints
  • Loads
    • Cases
      • Load Cases
      • Analysis Cases
      • Combinations
    • Point loads
      • Point Loads
      • Settlements
    • Bar loads
      • Dist. Loads
      • Elem. Point Loads
      • Temperature
      • Line loads
      • Line temp.
    • Area loads
      • Temperature (areas)
      • Edge loads
      • Pressure
      • Object temp.
  • Results
    • Displacements
    • Reactions
    • Constraint forces
    • Element forces
    • Panel stresses
    • Modal
    • Span extremes
    • Reaction sums
    • Info
  • Design
    • Concrete
      • Reinforcement
      • Shell reinf.
      • Crack width
      • Columns
      • Beam bars
      • Suggested rebar
      • Punching
    • Steel
    • Timber
  • Model
    • Cuts
    • Fields
  • Properties: the project information, the materials, and the sections of bars and of areas.
  • Geometry: the nodes, the bars, the area elements (triangles and quads), the geometry objects (one table for each kind), the supports, the springs (of nodes and of elements) and the constraints.
  • Loads: the cases (load cases, analysis cases, combinations), then the loads by what they act on: point loads (and settlements), bar loads, area loads. The same loads are in the Loads menu.
  • Results: the tables of the analysis: displacements, reactions, forces of the constraints, forces of the elements, stresses of the panels, modal results, the extremes along each span, the sums of the reactions, and an Info page. See Results.
  • Design: the results of the designs. Concrete has a tab for each of its designs: the reinforcement of the bars, the shell reinforcement of walls and slabs, the crack width, the columns, the beam bars, the suggested column reinforcement and the punching; Steel and Timber have one table each. Running a design from the Design menu fills its table. See Design.
  • Model: the section cuts you have defined and the fields.

The names follow the domain: a bar is a Beam in a plane model and a Grid member in a plate model, an area is a Panel or a Slab. (The list above is written from the application, for a plane model.)

docs.title: The panels that open when a command asks for them
docs.text:
Some commands open a panel of their own in the left panel, as one more tab beside AI and Tables. The tab opens in front, and reopening the command brings it back; it closes with its own Close button, which returns you to Tables. Several can be open at once. They are panels, not windows: the canvas stays in view, so you can pick things on it.

Tab Opened by What it is for What is in it Support sets Analysis ▸ Support Sets…, or Edit in the Variants panel named sets of restraints, for variants and for construction phases the list of sets (Add, Rename, Delete) and, for the selected one, its Name and the table of its supported nodes (a node not listed is free), with Show (select them on the canvas), Add node (click one on the canvas), Remove node, Load from selection and Apply to all; and, optionally, node springs and element (Winkler) springs Variants Analysis ▸ Variants… parallel what-if scenarios of the model the list of variants (New, Rename, Delete), its description, Support set, All elements or the Active elements (Use selection, Remove selection), Seed from the base model, and Sync with base, Save variant, Export as .x2d… and Variant combinations… Sequences Analysis ▸ Construction Sequences… construction sequences, phase by phase the list of sequences, the construction stages (Stage, Assign to the selected elements, View all stages) and the table of phases (number, time in days, name), with Add…, Edit…, Remove, Duplicate, Up, Down and Save sequence Cuts Analysis ▸ Cuts ▸ Results… the resultant of the forces across a section cut the Cut, the Case and the Plot field; Add… and Manage… cuts; the table of Bars, Areas and Total; a plot along the cut; and CSV (this case), CSV (all cases) and Graphics Beams Design ▸ Beam definitions which bars form one continuous concrete beam the table of bars (element, length, span, beam, section, status); Replace list with selection, Add selection to list, List defined beams; Assign to beam, Rename, Remove from beam; Detect beams automatically…; and Open detailing window… Timber beams Design ▸ Special timber beams pitched, tapered and curved timber beams the same panel in timber mode, with the parameters of the beam: lateral-restraint spacing, lamination thickness, inner radius, type, inclined edge, depth change, the apex reinforcement (bonded-on plane, or screws and rods), and Apply to beam Buckling Design ▸ Buckling lengths… the buckling-length factors of steel, timber and column members the table of members with their lengths, K_y, K_z, K_LT, LTB and column flag, and the buttons to apply, reset and load them Punching Design ▸ Punching… (plate models) the columns of a slab, for the punching check the list of columns (Add…, Edit…, Delete), Calculate, Draw the control perimeters, Clear, and Show columns on canvas Design report Design ▸ Design report… the step-by-step calculation of the design checks the materials (which designs), Summary tables, Overview diagrams, the scope, the detail, the combinations, the format, and Preview and Export…

Three of them change how the program lets you work:

  • While Variants or Sequences is open, the model is locked for editing, so that nothing changes under the panel, and the variant selector goes back to the base model. Closing the last of them unlocks it.
  • Beams, Timber beams and Buckling edit design-only data, which does not change the analysis, so they work on a locked model and keep the results; run the design again to apply what you set.
  • Cuts and Design report only read the results, so they also work on a locked model.

The Beam bars detailing… command, and the Open detailing window… button of the Beams panel, open the detailing of the bars of each beam in a window of its own, not a panel: see Concrete: beams and columns. What each panel does in detail is on the page of its subject: Variants & construction sequences, Results ▸ Cuts, Design, Buckling lengths, Concrete: punching and Design reports.

docs.title: The canvas
docs.text:
Action Control Select Left-click an item, or drag a selection rectangle. Dragging to the right selects what the rectangle encloses, to the left what it crosses Edit an item Double-click it (a node, a bar, an area, an object) Commands for an item Right-click it: a menu with the commands for that kind of item (edit, divide, select what it is made of, …) Zoom (anchored at cursor) Mouse wheel Pan The Pan button, then drag; or hold the middle button (wheel) and drag Zoom to a window The Zoom window button, then drag a rectangle Zoom in / out / fit The buttons of the Zoom group, or = / - / 0 Leave an add mode Esc

The selection count is on the right of the status bar. With the keyboard, Selection ▸ Find entity… (Ctrl+F) selects an item by its name. The Selection menu has the rest: select by a property, the previous selection, invert, edit and divide.

docs.title: Display panel
docs.text:
A dockable Display panel (toggle with View → Display panel) has two tabs.

Model — what is drawn in the scene, in one row per kind of entity: Nodes (markers, labels), Bars (shown, labels), Areas (shown, labels, borders), Objects (shown, labels), Supports (markers, constraints), Springs (nodes, elements) and Cuts; hover a box for its full name. The title of a row is faded only when the model has nothing of that kind. In the deformed and modal views an Undeformed structure toggle draws the reference geometry behind the deformed shape. When the model has geometry objects, the Structure view gains a Mesh checkbox that overlays the finite-element mesh generated from those objects (visual only — picking stays on the objects). Below the layers:

  • Colour by — Model (one colour), Sections or Materials. Bars, areas (triangles and quads) and geometry objects take the colour of their section or material — the surface of a rectangle or polygon object is filled like an area element (and its mesh, when shown, lies over that fill), not only outlined; where a result field colours the areas (stresses, shell reinforcement), the field wins. A colour stays with its section for as long as the section is in the model, so adding or removing another one does not change it; with more than 15 in use the colours repeat. The key is drawn on the canvas, lower right (the support key is upper right), so it is part of any image exported from it, and the Legend checkbox hides it; past 12 entries it says +N more. The list under the box shows every section or material in use — a section with its size (S1 · 0.30×0.50, a catalogue profile, or t=0.20 for an area) — with how many items use it; click an entry to select them on the canvas (Ctrl or Shift for several).
  • Grid — a section that opens and closes: gridlines, spacing, minor (snap) spacing, snap to grid, and the reference lines with their snap.
  • Legend and Reset display, which turns the layers back to their defaults.

Style — live, session-only styling of the active view, in two sections:

  • Colour maps — the colour map of the active view's field. Stresses/forces, shell reinforcement, plate displacements, scalar fields and pressure / temperature loads each keep their own colour map, chosen from one curated, science-friendly list (perceptually-uniform, diverging and sequential palettes, each shown with a preview swatch; no rainbow maps). Also here: continuous vs. discrete (banded) fill, number of levels, contour lines, nodal smoothing, and a manual colour-scale range. The section is enabled only in views that actually draw a colour-mapped field.
  • Diagrams — styling for the bar views. For force diagrams (M/V/N): positive / negative colours, fill opacity, line width, filled band vs. outline, and value labels. For utilisation-ratio colouring (steel / timber design): the colour scheme (traffic-light green→red, or any colour map), the pass/fail threshold, the over-limit colour and the bar width. Each sub-panel is enabled only for the view it applies to.

At the bottom, Save style… / Load style… / Set as default export or import the whole visualization style (colour maps, diagram and ratio styling, and the colour registry) as a portable .json preset, or persist the current style as the startup default. Ready-made presets (publication, presentation, colorblind-safe, grayscale, high-contrast, blueprint) come with the application.

Changes made in the Style tab apply only for the current session; the persistent defaults live in Preferences ▸ Display (and Set as default writes the current style there).

Where to look for what:

  • Making the model: Structure (materials, sections, geometry, supports, constraints) and Loads. Both open the table of what they manage; Add… creates one, Manage… lists them.
