  • The same commands, from words: the Assistant and the Agent can do most of what the menus do.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
File → Preferences is organised in tabs: General, Display, Design, Colors, AI Assistant and Dependencies.

The General tab holds the theme, the default file location, the coincident-node tolerance, the default grid spacing and snap, and whether to open the last model at startup. View options says what is shown when the application starts: the Panels (Tables, AI, Display) and the Tool bars (Add, Edit / Delete, Transform, Scene, Variants, Sequences). It also lists the last used model and the recent models, with buttons to clear the list or drop the files that no longer exist.

The Colors tab sets the colour of each kind of entity in the drawing. The Display tab holds the display sizing defaults (text, marker and line sizes) and the persistent style defaults — the colour map for each field, the default number of levels, continuous vs. banded fill, smoothing, and the bar-diagram and utilisation-ratio styling. The Design tab holds the default design code per material (concrete, steel, timber), whose options come from the same registry as Design → Code preferences; a code stored inside an opened .x2d takes precedence over this default.

docs.title: Preferences, this session, and what the application remembers
docs.text:
Three different things are kept apart:

  • Preferences (~/.xdfem2d/preferences.json) are what a launch starts with. They change only in the Preferences dialog: OK saves them, Cancel changes nothing. The one other way is the explicit Set as default of the Style tab.
  • This session. Whatever you change while the application runs — View ▸ Theme, the panel and tool-bar toggles of the View menu, the assistant's temperature, Think, Task and model in the Assistant tab, the tolerance asked for when you merge coincident nodes — lasts until you close the application and is not saved. When you change the same setting in the Preferences dialog and press OK, that choice replaces the session's; the settings you did not touch keep the value you chose in the session. To make a toggle permanent, set it in Preferences.
  • What the application remembers (~/.xdfem2d/state.json) is not a choice of yours: the recent files and the last folder, the acceptance of the liability notice, the licence cache, the first-run check for the optional tools, and the assistant warnings you switched off with Don't show this again (Preferences ▸ AI Assistant ▸ Show the assistant's warnings again brings them back). The application writes it when it needs to.

Older versions kept all of this in preferences.json; the first launch of a newer one moves the remembered part to state.json and leaves the preferences alone.

The folder also has config.ini, a file of advanced settings for the AI features (every line is commented out and the defaults apply until you change one; an environment variable of the same name wins over it). The rest of the folder is the Assistant's history and caches.

docs.title: JSON data structure
docs.text:
The model as the engine stores it: the structure.json inside a .x2d file (see File Formats) and a plain .json export are this same object. You can write one by hand, or from any program, and open it in the application; it is also what the engine's save() and load() use (see Scripting with the engine).

save() writes a single JSON object and load() reads it. Absent keys take their defaults, so a file stays readable as the format grows (for example, domain absent means plane).

docs.title: Top level
docs.text:
The list below is written from the engine (what save() writes), so it has every list the file can hold and every field of its entries. A list is [ {fields} ], one object per entry, and a map is { id: {fields} }. A name followed by ? is written only when it has a value; … is a value that is not a flat record.

{
  "domain": "plane" | "plate",
  "project_info": { … },
  "propagate_edge_supports": …,
  "propagate_edge_springs": …,
  "nodes": [ {"id", "x", "y"} ],
  "materials": [ {"name", "elastic_modulus", "unit_weight", "alpha", "unit_mass", "material_type", "poisson", "design"} ],
  "sections": [ {"name", "material_name", "b", "h", "area_override", "inertia_override", "inertia_minor_override",
                 "torsion_override", "wel_y_override", "wpl_y_override", "wel_z_override", "wpl_z_override",
                 "av_y_override", "av_z_override", "warping_override", "wt_override", "curve_y_override",
                 "curve_z_override", "profile_name", "angle", "shape", "tw", "tf", "rc_cover", "rc_alpha_s",
                 "rc_bar_phi", "rc_shear_min", "rc_torsion_distribution", "is_column", "rc_phi_ef", "rc_n_bars",
                 "rc_n_bars_y", "rc_n_bars_z", "rc_second_order_method", "timber_service_class", "beam_overrides"} ],
  "bar_elements": [ {"id", "node_i", "node_j", "section_name", "hinge_i", "hinge_j", "rc_design", "rc_cover",
                     "rc_cotg_theta", "rc_alpha_s", "sd_ky", "sd_kz", "sd_klt", "sd_ltb", "is_column", "beam", "stage"} ],
  "tri_sections": [ {"name", "material_name", "thickness", "plane_strain", "formulation", "rc_cover", "rc_alpha_s",
                     "rc_bar_phi", "rc_shear_min", "rc_cover_top_x", "rc_cover_top_y", "rc_cover_bot_x",
                     "rc_cover_bot_y"} ],
  "tri_elements": [ {"id", "node_i", "node_j", "node_k", "section_name", "stage"} ],
  "quad_sections": [ {"name", "material_name", "thickness", "plane_strain", "formulation", "rc_cover", "rc_alpha_s",
                      "rc_bar_phi", "rc_shear_min", "rc_cover_top_x", "rc_cover_top_y", "rc_cover_bot_x",
                      "rc_cover_bot_y"} ],
  "quad_elements": [ {"id", "node_i", "node_j", "node_k", "node_l", "section_name", "stage"} ],
  "tri_edge_loads": [ {"id", "tri_id", "node_a", "node_b", "load_case_id", "fx", "fy", "coord_sys", "pn", "pt"} ],
  "quad_edge_loads": [ {"id", "quad_id", "node_a", "node_b", "load_case_id", "fx", "fy", "coord_sys", "pn", "pt"} ],
  "surface_edge_loads": [ {"id", "object_id", "node_a", "node_b", "load_case_id", "fx", "fy", "coord_sys", "pn", "pt"} ],
  "tri_area_loads": [ {"tri_id", "load_case_id", "pz"} ],
  "quad_area_loads": [ {"quad_id", "load_case_id", "pz"} ],
  "surface_area_loads": [ {"object_id", "load_case_id", "pz"} ],
  "tri_area_springs": [ {"tri_id", "kz"} ],
  "quad_area_springs": [ {"quad_id", "kz"} ],
  "surface_area_springs": [ {"object_id", "kz"} ],
  "punch_columns": [ {"id", "node_id", "shape", "bx", "by", "position", "force", "dx", "dy", "beta_min"} ],
  "fields": [ {"name", "expression"} ],
  "geometry_objects": [ {…} ],
  "beams": { id: {"name", "overrides", "timber"?} },
  "beam_detail"?: …,
  "supports": [ {"name", "ux", "uy", "tz"} ],
  "support_assignments": [ {"node_id", "support_name"} ],
  "node_springs": [ {"node_id", "kx", "ky", "kt", "mode_x", "mode_y"} ],
  "element_springs": [ {"element_id", "kx", "ky", "coord_sys", "mode_x", "mode_y"} ],
  "constraints": [ {"id", "kind", "terms", "value", "master", "slaves", "nodes", "components", "enabled"} ],
  "load_cases": [ {"id", "self_weight_factor", "action_type", "load_duration"?, "category"?, "psi0"?, "psi1"?, "psi2"?} ],
  "point_loads": [ {"node_id", "load_case_id", "fx", "fy", "mz"} ],
  "distributed_loads": [ {"element_id", "load_case_id", "fxe", "fxd", "fye", "fyd", "coord_sys"} ],
  "element_point_loads": [ {"element_id", "load_case_id", "a", "fx", "fy", "mz", "coord_sys"} ],
  "load_combinations": [ {"id", "combo_type", "coefficients", "analysis_coefficients"} ],
  "cuts": [ {"id", "name", "x1", "y1", "x2", "y2"} ],
  "support_settlements": [ {"node_id", "load_case_id", "ux", "uy", "tz"} ],
  "temperature_loads": [ {"element_id", "load_case_id", "delta_t_uniform", "delta_t_gradient"} ],
  "tri_temperature_loads": [ {"tri_id", "load_case_id", "dt_i", "dt_j", "dt_k", "dt_gradient"} ],
  "quad_temperature_loads": [ {"quad_id", "load_case_id", "dt_i", "dt_j", "dt_k", "dt_l", "dt_gradient"} ],
  "area_temperature_loads": [ {"object_id", "load_case_id", "dt_uniform", "field_name", "dt_gradient",
                               "grad_field_name"} ],
  "line_temperature_loads": [ {"object_id", "load_case_id", "dt_uniform", "dt_gradient", "field_name",
                               "grad_field_name"} ],
  "line_distributed_loads": [ {"object_id", "load_case_id", "fx", "fy", "fx_field", "fy_field", "coord_sys"} ],
  "line_element_springs": [ {"object_id", "kx", "ky", "kx_field", "ky_field", "coord_sys", "mode_x", "mode_y"} ],
  "spectral_functions": [ {"id", "description", "damping", "points"} ],
  "nodal_masses": [ {"node_id", "mass_case_id", "mx", "my", "mtz"} ],
  "analysis_cases": [ {"id", "analysis_type", "coefficients", "num_modes", "modal_case_id", "spectrum_id",
                       "combination_rule", "direction", "damping", "nl_method", "max_iterations", "tolerance",
                       "beam_stiffness_factor", "column_stiffness_factor", "stored_stiffness_id", "sequence_id",
                       "phase_id", "solved"} ],
  "concrete_materials": [ {"material_name", "concrete_class", "steel_class", "gamma_c", "gamma_s", "alpha_cc"} ],
  "support_sets": [ {"id", "description", "restraints", "assignments", "node_springs", "element_springs"} ],
  "variants": [ {"id", "description", "active_elements", "support_set_id", "model"?, "synced_base_sig"?} ],
  "construction_sequences": [ {"id", "displacement_method", "phases"} ],
  "variant_combinations": { id: {"op", "terms"} }
}

Triangles, quads and objects have each their own lists. A load or a spring on an area element is kept in the list of the kind of element it acts on: tri_* for a triangle (keyed by tri_id), quad_* for a quad (keyed by quad_id) and surface_* for a meshed surface object (keyed by object_id). So tri_area_loads, quad_area_loads and surface_area_loads hold the same kind of entry (a pressure pz on a tri_id, a quad_id or an object_id), and likewise the edge loads, the temperature loads and the area springs. Bars and line objects have distributed_loads and line_distributed_loads, and so on.

docs.title: Entries inside other entries
docs.text:
// one phase of a construction sequence (an entry of `phases`)
{"id", "operations", "active_elements", "applied_cases", "case_factors", "support_set_id", "inherits_from", "reapply_self_weight", "release_supports", "time", "initial_state"}
// one operation of a phase (an entry of `operations`)
{"id", "action", "target", "group_kind", "ids", "factor", "note"}
// one support set (an entry of `support_sets`)
{"id", "description", "restraints", "assignments", "node_springs", "element_springs"}

In a .x2d file the list is split. structure.json has everything above except support_sets, variants, variant_combinations and construction_sequences, which are in variants.json and sequences.json, and the decisions of the beam-bars detailing, which are in beam_detail.json (see File Formats). A plain .json export has them all in one object.

docs.title: Notes on the slots
docs.text:
• The three per-node components are positional: they are written with the canonical (plane) names ux/uy/tz, fx/fy/mz, kx/ky/kt in both domains. In a plate model read them as w/θx/θy, fz/mx/my, kz/kθx/kθy. Readers also accept the plate aliases on input.
  • geometry_objects[].kind is one of segment, arc, multisegment, rectangle, polygon (the old spellings line, polyline, surface are still read). The objects are node-driven: they carry node_ids and their parameters, and the geometry is in the nodes.
    • A curve (segment, arc, multisegment) has id, section_name, divisions, max_chord, loads, intersect_crossings, is_column, sd_ky, sd_kz, sd_klt, sd_ltb, beam and node_ids. A multisegment also has closed, and span_divisions when it was set.
    • A surface (rectangle, polygon) has id, tri_section_name (a triangle or a quad section), target_size, prefer_quad, edge_support_mode, edge_spring_mode and node_ids, and edge_supports (one support name or "free" per edge, in perimeter order) when it was set.
  • tri_sections[].formulation is CST, Allman or ES-FEM (panel / membrane) in the plane domain, or a plate-bending element in the plate domain: MITC3 (shear-deformable, the default — valid for thin and thick slabs) or DKT (thin-plate / Kirchhoff).

docs.title: Licenses & Disclaimer
docs.text:
xdfem2D is made of two parts, published under different licenses: the desktop application, which is freeware, and the calculation engine, which is free software. This page says which is which, what you may do with each, and what the results of the program are, and are not.

Everything that is public is at github.com/pcachim/xdfem2D: the source of the engine, the Releases with the application for macOS, Windows and Linux, the Issues for bugs and questions, and the changelogs.

docs.text:

Freeware: free to use for personal, academic or commercial work, distributed only as a compiled application, without rights to redistribute or modify it. The Freeware License Agreement, shown the first time you start the application and under Help ▸ License Agreement. A summary is below xdfem2d, the engine The 2D finite-element calculation library at the core of the application. Its source is in the public repository, and it is on PyPI. The engine has no interface and no dependency on one; to use it, see Scripting with the engine. If it contributes to published work, please cite it:

Cachim, P. (2026). pcachim/xdfem2D [Computer software]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23511092

The DOI covers all versions and always resolves to the latest release.

docs.title: Third-party components
docs.text: The application bundles open-source libraries, notably Qt/PySide6 (LGPLv3), and each stays under its own license, which the third-party notices list, with what the LGPL asks of the application and of you (among it, the right to replace the Qt libraries with a compatible version).

docs.title: AI features and other people's models
docs.text:
The Assistant, the Agent and the MCP server are optional, and nothing is turned on until you use them. They work with language models and services that are not part of xdfem2D: a model that runs on your computer through Ollama, the cloud models of Ollama, a remote provider with your own API key, or an agent such as Claude Code or OpenCode. Each of them has its own terms of use and privacy policy, and the license of xdfem2D does not change them. A remote model or agent receives your question and a description of your model, and the application tells you so before the first message (see Where the model runs). What those models are free to do with it is for their terms to say.

xdfem2D itself does not collect, store or process your data on the author's behalf: your models, results and conversations stay on your computer, except what you yourself send to a remote model or agent.

docs.title: Disclaimer
docs.text:
xdfem2D computes structural analysis and design results: displacements, reactions, forces, modes, and reinforcement, steel and timber design. Producing a number is not the same as the number being right for your problem: none of it is verified, certified or checked against any code of practice by the mere fact of being produced.

The results depend on what you give the program. The geometry, materials, supports, actions and combinations are your assumptions, and the model is only as good as they are. The program is two-dimensional, so effects that need a three-dimensional model are not captured, and its methods are simplified where the documentation says so. It may also contain errors.

Conformity with a code is yours to establish. The design checks follow the Eurocodes as implemented in eurocodepy, in the edition and with the national parameters you choose (see Design codes). The program does not cover every clause or every case of a code, and choosing the edition and the national annex, and deciding that a design complies, is up to you.

All of this applies to the whole program, not just one module: analysis results, dynamic and seismic results, member design (concrete, steel, timber), and everything the Assistant, the Agent or an agent working through the MCP server says or does with a model. An agent can build, change and analyse your model by itself (every change is one step of Undo, and what it produced you read, not take on trust). All of it is an aid to calculation, not a substitute for engineering judgement. Anyone using the output of this software in the design, verification or construction of a real structure must be a qualified engineer, is responsible for verifying it independently (checking that the model and its assumptions are reasonable, for instance with a simplified calculation or an order-of-magnitude check), and remains the engineer of record.

The software is provided "as is", without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including as to accuracy, reliability or fitness for a particular purpose, and the author is not liable for damages arising from its use or from the inability to use it, to the extent the law allows. The terms are those of the agreement, in Help ▸ License Agreement, and prevail over this summary.

Errors are corrected in new versions, so use the current one (each version is valid until a date).

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: For bugs and questions, open an issue, or write to eurocodepy@gmail.com.

docs.title: Loads
docs.text: All loads belong to a load case. A load case is purely a definition of loads — it does not produce results on its own; an analysis case solves it.

docs.title: Load cases
docs.text:
Create load cases on the Loads tab. A load case has:

  • a name,
  • a self-weight multiplier (e.g. 1.0 to include full self-weight, 0.0 to exclude it), and
  • an action type (G permanent, Q live, W wind, E seismic, T temperature) used by the automatic Eurocode combination generator.

Note

Adding a load case automatically creates a matching Linear analysis case of the same name (factor 1.0), so the load case can be solved and combined right away.

docs.title: Load types
docs.text:
The same load types exist in both domains, read in the domain's own terms: the three components of a node are Fx, Fy, Mz in a plane model and Fz, Mx, My in a plate model. The dialogs show the names of the active domain.

Load Applies to Plane Plate Point load a node Fx, Fy, Mz Fz, Mx, My Distributed load an element trapezoidal Fy / Fx, start→end, global or local axes transverse intensity qz on a grid member Element point load a point along an element, at distance a Fx, Fy, Mz a transverse force and a concentrated bending moment Edge load a triangle or quad edge, or a surface boundary side traction Fx, Fy per unit length not used: a slab is loaded by area pressure Area pressure a slab region (a surface object, or a single triangle or quad) not used: a wall takes edge loads pz [kN/m²] Temperature (bars) an element uniform ΔT and gradient ΔT the same two values Temperature (areas) a triangle, a quad or a surface uniform ΔT over the element a through-thickness gradient ΔT = T_top − T_bottom Support settlement a supported node prescribed ux, uy, θz prescribed w, θx, θy Nodal mass a node (for a Mass case) Mx, My (masses on ux, uy), Mtz (rotational inertia) Mx (the mass on w), My, Mtz (rotational inertias about x and y)

Add each from its sub-table on the Loads tab, or from the Loads menu (Manage… / Add… per type), selecting the load case it belongs to.

docs.title: Surface loads
docs.text:
Edge loads (plane) are the surface-element counterpart of a distributed load: pick the two end nodes of a triangle or quad edge or a surface boundary side — the Add edge load tool lets you click them on the canvas — and give the traction per unit length. They are the way to apply pressure to a wall.

Area pressure (plate) pz [kN/m²] on a slab region is the everyday slab load, drawn as a colour map over the region. Add it from Loads → Area Pressure (Manage… / Add…). A constant pressure is lumped as pz·A/3 to each vertex of a triangle and pz·A/4 to each vertex of a quad.

Area temperature. In a plane model a uniform ΔT over a triangle or quad is a strain that stresses the element if it is restrained. A slab does not stretch, it bends, so there a triangle or surface temperature is the through-thickness gradient, which curves the plate element (a uniform rise is stress-free).

Field temperatures need the mesh

A field-driven temperature on a surface object only resolves once the object is meshed into triangles or quads. Before that the loads view shows a note asking you to Generate mesh (F6); a constant pressure or gradient draws immediately.

The Winkler area spring kz of a slab on grade is applied over a region in the same way as an area pressure, but it is a support, not a load: see Plate models.

docs.title: Self-weight
docs.text: Self-weight is applied per load case through its self-weight multiplier, using each element's section area and material unit weight. There is no separate self-weight load to add — set the multiplier on the load case.

docs.title: Viewing loads
docs.text: Switch the View dropdown to Loads and pick a load case (or all load cases) to draw arrows and value labels on the canvas.

docs.title: The MCP server (for external agents)
docs.text:
xdfem2D can be driven by an AI agent such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The agent builds a model with the same command language the Assistant writes, analyses it, designs it, reads the results and writes files, calling tools instead of clicking menus.

It is not the Assistant. The Assistant is a panel inside the application, meant for the small models that run on your computer. The MCP server is for an agent that you already use (a capable cloud model works best), which then has xdfem2D as one more tool.

The server is part of the application: the same program that opens the window starts it when it is given --mcp. Nothing else has to be installed.

docs.title: What it is, and what it is not
docs.text:
• One model in memory, separate from the window. The server keeps its own model, its results and an undo list. It does not see the model open in the application, and the application does not see the agent's. The two meet through .x2d files: the agent saves, you open; you save, the agent loads. If both edit the same file, whoever saves last wins.
  • Edits drop the results. Results belong to the model they were computed from. After any edit the agent runs the analysis again before asking for forces.
  • Nothing is lost silently. new_model and load_model refuse to throw away edits that were not saved (force=true discards them), and undo brings back the last edit.
  • It writes files where the agent says, unless you give it a folder (--root, below). save_model, export_file and export_figure take any path, and the agent chooses it.

docs.title: Work on the model that is open in the window
docs.text: --mcp gives the agent a model of its own. The other way is to let it work on the model you have open, from the Agent tab of the application: you see what it does as it does it, you can edit in between, and it sees what you did. That tab, its agents (Claude Code, Ollama's cloud models), its options and what to know about it are in The Agent tab. It uses the same tools as this page, plus ui_action, which only works in the window.

docs.title: Register it with your agent
docs.text:
First, open xdfem2D once and accept the notice. The server will not start before that, and it cannot show the notice itself. It also checks, as the window does, that the version has not expired; if it refuses, it says why on its standard error (the agent's log).

The program to register is the application's own executable, with --mcp:

System Program macOS /Applications/xdfem2D.app/Contents/MacOS/xdfem2D Windows C:\Program Files\xdfem2D\xdfem2D.exe (the folder the installer used) Linux /usr/bin/xdfem2D after the .deb, or xdfem2D in the folder you unpacked it in

Claude Code (macOS shown):

claude mcp add xdfem2d -- /Applications/xdfem2D.app/Contents/MacOS/xdfem2D --mcp

Add --scope user after the name to have it in every project. claude mcp list shows whether it connected. Open a new session: the tools appear when it starts.

Claude Desktop, in claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "xdfem2d": {
      "command": "/Applications/xdfem2D.app/Contents/MacOS/xdfem2D",
      "args": ["--mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Any other MCP client works the same way: the server speaks MCP over standard input and output.

docs.title: From a source checkout
docs.text:
If you run xdfem2D from its source, install the environment (uv sync, which includes the mcp package) and register the Python module instead:

claude mcp add xdfem2d -- /path/to/project/.venv/bin/python -m xdfem2d_app.mcp_server

python -m xdfem2d_app.gui --mcp does the same as the executable, notice and expiry check included; python -m xdfem2d_app.mcp_server skips both, since a checkout has neither.

docs.title: Check that it works on your machine
docs.text:
/Applications/xdfem2D.app/Contents/MacOS/xdfem2D --mcp-check

starts the server as an agent would, talks to it, and tries what an agent does: it builds a beam, analyses it, reads a reaction, designs it, writes a DXF, an Excel file and a Word report, draws a figure (which makes the server start the program a second time) and tries a path outside --root. Every step is reported as ok or FAIL with the reason, on the screen and in a file, ~/xdfem2d_mcp_check.txt (--log FILE chooses another). The file is what to look at, and to send if something fails: a Windows build has no console, and nothing it prints is seen.

The check refuses, like the server, if the notice has not been accepted in the window (exit code 2), and says so. The code is 0 when every step passes and 1 when one fails.

docs.title: Keep the agent's files in one folder
docs.text:
--root FOLDER (after --mcp) is the only folder the agent may read or write files in:

claude mcp add xdfem2d -- /Applications/xdfem2D.app/Contents/MacOS/xdfem2D --mcp --root ~/Structures

A relative path (beam.x2d, reports/beam.docx) is relative to that folder, and the folders it needs are created inside it. A path that leaves it (../x.x2d, ~/Desktop/x.docx, an absolute path elsewhere, or a link that points out) is refused, with a message that names the folder. The folder must exist; if it does not, the server says so and does not start. Without --root the agent can use any path. Use it for an agent you do not follow step by step, or one other people share.

summary tells the agent which folder it is limited to.

docs.title: How much the server tells the agent
docs.text:
--instructions short|grammar|full (after --mcp) sets what the server says when a client connects:

Level What the agent receives short A line that points to the reference tool grammar The command language and its rules full (default) The above, and to read the model with summary before editing one that already has things

Models that do not read the documentation on their own do much better with full. Put it in the registration if you want another: ... xdfem2D --mcp --instructions grammar.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text: Tool What it does reference The command language: one line per verb and object, with an example summary What is loaded: the model (nodes with coordinates, bars, supports, sections, cases), the names get understands for its domain, variants, sequences, punching columns new_model An empty model. domain is plane (frames and walls) or plate (slabs and grillages) and cannot change afterwards load_model, save_model Open and save a .x2d file, with its results and design settings commands Edit the model with the command language, one per line. All or nothing: on an error the model is untouched and the answer names the line check Try commands on a copy and report the problems get Read the model and its results: reactions, displacements, forces, design, lists. The word get may be left out. variant=ID reads a variant undo Undo the last edit ui_action Only in the window: change what it shows (a view, the layers, the colours of the results, the grid, the zoom), as the Display panel and the View menu do. It never changes the model. With no action it lists them lock_model Lock the model against changes (commands, undo, design settings, a new or another model are refused; reading and analysing go on), or unlock it. Unlocking discards the results, so it is refused while there are some unless force=true. In the window it is the Lock of the toolbar, and you can unlock it there auto_combinations The EN 1990 combinations (ULS, SLS-K, SLS-FR, SLS-QP) of the model's cases run_analysis Analyse. scope="all" also solves the variants and their combinations set_design Design preferences (γc, γs, αcc, the code editions, the crack-width limit ...), the combinations to design for and those for the crack width (SLS) run_design Design: concrete (beams and columns), bars, areas (slabs and walls), crack, punching, steel, timber beam_bars The bars proposed for each beam by zone, a page at a time add_punch_column A column for the punching check of a slab add_variant A variant: elements switched off, a support taken away, or other supports add_variant_combination A combination across variants set_stages, add_sequence Construction stages of the elements, and a sequence made from them remove_overlay Remove a variant, a combination across variants, a sequence or a punching column export_file A Word report (with figures if asked), the tables in Excel, a step-by-step design report (design-concrete, design-steel or design-timber, as .docx or .html), a DXF export_figure A view of the model as the window draws it. In the window it shows the view there, and writes a picture file (PNG, PDF or SVG) if you give a path; with --mcp it writes the file, so the path is needed

docs.title: Copying and transforming
docs.text:
Beyond the commands the Assistant knows, the agent has the Edit menu as commands (reference lists them): copy, array (rectangular or circular), rotate, scale, mirror and divide. They work on nodes, and on bars, slabs and walls through the nodes they are made of; a copy brings the bars, slabs and walls made of the copied nodes, and their loads if you add loads. The answer names the new ids (A_c2, E1_c2 ...), so that the next line can use them.

copy bar E1 by 0 3 loads
array nodes A,B rect 1 0 3 3        # three storeys, 3 m apart
mirror nodes all about x=6 copy
rotate nodes all about 0 0 by 90

docs.title: Dynamics and second order
docs.text:
The agent can also set up the seismic and second-order analyses, which the Assistant does not:

add analysis M mass = 1 G + 0.3 Q                 # the mass of the loads (kN / 9.81)
add mass B,C mx 2 my 2 case M                     # a concentrated mass, in tonnes
add analysis Modes modal mass M modes 6           # the vibration modes: get modal
add spectrum EC8 ec8 ag 1.5 S 1.2 TB 0.15 TC 0.5 TD 2 [q 3]
add spectrum SP points 0 1  0.5 2.5  2 1          # or a spectrum of your own
add analysis Sx spectrum modal Modes function EC8 direction X rule CQC
add analysis P pdelta = 1.35 G + 1.5 Q beams 0.8 columns 0.8

Run the analysis, then read them with get modal, get spectrum case Sx, or get max ux on nodes all case Sx. A case that cannot be solved (for instance a modal case whose mass case has no mass) does not stop the run: the answer of run_analysis lists it in case_errors. P-Delta is for plane models.

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
get takes the same questions as the command language. A few:

get sum reaction fy on nodes all case ULS
get max M on bars all case C1
get absmax uy on nodes all case C1
get design concrete bars longitudinal
get design concrete areas punching worst 3
get list bars

The summary tool lists the names a model understands (a plate has other reactions and displacements than a frame). Results are read per case or combination; a design is computed per combination, never per analysis case.

docs.title: Variants and construction sequences
docs.text: add_variant makes a variant of the model with its own supports or with some elements off, and run_analysis with scope="all" solves it; get ... variant=ID reads it, and the base model is read without variant. A construction sequence is set up from stages: set_stages({"1": ["E1"], "2": ["E2"]}), then add_sequence("SEQ", {"1": ["G"]}), and the phases are cases named seq__SEQ__Stage1, seq__SEQ__Stage2 ...

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
export_figure and the figures of a report are drawn by the application's own canvas, so they look as they do in the window. Writing a file takes a few seconds, because the canvas is opened off screen, in a process of its own. In the window, export_figure also shows the view there, as ui_action does.

The views are structure, loads, deformed, displacements, reactions, bending, shear and axial (the result ones need an analysis first). After a design, reinforcement (and shear_reinf), crack, tri_reinf (slabs and walls), steel_design, timber_design and column_design; and stress, fields, modal and constraints when the model has them. case is the load case, analysis case or combination (empty is the first). A view the model does not have is refused with the list of the ones it has.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
A conversation with an agent could go like this (the tool the agent chose is in brackets):

You: A simply supported concrete beam of 6 m, section 0.3 × 0.5, dead load 12 kN/m and live load 5 kN/m. Design it and write a report with the drawings to ~/Desktop/beam.docx.

  1. reference, summary (empty model)
  2. commands: add material ..., add section ..., nodes, bar, supports, cases, loads
  3. auto_combinations, run_analysis
  4. run_design concrete, run_design crack, run_design bars, beam_bars
  5. export_file report ... figures=true

docs.title: What to know
docs.text:
• Big models are read in pages. An answer has a size limit: a longer list is cut to its first items, with a note (rows_cut: first 100 of 2000) that says how to ask for less, and beam_bars returns a page at a time (offset, limit).
  • Not everything is covered. The diagrams of the bars of a combination across variants cannot be read with get (reactions and displacements can). A beam's bars are a proposal: the detail stored in the model is not changed, as the menu does.
  • Design preferences. A model loaded from a file brings the design settings saved in it. A new model uses the engine's defaults, which are the application's.
  • Optional packages. Word and Excel files need python-docx and openpyxl, DXF needs ezdxf, and the figures need the interface (pyside6). They come with the application's dependencies. If one is missing, the answer says which. A pandoc on the path is used for the design reports, when there is one.

docs.title: If something does not work
docs.text: What you see Why The server is listed but fails to connect Run xdfem2D --mcp-check: it says which step fails and why. Or run the registered command in a terminal: it prints why on standard error (the notice not accepted, an expired version, a wrong path) From a checkout: No module named 'mcp' The environment lacks the package: uv sync A file is refused as "outside the folder this server may use" The server was started with --root: use a path inside it, or a relative one The agent does not use the tools The session was open before the registration: start a new one The agent writes commands the server refuses Use --instructions full, and ask it to call reference An export says a package is not installed Install what the answer names A figure is refused The view needs results (run the analysis) or a design that has not been run

docs.title: Modelling the Structure
docs.text:
Build a model from the Geometry and Properties tabs, or directly on the canvas. The model must be unlocked to edit (toggle with Ctrl+L); running an analysis locks it.

This page is what both domains share: materials, sections, nodes, the families of elements, and the editing tools. What belongs to one domain is on its own page, with the same layout: Plane models (frames and walls) and Plate models (slabs and grillages). The mechanisms that act the same way in both are on Supports, springs and constraints and Geometry objects. The domain is chosen once, in New model (see Domains).

docs.title: Materials and sections
docs.text:
Define these first, on the Properties tab.

  • Material — elastic modulus E (kN/m²), unit weight γ (kN/m³), and thermal expansion α (1/°C).

  • Section — a cross-section linked to a material. A Shape field selects the geometry and which dimensions are needed; the area and second moment of area are derived automatically and shown as read-only labels:

    Shape Dimensions used Generic b × h (or a steel-profile override) Rectangular width b, height h Circular diameter d Rectangular hollow b × h, wall thickness t Circular hollow diameter d, wall thickness t I flange width b, total height h, flange tf, web tw T flange width b, total height h, flange tf, web tw

    A steel profile picked from the library still fills the area/inertia directly. The separate Type field (Concrete / Steel / Timber / Other) is for material /design classification and is independent of the shape.

Built-in Rigid and Dummy

Every model is seeded with two reserved entries — a material and a section — called Rigid (numerically very stiff, for near-rigid links) and Dummy (zero stiffness, for a member that must be otherwise restrained). They are opened read-only, cannot be renamed or deleted, and are shown at the bottom of the material and section lists.

A surface section (the section of a triangle or a quad) is different: it carries a thickness, a material and a formulation, and it is described on the page of the domain, because the formulations are not the same (see below).

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
A node has an (x, y) position. Add nodes from the Nodes sub-tab, the Structure menu, or with the Add node tool: enable it and click on the canvas to place nodes; press Esc to stop.

Double-click a node on the canvas to edit its position, support, or spring.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
An element's role follows from what it spans and the model's domain: a line element is a Beam in a plane model and a Grid member in a plate model; an area element — a triangle or a quad — is a Panel in a plane model and a Slab in a plate model. The tabs, menus and section dialogs use these names, so the same primitives read correctly in either domain.

A bar element connects two nodes and references a section. Add elements from the Beams / Grid sub-tab or with the Add element tool: enable it, click the start node, then the end node.

Each element end can carry a moment release (hinge), drawn as a small open circle near the node.

A triangle and a quad are the same modelling role, so they share one selection, one Manage area elements… manager, one bulk/individual editor, and the same result views — pick the shape per element or per surface.

Panel and Slab sections

In the GUI a Panel (plane) or a Slab (plate) pairs a triangle section and a quad section under one name (one material/thickness choice), and the surface's Mesh as: Triangles / Quads selector decides which is used. Programmatically they are two sections (tri_sections / quad_sections) that may share a name.

docs.title: What each domain has
docs.text: Plane Plate What it models a frame or wall in its own plane a slab or grillage bending out of plane DOFs per node ux, uy, θz w, θx, θy Line element Beam: axial, bending and shear Grid member: bending, shear and St-Venant torsion Triangle Panel: CST, Allman, ES-FEM Slab: MITC3 (default), DKT Quad Panel: QM6 (recommended), Q4 Slab: MITC4 (recommended), DKT4 Supports PIN, FIXED, ROLLER-X/Y, GUIDED-X/Y, BLOCK SIMPLE, CLAMPED, CLAMP-X/Y, SYM-X/Y, BLOCK Node springs Kx, Ky, Kt kz, ktx, kty Foundation element spring along a bar (Kx, Ky) element spring along a grid member (transverse, w only); area spring kz under a slab Loads Fx, Fy, Mz; distributed; edge tractions Fz, Mx, My; qz; area pressure pz Constraints rigid link, equal DOF, equation equal DOF, equation (a rigid link is in-plane kinematics) Analyses Linear, NonLinear, Mass, Modal, Spectrum, P-Delta the same, with vertical modes; no P-Delta Triangle and quad results membrane stresses σ (with an N = σ·t force toggle) slab forces: moments, shears, Wood–Armer Bar results M, V, N diagrams M, V, T diagrams Details Plane models Plate models

docs.title: Editing on the canvas
docs.text:
• Click to select; drag a rectangle for a window selection (left-to-right encloses, right-to-left crosses).
  • Selection menu / panel: Select all, Invert, Clear, Edit nodes, Edit elements, Delete.
  • Cut/Copy/Paste (Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V) duplicate a selection with an offset. Undo/Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) cover all edits.

docs.title: Transforms and bulk edits
docs.text:
The Edit menu applies geometric transforms to the current selection:

Command Effect Move Translate by a vector Array Replicate along a grid (copies at a spacing, a count in each direction) Rotate Rotate about a point Scale Scale about a point Mirror Reflect across an axis

Two commands bake parametric objects into ordinary, individually-editable elements: Line to bar (segment / arc / multisegment → bars) and Surface to mesh (rectangle / polygon → triangles and/or quads); the object is then removed. See Geometry objects.

To change many entities at once, select them and use Selection → Edit selected nodes / bars / triangles… for a bulk editor, or Divide bars… to subdivide selected members into several elements.

docs.title: Checking and meshing the model
docs.text:
• Structure → Model check (also in the Analysis menu) reports topology issues that are not auto-fixed: isolated nodes, coincident nodes, unconnected T-junctions and crossings, duplicate bars, masses on restrained DOFs, and the constraint checks above.
  • Analysis → Generate mesh (F6) compiles the geometry objects into the concrete mesh the solver uses, so you can inspect it before running — it is shown via the Mesh overlay checkbox on the Structure view (Display panel ▸ Model tab), which draws the generated mesh over the geometry objects.
  • Analysis → Model info shows a summary of the model's size and contents.

docs.title: Plane models: frames and walls
docs.text:
A plane model is a frame, truss, arch or wall in its own plane: the nodes carry ux, uy and θz. It is one of the two domains, chosen in New model (Frame / Wall, in-plane). This page is the reference for it, in the same order as Plate models: the elements, the supports, the springs, the loads, the analyses, the results and design, the templates, and a script.

What both domains share is on Modelling the structure, Supports, springs and constraints and Geometry objects.

docs.title: Line elements: beams
docs.text: A beam is an Euler–Bernoulli beam-column with axial, bending and shear behaviour, six degrees of freedom (three per node). It references a section (materials and sections are on Modelling). Each end can carry a moment release (hinge). Its results are the M, V and N diagrams.

docs.title: Surface elements: panels
docs.text: A panel is a surface that carries forces in its own plane: a wall, a shear wall, a deep beam. Its sections carry a thickness, a material, a plane-stress / plane-strain flag and a formulation.

docs.title: Triangles
docs.text:
Formulation DOFs per node Notes CST (constant-strain triangle) ux, uy Fast, robust; overly stiff in bending. The node's rotation is left free (auto-restrained) unless a bar also frames in. Allman ux, uy, θz Adds an in-plane drilling rotation, so it can transfer moment to a frame member and converges faster in bending. ES-FEM (edge-based smoothed) ux, uy Smooths CST over edge domains — softer, more accurate in bending — without adding a DOF.

Add triangles one by one (three node picks) on the Triangles sub-tab, or let a polygon geometry object mesh itself automatically.

docs.title: Quads
docs.text:
A quad is the 4-node counterpart of the triangle. Its advantage is on a regular, structured mesh (a rectangular wall panel): a triangle split introduces a directional (diagonal) bias in the stress field near supports and point loads that a quad avoids. Prefer quads on regular grids; keep triangles for irregular or concave outlines (the quad mesher is structured-only).

Formulation Notes QM6 (incompatible-modes Q4) The recommended membrane quad — four internal bubble DOFs, condensed out, fix the bending-lock that plain Q4 suffers. Q4 (bilinear) Reference/patch-test element only — locks in bending, not recommended as the default.

Add quads one by one (four node picks, i → j → k → l counter-clockwise) from Structure ▸ Triangles ▸ Add quad, or let a rectangle/polygon object mesh into quads.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text: Supports restrain ux, uy and θz. The canonical names are FIXED (all three), PIN (both translations), ROLLER-X / ROLLER-Y (one translation), GUIDED-X / GUIDED-Y (a translation and the rotation) and BLOCK (rotation only, free to move). The quick presets of the support dialog are PIN, ROLLER-X and FIXED. The mechanism, the other tables and the on-canvas legend are on Supports, springs and constraints.

docs.title: Springs and foundations
docs.text: A node spring has Kx, Ky and Kt. An element spring is a Winkler foundation along a bar, per unit length, with Kx and Ky in global or local (axial / transverse) axes. Both can be tension-only or compression-only, which a NonLinear case honours (a footing that lifts off the soil is the typical use). See Springs.

docs.title: Loads
docs.text:
Load Applies to Parameters Point load a node Fx, Fy, Mz Distributed load a bar trapezoidal Fy / Fx, global or local axes Element point load a point along a bar Fx, Fy, Mz at distance a Edge load a triangle or quad edge, or a surface boundary traction Fx, Fy per unit length Temperature a bar, or an area uniform ΔT (and a gradient on bars) Support settlement a supported node prescribed ux, uy, θz Nodal mass a node, for a Mass case Mx, My, Mtz

Everything about load cases, self-weight and the loads view is on Loads.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: All the analysis cases are available: Linear, NonLinear (unilateral springs), Mass, Modal, Spectrum (EC8) and Geometric Nonlinear (P-Delta). P-Delta is built from the axial force of the bars, which is why it exists only in this domain. See Analysis.

docs.title: Results and design
docs.text:
• Bars: M, V and N diagrams, displacements, reactions.
  • Triangles and quads: membrane stresses σx, σy, τxy, σ1, σ2, von Mises (kN/m²), and, with the Forces (N = σ·t) toggle, forces per unit width Nx, Ny, Nxy, N1, N2.
  • Design: concrete beams and columns (EC2) with flexure, shear, crack width and the suggested column reinforcement; membrane (Wood/Baumann) reinforcement of triangles; steel (EC3) and timber (EC5) members; punching.

See Results and Design.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Beams & Frames, Walls, Trusses and Arches build plane models (see Templates).

docs.title: By script
docs.text:
from xdfem2d import Structure2D

s = Structure2D(domain='plane')
s.add_material('C30', elastic_modulus=30e6, unit_weight=25.0)
s.add_section('S1', material_name='C30', b=0.3, h=0.6)
s.add_node('N1', 0.0, 0.0)
s.add_node('N2', 5.0, 0.0)
s.add_bar_element('E1', node_i='N1', node_j='N2', section_name='S1')
s.add_support('PIN', ux=True, uy=True)
s.add_support('ROLLER', uy=True)
s.assign_support('N1', 'PIN')
s.assign_support('N2', 'ROLLER')
s.add_load_case('LC1', self_weight_factor=0.0)
s.add_distributed_load('E1', 'LC1', fye=-10.0, fyd=-10.0)   # 10 kN/m downward
r = s.calculate()
print(r['reactions']['LC1']['N1'])                          # [Rx, Ry, Mz]

Runnable examples are in the examples/ folder: example-simple_beam_plane.x2d, example-continuous_beam.x2d, example-frame_and_wall.x2d, example-truss.x2d, example-arch.x2d, example-modal_frame.x2d and example-tension.x2d.

docs.title: Plate models: slabs and grillages
docs.text:
A plate model bends out of its plane: a slab (plate-bending triangles and quads) or a grillage (beams carrying transverse load and torsion). The nodes carry w, θx and θy. It is one of the two domains, chosen in New model (Slab / Grillage, out-of-plane). This page is the reference for it, in the same order as Plane models: the elements, the supports, the springs, the loads, the analyses, the results and design, the templates, and a script.

What both domains share is on Modelling the structure, Supports, springs and constraints and Geometry objects.

docs.title: Line elements: grid members
docs.text: A grid member is a beam of a grillage: it carries bending and shear for the transverse load and St-Venant torsion. It reuses the bar section and gains a torsion constant J = β·b·h³ (with G = E/2(1+ν)). A hinge at an end releases the bending rotation; there is no torsion release. Its results are the M, V and T diagrams.

docs.title: Surface elements: slabs
docs.text: A slab is a surface that bends under transverse load. Its sections carry a thickness, a material and a formulation: the plate-bending element.

docs.title: Triangles
docs.text:
Formulation Notes MITC3 (the default) Shear-deformable (Mindlin–Reissner): valid for thick slabs as well as thin ones, and reports a genuine shear field vx, vy. It converges to the exact Mindlin solution and passes the constant-moment patch test. DKT The thin-plate (Kirchhoff) element: no shear deformation, very accurate for thin slabs on coarse meshes.

Use the default (MITC3) unless the slab is very thin and the mesh is coarse, where DKT converges with fewer elements. Both share the same nodes, DOFs, results and Wood–Armer design moments, so switching is just the section's formulation.

Add triangles one by one (three node picks) on the Triangles sub-tab, or let a polygon geometry object mesh itself automatically.

docs.title: Quads
docs.text:
A quad is the 4-node counterpart of the triangle. On a regular grid it avoids the diagonal bias that a triangle split introduces near supports and point loads; prefer quads on regular grids and keep triangles for irregular or concave outlines (the quad mesher is structured-only).

Formulation Notes MITC4 (Mindlin, shear-locking-free) The recommended slab quad — the 4-node analogue of MITC3. DKT4 (thin, Kirchhoff) Four DKT triangles condensed to a quad; the thin-plate analogue of DKT.

They carry the same moments and shears, Wood–Armer design and result views as the triangles, so a mixed tri/quad slab (quads in the regular field, triangles at an irregular edge) is one continuous model. Add quads one by one (four node picks, i → j → k → l counter-clockwise) from Structure ▸ Triangles ▸ Add quad, or let a rectangle/polygon object mesh into quads.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text: Supports restrain w, θx and θy. The canonical names are CLAMPED (all three), SIMPLE (w only), CLAMP-X / CLAMP-Y (w and one rotation), SYM-X / SYM-Y (one rotation: a symmetry line) and BLOCK. On the canvas the symbols read as slab edges: a simply-supported knife-edge (SIMPLE), a hatched clamp (CLAMPED), a supported edge with one rotation held (CLAMP-X/Y), and a dash-dot symmetry line (SYM-X/Y), which lets you model a whole slab from one wedge. The quick presets of the support dialog are SIMPLE, CLAMPED and SYM-X. The mechanism, the other tables and the on-canvas legend are on Supports, springs and constraints.

docs.title: Springs and foundations
docs.text: A node spring has kz (transverse) and ktx, kty (rotations). An element spring under a grid member resists the transverse deflection w only. A Winkler area spring kz [kN/m³] under a slab (a slab on grade) is lumped kz·A/3 at each triangle vertex and kz·A/4 at each quad vertex. It is a support, not a load, but it is applied over a region the same way as an area load. See Springs.

docs.title: Loads
docs.text:
Load Applies to Parameters Point load a node Fz, Mx, My Distributed load a grid member transverse intensity qz Area pressure a slab region (a surface object, or a single triangle) pz [kN/m²]: the everyday slab load, drawn as a colour map Temperature a slab (a triangle, a quad or a surface); a grid member takes the same two values as a bar through-thickness gradient ΔT = T_top − T_bottom, which curves the plate (a uniform rise is stress-free) Support settlement a supported node prescribed w, θx, θy Nodal mass a node, for a Mass case Mx (the mass on w), My, Mtz (rotational inertias about x and y)

A slab is loaded by area pressure (edge tractions are a plane-domain load). Everything about load cases, self-weight and the loads view is on Loads.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Linear, NonLinear, Mass, Modal, Spectrum and Sequence are available. The mass sits on the transverse DOF w, so the modes are the out-of-plane (vertical) vibration and the response spectrum is vertical. P-Delta is not available: its geometric stiffness is built from in-plane axial force, which a plate model does not carry. See Analysis.

docs.title: Results and design
docs.text:
• Grid members: M, V and T diagrams, deflection, reactions Rz, Mx, My.
  • Triangles and quads: the deflection field w, θx, θy, and the slab forces mx, my, mxy, m1, m2 (kNm/m) and vx, vy (kN/m). They are already stress resultants, so there is no force toggle.
  • Wood–Armer (W-A) design moments m*x,bot, m*y,bot, m*x,top, m*y,top, per element: the orthogonal-reinforcement moments an EC2 slab check consumes.
  • Design: the grillage members are designed as bars, with torsion (Concrete: beams and columns); the slab is designed for bending and out-of-plane shear (Concrete: slabs and walls), and checked for punching at its columns (Concrete: punching).

See Results.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Slabs (rectangular slab, rib-stiffened, flat slab on columns, slab on grade, circular sector) and Grillages (beam grid, bridge deck) build plate models (see Templates).

docs.title: By script
docs.text:
from xdfem2d import Structure2D

# A cantilever grillage member with a tip load (see examples/example-grillage-cantilever.py)
s = Structure2D(domain='plate')
s.add_material('C30', elastic_modulus=33e6, unit_weight=25.0, poisson=0.2)
s.add_section('BEAM', material_name='C30', b=0.3, h=0.5)     # grillage bar: gains J
s.add_node('N0', 0.0, 0.0)
s.add_node('N1', 3.0, 0.0)
s.add_bar_element('G1', node_i='N0', node_j='N1', section_name='BEAM')
s.add_support('CLAMPED', w=True, tx=True, ty=True)
s.assign_support('N0', 'CLAMPED')
s.add_load_case('LC', self_weight_factor=0.0)
s.add_point_load('N1', 'LC', fz=-10.0)                       # 10 kN down at the tip
r = s.calculate()
print(r['displacements']['LC']['N1'])                        # [w, θx, θy]

# For a slab: add_plate_section / add_quad_section, nodes, add_tri_element (3 nodes) or
# add_quad_element (4 nodes, counter-clockwise), supports, then the area pressure:
#   s.add_plate_section('SLAB', 'C30', thickness=0.20)         # MITC3; formulation='DKT' for thin plates
#   s.add_quad_section('SLABQ', 'C30', thickness=0.20, formulation='MITC4')   # DKT4 for thin
#   s.add_area_load('S1', 'LC', pz=-10.0)                      # a triangle OR a quad id (or a surface object)

Runnable examples are in the examples/ folder: example-slab.py (thin slab with the DKT element, checked against the Kirchhoff Navier series), example-slab-mitc3.py (thick slab with MITC3, checked against the exact Mindlin series — the transverse-shear deflection the DKT misses), example-slab-quad.py, example-grillage.py (crossed two-beam grillage, load split) and example-grillage-cantilever.py (cantilever bar checked against the bending F·L³/3EI and the St-Venant torsion T·L/GJ).

docs.title: Python API: loads and analysis
docs.text:
How to apply loads and set up the analysis in code: load cases, the loads themselves, analysis cases, combinations, masses and spectra. Building the model is on Python API: building a model. The conventions that apply to every call (signs, domains, create_* and add_*) are on Scripting with the engine.

The signatures on this page are written from the engine, so they are complete: every parameter, with its type and default. Python API: reference lists every call.

Every load belongs to a load case, so that comes first. A load case is only a definition of loads; an analysis case is what gets solved (see Analysis).

To apply… Shortcut Fundamental A load case create_load_case add_load_case A uniform load on a bar or a slab create_uniform_load add_distributed_load, add_area_load, add_line_distributed_load A trapezoidal or point load on a bar create_bar_distributed_load, create_bar_point_load add_distributed_load, add_element_point_load A load on a node or an edge create_node_load, create_edge_load add_point_load, add_tri_edge_load, add_surface_edge_load Self-weight, temperature, settlement create_self_weight, create_temperature, create_support_settlement add_temperature_load and its relatives, add_support_settlement An analysis case create_analysis_case add_analysis_case A combination, a nodal mass, a spectrum add_load_combination, add_nodal_mass, add_spectral_function

docs.title: Convenience call (create_*)
docs.text:
create_load_case(
    id: str | None = None, self_weight_factor: float = 0.0, action_type=None,
    create_analysis_case: bool = True) -> LoadCase

id optional — auto-assigned ("LC1", "LC2", …) when omitted. action_type accepts the Eurocode letter ("G"/"Q"/"W"/"E"/"T"), the word ("permanent"/"live"/"wind"/"seismic"/"temperature", case-insensitive), or the old dashed label — whichever is written, the stored value is always the letter. create_analysis_case=True also creates a matching AnalysisCase with the same id (see Analysis cases below) so a new load case is solvable right away, without a separate call.

docs.title: Fundamental call
docs.text:
add_load_case(
    id: str, self_weight_factor=0.0, action_type=None, create_analysis_case: bool = True,
    load_duration=None, category: str = '', psi0=None, psi1=None, psi2=None) -> LoadCase

id required — what create_load_case above forwards to.

docs.title: Convenience calls (create_*)
docs.text:
create_uniform_load(targets, load_case, value, direction: str = 'down', coord_sys: str = 'global')
create_bar_distributed_load(
    elements, load_case=None, q_i: float = None, q_j: float = None, direction: str = 'down')
    # trapezoidal; bars only
create_bar_point_load(
    elements, load_case=None, p: float = None, at: float = 0.5, direction: str = 'down')
    # bars only; at = fraction of the span

create_uniform_load is the one to use for a constant load. value is a force per length [kN/m] on a bar-like target (a bar, or a geometry line, segment, multisegment or arc) and a pressure [kN/m²] on an area-like target (a slab region, a triangle or a quad), and the call routes each target by its own kind, so one call may mix both. It checks every target before applying anything, so it either applies everything or raises. It returns a dictionary from each target id to 'bar' or 'area'.

direction is "down" or "up" (the gravity axis: −Y in a plane model, −Z in a plate model) for both kinds, or "perp" and "axial" (local axes, bars only, plane domain). coord_sys ("global" or "local") only matters for bars.

targets and elements take a single id or object, or a list of either (a list in gives a list out). load_case is the load case, as an id or a LoadCase; where it is optional, leaving it out uses a default case that is created on first use. create_bar_distributed_load only takes "down" and "up".

docs.title: Fundamental calls
docs.text:
add_distributed_load(
    element_id: str, load_case_id: str, fxe=0.0, fxd=0.0, fye=0.0, fyd=0.0, coord_sys='global',
    fze=None, fzd=None) -> DistributedLoad
add_element_point_load(
    element_id: str, load_case_id: str, a: float, fx=0.0, fy=0.0, mz=0.0, coord_sys='global',
    fz=None) -> ElementPointLoad
add_area_load(target_id: str, load_case_id: str, pz: float = 0.0)
    # slab pressure (plate); a surface object, a triangle id or a quad id
add_line_distributed_load(
    object_id: str, load_case_id: str, fx=0.0, fy=0.0, fx_field='', fy_field='',
    coord_sys='global') -> LineDistributedLoad

Signed components (fx, fy, …) in a chosen frame (coord_sys), not a named direction: what the shortcuts above forward to. Reach for these directly for a load the shortcuts cannot express, such as a trapezoidal axial load or a point load in a local frame with both fx and fy. Negative pz is downward; a new area load replaces an existing one on the same target and case.

docs.title: Convenience calls (create_*)
docs.text:
create_node_load(nodes, load_case=None, p: float = None, direction: str = 'down')
create_edge_load(object_id: str, edge, load_case=None, p: float = None, direction: str = 'perp')

create_node_load direction: "down"/"up" (both domains — plane: global ∓Y; plate: transverse, ∓Z). "left"/"right" (global ∓X) are plane domain only. create_edge_load's edge: 'all' | 'bottom'/'right'/ 'top'/'left' | an integer index — same vocabulary as support_edge. direction: "perp" (outward normal) or "tang" (along the edge, sign follows the edge's own winding, not a global direction — for a rectangle, 'top' is −X, not +X; use create_node_load on the corner node for an unambiguous global push instead of guessing "tang"'s sign).

docs.title: Fundamental calls
docs.text:
add_point_load(
    node_id: str, load_case_id: str, fx=0.0, fy=0.0, mz=0.0, fz=None, mx=None,
    my=None) -> PointLoad
add_tri_edge_load(
    id: str, tri_id: str, node_a: str, node_b: str, load_case_id: str, fx: float = 0.0,
    fy: float = 0.0, coord_sys: str = 'global', pn: float = 0.0, pt: float = 0.0) -> TriEdgeLoad
add_surface_edge_load(
    id: str, object_id: str, node_a: str, node_b: str, load_case_id: str, fx: float = 0.0,
    fy: float = 0.0, coord_sys: str = 'global', pn: float = 0.0, pt: float = 0.0)

add_point_load is the only way to put a moment (mz/mx/my) or an in-plane force on a plate node — what neither create_node_load nor create_uniform_load can express. add_tri_edge_load addresses an already-meshed triangle's edge (post-solve ids); create_edge_load above works pre-mesh, on the geometry object itself.

docs.title: Convenience calls (create_*)
docs.text:
create_self_weight(factor: float = 1.0, load_case=None) -> LoadCase
    # sets/creates self_weight_factor
create_temperature(target, uniform: float = 0.0, gradient: float = 0.0, load_case=None)
create_support_settlement(
    nodes: str | Node | list, load_case=None, ux=0.0, uy=0.0, tz=0.0, w=None, tx=None, ty=None)

create_temperature dispatches by target type: bar → add_temperature_load, triangle → add_tri_temperature_load, quad → add_quad_temperature_load, geo line object → add_line_temperature_load, geo area object → add_area_temperature_load. It only takes a single uniform/gradient value, never a field: add_area_temperature_load/add_line_temperature_load below are the ones that accept field_name/grad_field_name for a ΔT that varies spatially (sampled per generated mesh node/bar); use them directly for that case, the same way create_bar_distributed_load above is the one to reach for when create_uniform_load's "down"/"up"-only direction is not enough. create_support_settlement's nodes: a single id/Node, or a list of either; w/tx/ty are the plate-domain aliases of ux/uy/tz.

docs.title: Fundamental calls
docs.text:
add_temperature_load(
    bar_id: str | None = None, load_case_id: str | None = None, dt_uniform=0.0, dt_gradient=0.0,
    alpha=None, *, element_id: str | None = None, delta_t_uniform: float | None = None,
    delta_t_gradient: float | None = None) -> TemperatureLoad
    # bars — alpha: accepted, no effect (see below)
add_tri_temperature_load(
    tri_id: str, load_case_id: str, dt_i=0.0, dt_j=0.0, dt_k=0.0,
    dt_gradient=0.0) -> TriTemperatureLoad
    # triangles
add_quad_temperature_load(
    quad_id: str, load_case_id: str, dt_i=0.0, dt_j=0.0, dt_k=0.0, dt_l=0.0,
    dt_gradient=0.0) -> QuadTemperatureLoad
    # quads
add_area_temperature_load(
    object_id: str, load_case_id: str, dt_uniform=0.0, dt_gradient=0.0, field_name='',
    grad_field_name='') -> AreaTemperatureLoad
add_line_temperature_load(
    object_id: str, load_case_id: str, dt_uniform=0.0, dt_gradient=0.0, field_name='',
    grad_field_name='') -> LineTemperatureLoad
add_support_settlement(
    node_id: str, load_case_id: str, ux=0.0, uy=0.0, tz=0.0, w=None, tx=None,
    ty=None) -> SupportSettlement

bar_id/dt_uniform/dt_gradient are the canonical names for add_temperature_load now — matching tri_id/quad_id and dt_uniform/dt_gradient elsewhere in the temperature-load family, instead of the bar's old generic element_id and delta_t_uniform/ delta_t_gradient. The old element_id=/delta_t_uniform=/ delta_t_gradient= keywords still work (same pattern as tri_section_name= above); the stored TemperatureLoad attributes and the .x2d field keep the names element_id/delta_t_uniform/delta_t_gradient.

alpha is a different thing from a deprecated alias — it is accepted but has no effect at all. Unlike the keywords above (each still sets the value it names, just under an old spelling), passing alpha to add_temperature_load changes nothing: the thermal expansion coefficient always comes from the element's material (Material.alpha) at analysis time. The parameter exists only so old call sites that already pass alpha keep working: TemperatureLoad has nowhere to store it.

docs.title: Analysis cases, combinations and dynamics
docs.text: AnalysisCase controls how a model is solved (linear, modal, spectrum, …). It is a different concept from a LoadCase, which only says what loads exist; the two only share the word "case".

docs.title: Analysis case: convenience call
docs.text:
create_analysis_case(
    id: str | None = None, analysis_type: str = 'Linear', coefficients: dict | None = None,
    **kwargs) -> AnalysisCase

id optional — auto-assigned ("AC1", "AC2", …) when omitted. create_load_case's create_analysis_case=True (see Load cases above) already creates one of these with a matching id for the common case; call this directly only for a case that needs a different id or a non-default analysis_type.

docs.title: Analysis case, fundamental
docs.text:
add_analysis_case(
    id: str, analysis_type: str = 'Linear', coefficients: dict | None = None,
    **kwargs) -> AnalysisCase
    # analysis_type: Linear | NonLinear | Mass | Modal | Spectrum | GeometricNonlinear

id required — what create_analysis_case above forwards to.

docs.title: Combinations, masses and spectra
docs.text:
add_load_combination(
    id: str, coefficients: dict[str, float], combo_type='LinearSum') -> LoadCombination
add_nodal_mass(
    node_id: str, mass_case_id: str, mx: float = 0.0, my: float = 0.0,
    mtz: float = 0.0) -> NodalMass
add_spectral_function(
    id: str, description: str = '', damping: float = 0.05,
    points: list | None = None) -> SpectralFunction

No create_* layer for these three — no auto-id convenience has been needed for them yet.

docs.title: Python API: building a model
docs.text:
How to build a model in code: materials, sections, nodes, elements, geometry objects, supports, springs, constraints and fields. Loads and analysis are on Python API: loads and analysis; solving, reading the results, designing and editing are on Python API: results and design. The conventions that apply to all of them, and an end-to-end example, are on Scripting with the engine.

The signatures on this page are written from the engine, so they are complete: every parameter, with its type and default. Python API: reference lists every call.

To create… Shortcut Fundamental A material create_rc_material, create_steel_material, create_timber_material add_material, add_concrete_material A section create_bar_section, create_area_section, create_rc_section, create_steel_section, create_timber_bar_section add_section, add_tri_section, add_plate_section, add_quad_section, add_area_section A node, a bar, a triangle or a quad create_node, create_node_list, create_bar_element, create_area_element add_node, add_bar_element, add_tri_element, add_quad_element, add_area_element A wall or a slab region create_polygon (alias create_panel) add_geo_rectangle, add_geo_polygon A line or an arc add_geo_segment, add_geo_arc, add_geo_arc_3pts, add_geo_multisegment A support pin, fix, roller, symm, create_support; on an edge support_edge and its relatives add_support, assign_support A spring add_node_spring, add_element_spring, add_line_element_spring, add_area_spring A constraint or a field add_rigid_link, add_equal_dof, add_constraint_equation, add_field A whole standard structure create_from_template

docs.title: Convenience calls (create_*)
docs.text:
create_material(
    name: str, elastic_modulus: float, unit_weight: float, alpha: float = 1e-05, unit_mass=None,
    material_type=None, design=None, poisson: float = 0.2) -> Material
    # == add_material, pure alias
create_rc_material(
    concrete: str = 'C30/37', steel: str = 'B500B', name: str | None = None) -> Material
    # get-or-create, deduped by name
create_steel_material(steel: str = 'S275', name: str | None = None) -> Material
create_timber_material(timber: str = 'C24', name: str | None = None) -> Material

name=None derives the name from the class string (e.g. "C30/37"). Get-or-create: two calls with the same class dedupe to one Material.

docs.title: Fundamental calls (add_*)
docs.text:
add_material(
    name: str, elastic_modulus: float, unit_weight: float, alpha: float = 1e-05, unit_mass=None,
    material_type=None, design=None, poisson: float = 0.2) -> Material
add_concrete_material(
    material_name: str, concrete_class: str, steel_class: str, gamma_c=1.5, gamma_s=1.15,
    alpha_cc=1.0) -> ConcreteMaterial

add_concrete_material links EC2 design metadata onto an already-existing material by name — a different job from create_rc_material, which makes the physical material itself.

docs.title: Convenience calls (create_*)
docs.text:
create_bar_section(name: str, material_name: str | Material, b: float, h: float, **kw) -> Section
    # material_name resolves an unrecognised Eurocode class automatically first
create_area_section(

    cover: float = 0.045) -> Section

    name: str, material_name: str, thickness: float = 0.1, plane_strain: bool = False,
    formulation: str = 'CST', quad_formulation: str = 'QM6', rc_cover: float = 0.045,
    rc_alpha_s: float = 90.0, rc_bar_phi: float = 16.0, rc_shear_min: bool = True,
    rc_cover_top_x: float = None, rc_cover_top_y: float = None, rc_cover_bot_x: float = None,
    rc_cover_bot_y: float = None) -> TriSection
    # add_tri_section + add_quad_section under one name; returns the TriSection,
    # the QuadSection is self.quad_sections[name]. A bad quad_formulation rolls
    # the tri half back rather than leaving an unpaired section.

The quad section fields mirror the triangle section's; a wall uses "QM6" (recommended) or "Q4", a slab uses "MITC4" (recommended) or "DKT4". Edge, area (pz), temperature and Winkler-spring loads all have quad targets, via the same add_area_load / create_temperature / add_area_spring dispatchers (the id resolves to the triangle or quad list) plus add_quad_edge_load / add_quad_temperature_load.

material_name must already exist. These are what every create_* call above forwards to.

docs.text:
create_node(x: float, y: float, id: str | None = None) -> Node
    # id auto-assigned: "1", "2", ...
create_node_list(outline, id_prefix: str | None = None) -> list[Node]
    # flexible outline, see Geometry objects
create_bar_element(
    section: str | Section, node_i: str | Node, node_j: str | Node, id: str | None = None,
    **kw) -> BarElement
    # id auto: "B1", "B2", ...; section first, then the nodes it applies to;
    # node_i/node_j: id or Node; section: name or Section
create_area_element(
    section: str | TriSection | QuadSection, node_i: str | Node, node_j: str | Node,
    node_k: str | Node, node_l: str | Node | None = None, id: str | None = None,
    **kw) -> TriElement | QuadElement
    # id auto: "T1", "T2", ... (triangle) or "Q1", "Q2", ... (quad); section first;
    # node_l is the only thing that decides triangle (3 nodes) vs quad (4 nodes) —
    # one call covers both instead of picking add_tri_element/add_quad_element
    # up front

id optional (auto-assigned), and node/section arguments accept the object returned by another create_* call as well as a raw id/name. Section comes first in both calls — the target it belongs to precedes the nodes it applies to, one order across the whole create_* element layer:

n = s.create_node_list([0,0, 5,0, 10,0])
sec = s.create_rc_section("B30x60", 0.30, 0.60)
s.create_bar_element(sec, n[0], n[1])

docs.text:
add_node(id: str, x: float, y: float) -> Node
add_bar_element(
    id: str, node_i: str, node_j: str, section_name: str, hinge_i=False, hinge_j=False,
    rc_design=False, rc_cover=0.025, rc_cotg_theta=1.0, rc_alpha_s=90.0, sd_ky=None, sd_kz=None,
    sd_klt=None, sd_ltb=True, stage: int = 1, is_column: Optional[bool] = None,
    beam: Optional[str] = None) -> BarElement
    # Beam (plane) / Grid (plate)
add_tri_element(id: str, node_i: str, node_j: str, node_k: str, section_name: str) -> TriElement
    # Panel/Slab
add_quad_element(
    id: str, node_i: str, node_j: str, node_k: str, node_l: str, section_name: str) -> QuadElement
    # 4-node area element; nodes counter-clockwise; Panel/Slab (see add_quad_section)
add_area_element(
    id: str, node_i: str, node_j: str, node_k: str, node_l: str | None = None, *,
    section_name: str) -> TriElement | QuadElement
    # 3 nodes -> add_tri_element, 4 (node_l given) -> add_quad_element;
    # section_name is keyword-only (its slot would otherwise shift depending
    # on which branch runs)

Element ids are unique across kinds — a bar, a triangle and a quad may not share the same id. A quad is validated at creation (4 distinct nodes, counter-clockwise winding, convex, positive Jacobian); a bad quad raises rather than being silently repaired.

add_area_element dispatches to the other two: three nodes make a triangle, four a quad. section_name is keyword-only on it, because its position would otherwise shift with the branch.

docs.title: Convenience call: create_polygon
docs.text:
create_polygon(
    outline, thickness: float, material: str = 'C30/37', target_size: float = 0.5,
    id: str | None = None)
    # exactly 2 points -> opposite corners of a rectangle; 3 or more -> a polygon

A region and its section in one call: the domain picks a slab (plate) or a wall (plane). create_panel and add_panel are the same call under older names. Keep the return: .node_ids are the real corner nodes (for a rectangle, counter-clockwise: bottom-left, bottom-right, top-right, top-left), for example to put create_node_load on one specific corner. Named edges (support_edge, below) work on this outline as long as the 4 points are given in that order.

material is an existing material name or a Material, or an unresolved Eurocode concrete class ("C30/37"), which is created for you with its steel fixed at "B500B". id names the geometry object, and its section <id>_sec; it is "Panel1", "Panel2", … when omitted.

outline (and any list of points, including create_node_list above) is flexible: [(x, y), …] pairs, a flat [x1, y1, x2, y2, …], {"x": …, "y": …} dicts, or two columns [[x1, x2, …], [y1, y2, …]] (for 3 or more points). Except in the flat form, an entry may instead be the id of an existing node, or a Node, mixed freely with coordinates.
