docs.title: A whole standard structure
docs.text:
create_from_template(kind: str, **params) -> Structure2D
    # on an EMPTY model

The parametric structures of File ▸ New from Template… as one call, with plain parameters: the material is a name (material='C30/37', 'S275', 'C24'), the lengths are the ones the problem states (spans=[4, 5, 6]), and a profile is profile='IPE300'. Linear structures come as nodes and bars, walls and slabs as one geometry object that is meshed when the model is solved. It fills an empty model only, and validates everything before building anything; an error says what the call takes.

s = Structure2D(domain='plane')
s.create_from_template('continuous_beam', spans=[4, 5, 6])

The kinds are listed by xdfem2d.template_api.template_kinds(): beam, continuous_beam, portal_frame, frame, truss_warren, truss_howe, truss_pratt, truss_long, truss_kingpost, truss_town, arch, wall, slab, wall_beam, wall_frame, slab_ribbed, flat_slab, slab_on_grade, slab_sector, beam_grid, bridge_grillage. The parameters of each are in xdfem2d.template_api.TEMPLATE_KINDS, and kind_signature(kind) prints one.

docs.title: Convenience calls (create_*)
docs.text:
pin(nodes: str | Node | list)
    # plane: ux,uy   · plate: w
fix(nodes: str | Node | list)
    # plane: ux,uy,θz · plate: w,θx,θy
roller(nodes: str | Node | list, free: str = 'x')
    # plane only — frees one translation
symm(nodes: str | Node | list, axis: str = 'x')
    # plate only — symmetry line (w free, θ about axis fixed)
create_support(
    nodes: str | Node | list, ux=False, uy=False, tz=False, w=None, tx=None, ty=None,
    name: str | None = None)

nodes: a single id/Node, or a list of either (same list-or-single rule as loads). pin/fix/roller/symm cover the common cases with an auto-assigned canonical support name ("PIN", "FIXED", "ROLLER-X", "SYM-X", …); create_support is the generic one-call create-and-assign underneath them.

True fixes that DOF, False frees it — every flag defaults to False, so create_support(nodes) on its own restrains nothing. A model that means to fully fix a node has to say ux=True, uy=True, tz=True (or just call fix(nodes)); writing all three explicitly as False "to be clear" restrains nothing and turns the structure into a mechanism — a real mistake a script has made. w/tx/ty are the plate-domain aliases of the same three (ux,uy,tz) slots.

docs.title: Fundamental calls
docs.text:
add_support(name: str, ux=False, uy=False, tz=False, w=None, tx=None, ty=None) -> Support
assign_support(node_id: str, support_name: str) -> SupportAssignment

The two calls every convenience wrapper above forwards to: create the named restraint, then assign it to a node. Reach for these directly to reuse one named Support across many assign_support calls without re-specifying its flags each time.

docs.title: On the edge of a region
docs.text:
support_edge(object_id: str, edge, kind: str = 'pin')
    # the general call
pin_edge(object_id: str, edge)
    # = support_edge(…, 'pin')   plate SIMPLE · plane PIN
fix_edge(object_id: str, edge)
    # = support_edge(…, 'fix')   plate CLAMPED · plane FIXED
roller_edge(object_id: str, edge, free: str = 'x')
    # = support_edge(…, 'roller-x'/'roller-y')  plane only
symm_edge(object_id: str, edge, axis: str = 'x')
    # = support_edge(…, 'symm-x'/'symm-y')      plate only
support_object_edge(object_id: str, edge, support_name: str)
    # any named support / 'free'
free_edge(object_id: str, edge)
    # remove — clear that edge

support_edge is the general call; pin_edge/fix_edge/roller_edge/ symm_edge are it with a fixed kind. edge: 'all' | 'bottom'/'right'/'top'/'left' | an integer index (vertex i → i+1, wrapping) — the same vocabulary create_edge_load (see loads) uses. kind: pin | fix | symm-x | symm-y | roller-x | roller-y. All are domain-aware (roller-* is plane-only, symm-* plate-only, exactly as the node methods are) and resolve to the canonical support (SIMPLE/CLAMPED/…).

They all write the object's per-edge edge_supports list, so every mesh node the edge generates is restrained, and restraints can differ per edge (e.g. clamped / simply / clamped / simply around a rectangle).

support_object_edge takes an explicit support name instead of a kind: any support already defined (or a canonical name such as SIMPLE / CLAMPED), or 'free' to clear that edge. free_edge is the inverse of the whole family — it frees an edge whether it was restrained through the edge_supports list or by corner-node assignments.

In a JSON model the same thing is the object's "edge_supports" key: a list with one entry per edge in perimeter order (a rectangle is bottom, right, top, left), each a support name or "free". For example, a slab simply supported on two opposite edges:

{ "kind": "rectangle", "id": "R1", "tri_section_name": "Slab",
  "node_ids": ["R1.p0", "R1.p1", "R1.p2", "R1.p3"],
  "edge_supports": ["SIMPLE", "free", "SIMPLE", "free"] }

When edge_supports is absent, edge_support_mode ("common" default / "equal" / "none") instead propagates each edge from whatever supports its two corner nodes carry — the older corner-propagation fallback, used when the corners are supported directly (assign_support/pin on the corner nodes) rather than through edge_supports.

docs.title: Python API: results and design
docs.text:
How to solve a model, read what comes back, design it, edit it afterwards, and use the variants and construction sequences, all without the interface. Building the model is on Python API: building a model, the loads and analysis cases on Python API: loads and analysis.

The signatures on this page are written from the engine, so they are complete: every parameter, with its type and default. Python API: reference lists every call.

docs.title: Solving and reading the results
docs.text:
Structure2D(domain="plane")                 # or "plate"; fixed for the model's life
calculate() -> dict
    # assemble and solve every analysis case; returns the results
check_references()
    # raise on dangling or invalid references
domain_problems() -> list[str]
    # features the model's domain does not support
save(path: str)
    # write a .x2d or .json
Structure2D.load(path) -> Structure2D       # read a file

calculate() returns a dictionary. The ones you will use most are keyed by analysis-case id and then by node or element id:

Key Holds displacements[case][node] [ux, uy, θz] (in a plate model [w, θx, θy]) reactions[case][node] [Rx, Ry, Mz] (plate: [Rz, Mx, My]) at a supported node element_forces[case][element] {'i': [N, V, M], 'j': [N, V, M]}: the end forces of a bar (plate: T in place of N) spring_forces, constraint_forces the reaction of springs and the force each constraint transmits tri_stress[case][element] the field of the triangles and quads: stresses in a plane model, moments and shears in a plate model combinations the results of the combinations, built from the analysis cases analysis_cases per case: its type and whether it was solved timing, system_size the size of the system and the time of each stage 
r = s.calculate()
print(r['reactions']['LC1']['N1'])                 # [Rx, Ry, Mz]
print(r['element_forces']['LC1']['E1']['i'])       # [N, V, M] at the start of the bar

docs.title: Running without a window: xdfem2d.workflows
docs.text:
The checks and the calculation that the application's Run and Design menu do, as functions that need no window:

validate_for_analysis(struc) -> list           # what stops the model from being analysed: [{'code', 'msg'}], empty when it can run
run_analysis(struc, scope="active" | "all", results=None) -> AnalysisOutcome
    # solves the model; "all" also solves the variants, the combinations across variants and the construction sequences.
    # given the previous results of a solved model, only the pending analysis cases are solved
run_design(struc, results, kind, prefs=None, combinations=None, sls_combinations=None) -> dict
    # designs the members of a kind and stores the outcome in `results`, where the design views read it.
    # kind: "concrete" | "bars" | "areas" | "crack" | "punching" | "steel" | "timber"
    # returns {'kind', 'designed', 'failing', 'combinations'}; raises ValueError for an unknown kind, no results, or no combination
available_combinations(struc, results) -> list  # the combination ids a design can use

The application's window calls the same functions, so the two cannot differ. Automatic EN 1990 combinations:

xdfem2d.combinations.auto_combinations(struc, types=("ULS",), replace=True) -> dict
    # types: any of "ULS", "SLS-K", "SLS-FR", "SLS-QP"; returns {'added', 'skipped', 'removed', 'errors', 'cases'}
    # replace=True first removes the combinations an earlier run generated (ids starting ULS:, ULS-E:, SLS-K:, SLS-FR:, SLS-QP:),
    # never one you named

docs.title: Editing and removing
docs.text: Nodes, elements, sections, materials, load cases, combinations, analysis cases and geometry objects have companion remove_* and rename_* methods, and so do loads (remove_point_loads, remove_distributed_loads, remove_area_load, the remove_*_temperature_load family) and springs (remove_node_spring, remove_element_spring, remove_area_spring, remove_line_element_spring). The load/temperature removes take a load_case_id="" that clears every case on the target, or one named case.

docs.title: Forgiving removal: delete_* and free_edge
docs.text:
The intent-level inverses of the create_*, pin and support layer, and what to reach for when undoing an edit:

delete_support(nodes)
    # unassign the support on a node / list of nodes
free_edge(object_id: str, edge)
    # free an edge (inverse of support_edge/pin_edge)
delete_area(object_id: str)
    # delete a region/line object (= remove_geo_object)
delete_load(target: str, load_case_id: str = '')
    # node / bar / area loads on a target
delete_temperature(target: str, load_case_id: str = '')
    # bar / triangle / quad / object
delete_spring(target: str)
    # node / element / area / line spring

Each is a forgiving wrapper over the low-level remove_*: removing what is not there is a no-op, so one delete_load('N1') clears whatever loads N1 carries without the caller first classifying the target. The low-level remove_* are the by-id/by-name primitives (used by the application); the delete_* and free_edge calls are the ones to use in a script.

docs.title: Variants, support sets and construction sequences
docs.text:
The variants and construction sequences of the application are plain objects of the engine, in xdfem2d.models: SupportSet, Variant, ConstructionSequence, ConstructionPhase, Operation, with OpAction (ADD, REMOVE) and OpTarget (ELEMENTS, SUPPORTS, LOADS).

add_support_set(support_set) -> object
add_variant(variant) -> object
add_construction_sequence(sequence) -> object
    # also keeps its analysis case of type 'Sequence'
derive_variant(
    variant, support_sets: Optional[dict] = None, filter_tri: bool = False) -> Structure2D
    # a new model for the variant; the original is untouched
with_active(active_elements) -> Structure2D
    # a copy with only those elements active
xdfem2d.workflows.run_sequence(struc, seq_id) -> dict                        # solve one construction sequence
xdfem2d.workflows.run_variant_combination(struc, terms, op, ...) -> dict     # combine variant results: terms are (variant_id, case_id, factor)
xdfem2d.phasing.resolve_phase_state(...)                                     # the state of a phase, replayed from its operations
xdfem2d.workflows.assign_stage(struc, element_ids, stage) -> int             # the `stage` of the elements, for phases that add a stage

A phase is a list of Operations, replayed from the top on top of the previous phase; see Construction sequences for what each one means. The cached state of a phase (its active elements, applied cases and case factors) is recalculated from its operations, which is what the Python export relies on.

docs.title: Section cuts
docs.text:
add_cut(id: str, x1: float, y1: float, x2: float, y2: float, name: str = '') -> Cut
remove_cut(cut_id: str)
rename_cut(old_id: str, new_id: str)

A Cut is a straight segment (x1,y1) -> (x2,y2) that reports the resultant of the internal forces crossing it — bars and areas, combined and separately — for one case (load case, analysis case, or LinearSum combination) at a time. Evaluation lives in the Qt-free xdfem2d.cuts module, not on Structure2D itself:

cut_result(struc, results, cut, case, ref_point=None) -> dict
    # {'domain', 'bars': [...], 'areas': [...],
    #  'resultant': {'bars', 'areas', 'total'}, 'reason'}
    # bars/areas per-crossing detail; resultant['total'] is what a Results
    # panel shows. ref_point defaults to the cut's own midpoint.
cut_distribution(cutres, n=101) -> dict
    # {'s', 'fields', 'markers'} — sampled per-length area fields (piecewise
    # constant per triangle) plus bar crossings as point markers, for
    # plotting the distribution along the cut.
cuts_report(struc, results, cases, ref_point=None) -> list[dict]
    # one row per (cut, case): cut_id, cut_name, case, total_<N|V|M or
    # V|Mb|Mt>, reason — every cut against every case id, for CSV export.
cut_bar_resultant(struc, results, cut, case, ref_point=None) -> dict
cut_area_resultant(struc, results, cut, case, ref_point=None) -> dict
    # the two halves cut_result sums; called directly only if you want one
    # side in isolation.
find_bar_crossings(struc, cut) -> list[dict]        # {elem_id, a, s, x, y}
find_triangle_crossings(struc, cut) -> list[dict]    # {tri_id, s0, s1, p0, p1}
    # pure geometry — every bar/triangle the cut crosses, no results needed.

Resultant keys are N, V, M for a plane cut (axial along the cut's normal, shear along its tangent, in-plane moment about ref_point) or V, Mb, Mt for a plate cut (transverse shear, bending and twisting moment — the same mn/mnt split slab results already use). struc must be the compiled model (geo_expand.expand_geometry's output) when the model has geometry objects, matching whatever handle the GUI already keeps for tri-field plotting — cuts are evaluated against the solved mesh, not the editable objects.

A cut has a tangent t = (P2 − P1)/L and a normal n, t rotated +90° (to the left of the drawing direction). The forces reported are those the positive side (the side n points to) exerts on the negative side, and moments are taken about the cut's midpoint unless ref_point is given. Bars crossing the cut contribute their internal forces at the crossing, rotated to the cut's axes (point contributions); areas contribute the line integral of the stress field along the part of the cut inside each triangle (per-length contributions). Bars and areas are always computed separately and then summed.

docs.title: Member buckling (steel EC3 and timber EC5)
docs.text:
The steel and timber member checks work on physical members — chains of collinear bars grouped by xdfem2d.member_utils.identify_members(struc). Each BarElement carries the per-member buckling-length factors used by the design (buckling length = K × physical-member length); leave them None to inherit the global default from the design preferences:

BarElement.sd_ky   # K for flexural buckling about y (major / in-plane)
BarElement.sd_kz   # K for flexural buckling about z (minor / out-of-plane)
BarElement.sd_klt  # K for the lateral-torsional length
BarElement.sd_ltb  # bool: member susceptible to lateral-torsional buckling

Free-end (cantilever) detection helpers in xdfem2d.member_utils:

member_free_ends(struc, member)   -> (free_i, free_j)   # a truly-free end node
member_has_free_end(struc, member) -> bool
cantilever_k_for(struc, member, prefs) -> float | None  # auto K (Ky, Kz) or None

A node is a free end when nothing is attached to it (a single incident bar and no support, node spring, triangle or constraint). When enabled (cantilever_auto, default on), such members take cantilever_k (default 2.0) for sd_ky/sd_kz unless an explicit value is set.

docs.title: Design reports (calculation trace)
docs.text:
Every design routine can, with with_reports=True, attach a full step-by-step calculation report for the governing case of each member / section / column / triangle. The report content — clause, symbolic expression, LaTeX and numeric substitution — is produced by eurocodepy through an optional trace (eurocodepy.calc_report.CalcReport): the check computes exactly as before and the trace only records what was computed, so the reported numbers are, by construction, the ones used. The app only gathers and renders; it never re-derives formulas.

The EC2 procedures are owned by eurocodepy composites, each taking an input dataclass and an optional trace:

eurocode2_shear_check(ShearInput, v_ed, trace=None)      # §6.2 shear
eurocode2_punching_check(PunchInput, n_ed, …, trace=None) # §6.4 / :2023 §8.4
eurocode2_membrane_check(MembraneInput, trace=None)       # §6.109 membrane (areas)
eurocode2_slab_check(SlabInput, trace=None)               # §6.1 slab flexure (areas)
calc_torsion(…, trace=None)                               # §6.3 grillage torsion
calc_asl_nm(…, trace=None)                                # §6.1 M-N flexure

Gathering and rendering live in xdfem2d.design_report (Qt-free):

build_reports(struc, results, material, prefs=None, combinations=None) -> {id: report}
    # material: "steel" | "timber" | "concrete" | "concrete_area" | "punching"
filter_reports(reports, material, struc,
               selected_bars=None, selected_nodes=None, selected_tris=None)
reports_from(design_output) -> {id: report}      # normalise a routine's output
report_base_id(report) -> str                    # member/element/column/triangle id
per_combination_key(base_id, combo) / merge_per_combination({combo: {id: report}})
render_html(reports, title)   / render_markdown(...) / render_pdf(...) / render_docx(...)
write_markdown_bundle(reports, md_path, title)   # .md + <stem>_assets/ figures
section_figure_png(geom)      # cross-section drawing (rect / I / RHS / SHS / CHS)
pandoc_available()            # gates the native editable-OMML Word route
EXPECTED_SCHEMA / schema_mismatches(reports)     # report-schema version guard

A report dict has the shape {schema_version, title, meta, sections:[{title, steps:[{symbol, value, unit, clause, expr, latex, subst, note, ok}]}]}. The GUI consumes these through the Design → Design report… side panel.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: After running an analysis (F5), review results on the canvas, in the Results tab, and through the exports.

docs.title: View modes
docs.text:
Switch with the View dropdown, View → View mode, or the accelerators Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+6 and Ctrl+9 (the modes without one are reached from the dropdown). The dropdown lists only the modes that have data for the current model, so entries appear and disappear as you mesh, run, or design.

Mode Shortcut Shows Case selector Structure Ctrl+1 Geometry only load cases Loads Ctrl+2 Applied loads load cases Fields A field expression mapped over the model — Modal shapes Ctrl+3 Mode shapes modal cases Deformed shape Ctrl+4 Cubic-Hermite deflected shape analysis cases / sequences / combinations Displacements Nodal-displacement diagram along members analysis cases / sequences / combinations Reactions Ctrl+5 Support reaction arrows + sum analysis cases / sequences / combinations Constraint forces Force each constraint applies at its nodes analysis cases / sequences / combinations Force diagrams Ctrl+6 the diagram along the members of the quantity chosen in the Diagram selector: bending moment M, shear force V, axial force N (torsion T in a plate model) analysis cases / sequences / combinations Stress (σ) / Forces Triangle field: plane membrane stresses σx, σy, τxy, σ1, σ2, von Mises (kN/m²); plate slab forces mx, my, mxy, m1, m2, vx, vy and Wood–Armer (W-A) design moments (kNm/m) analysis cases / sequences / combinations Reinforcement (As) Ctrl+9 EC2 bar flexural reinforcement envelope design results Shear reinf. (Asw) EC2 bar shear reinforcement design results Shell reinf. (As) EC2 membrane reinforcement of triangles design results Crack width (wk) EC2 SLS crack-width verification design results Steel design, Timber design, Column design the utilisation of each member, colour-coded design results

The Fields mode requires a compiled mesh; the stress mode needs triangle elements; the reinforcement and crack modes need the matching design run. The analysed mesh itself is inspected via the Mesh overlay checkbox on the Structure view (Display panel ▸ Model tab), not a separate view mode. The Constraint forces mode appears only when the model has constraints.

Only modes with available data are enabled. Use the Case dropdown to pick which analysis case, sequence, or combination to display; for Modal, choose the Mode number. When a construction sequence is selected, a phase selector appears in the toolbar to navigate phase by phase. A Cumulative / Increment toggle controls whether displacements show the running total (Σ Δu) or only the current phase's increment (Δu); forces and reactions always reflect the accumulated state up to the selected phase.

docs.title: What each view shows in each domain
docs.text:
The views are the same in both domains; the quantities they show follow the degrees of freedom (ux, uy, θz in a plane model, w, θx, θy in a plate model).

View Plane Plate Deformed shape, Displacements the deflected shape in the plane; ux, uy, rz the out-of-plane deflection w and the rotations θx, θy Modal shapes in-plane modes vertical (out-of-plane) modes Reactions Rx, Ry, Mz per support, and their sums Rz, Mx, My per support Bending moment, Shear force M, V diagrams along bars M, V diagrams along grid members Axial force / Torsion Axial force N Torsion T: the view reads Torsion in a plate model Triangle and quad field Stress σx, σy, τxy, σ1, σ2, von Mises (kN/m²) Forces mx, my, mxy, m1, m2, vx, vy (kNm/m, kN/m) and the Wood–Armer (W-A) design moments Reinforcement (As), Shear reinf. (Asw) beams and columns grillage beams Shell reinf. (As) membrane (Wood/Baumann) reinforcement: As,x, As,y and the concrete stress σc the bending reinforcement of the slab, by face (Concrete: slabs and walls) Cuts N, V, M V, Mb, Mt

The title of the triangle field reads Stress in a plane model and Forces in a plate model, and the component selector lists the matching quantities. In a plane model a Forces (N=σ·t) checkbox converts the membrane stresses into forces per unit width — Nx, Ny, Nxy, N1, N2 in kN/m, each scaled by the triangle's own thickness (von Mises is omitted, having no force meaning). Plate results are already stress resultants, so no toggle appears there.

docs.title: Scale and undeformed reference
docs.text:
For deformed and diagram views, the Scale spin box sets the magnification. With Auto on, the result is fitted to about 10 % of the model span. In the deformed and modal views, an Undeformed structure checkbox toggles the reference geometry; support markers stay visible if their layer is enabled.

The look of each result view — colour map, banded vs. continuous fill, levels, contour lines, smoothing and colour-scale range for the field views, and the sign colours, opacity, line width and value labels for the M/V/N diagrams and the utilisation-ratio colouring — is set live in the Style tab of the Display panel for the current session. Set as default there, or Preferences ▸ Display, keeps it for the next launches (see Preferences).

docs.title: Reactions and equilibrium
docs.text:
The Reactions view draws an arrow per support and a corner box with the Σ reactions (ΣRx, ΣRy, ΣMz) — the total support force, which doubles as an equilibrium check against the applied loads. In a plate model each support shows Rz, Mx and My instead.

Spring reactions are drawn too: node springs as labelled arrows, and element (Winkler) foundation springs as a distributed reaction diagram with numeric values (reaction per unit length) at each element end. The colour shows the state — blue for compression (the spring pushes the structure) and red for tension (it pulls). For a NonLinear case the unilateral state is respected: sections where a tension-/compression-only spring is inactive show zero reaction (e.g. the lifted part of a footing carries no soil reaction), instead of the spurious tension a Linear case would draw.

docs.title: Constraint forces
docs.text:
For a model with constraints, the Constraint forces view draws — in magenta — the force each constraint applies at the nodes it couples: an arrow for Fx and Fy and a label for the moment Mz. This is the force you could apply instead of the constraint to get the same displacements: for a rigid link it is the force and moment transmitted through the link; for an equal-DOF tie it is the internal tie force (equal and opposite between the tied nodes).

The value is recovered as the residual of the physical stiffness at the coupled DOFs — the same method used for support reactions — so it is well-conditioned despite the penalty. The same numbers appear in the Constraint forces table of the Results report and the Excel export (only when constraints exist).

docs.title: Cuts
docs.text:
A cut is a straight segment you draw across the model to read the resultant of the internal forces crossing it — bars and areas, combined and separately — for one case or combination at a time. Unlike everything else on this page, a cut needs no re-run when added, renamed or moved: it is a report definition over whatever is already solved.

Analysis → Cuts → Add cut… picks two points on the canvas (any two points, not necessarily nodes) and opens a small dialog for the cut's Name — the only field you set; there is no separate id to manage, and two cuts cannot share a name. Manage cuts… lists every cut with its endpoints for add/edit/delete. Cuts are drawn on the canvas as a plain segment with its name and a short arrow along the normal — the side the arrow points to is the positive side: results are reported as what the positive side exerts on the negative side.

Analysis → Cuts → Results… opens the results side panel: pick a cut and a case/combination, and a table shows the resultant in three rows — Bars, Areas, Total — with columns N, V, M for a plane cut (axial along the cut's normal, shear along its tangent, in-plane moment about the cut's midpoint) or V, Mb, Mt for a plate cut (transverse shear, bending and twisting moment — the same mn/mnt split the triangle stress view uses). Below the table, a small plot shows the chosen per-length area field along the cut, with a marker at every point a bar crosses it. Export CSV… writes the same table for the selected case, or every case at once, to a spreadsheet-ready file.

Sign conventions. A cut has a tangent t, from its first point to its second, and a normal n, t turned +90° (to the left of the drawing direction). What is reported is what the positive side (the side n points to) exerts on the negative side. Moments are taken about the cut's midpoint. Bars crossing the cut contribute their internal forces at the crossing, rotated to the cut's axes, as point contributions. Areas contribute the integral of their stress field along the part of the cut inside each triangle, as contributions per unit length. Bars and areas are always computed separately and then added for the total.

If you are scripting against a model instead of using the application, the cuts are in Python API: results and design (xdfem2d.cuts.cut_result and friends).

docs.title: The Results report
docs.text:
The Results tab (Analysis → Results) prints a full text report:

  • per load case, combination and analysis case: displacements, reactions (with a Σ row), and element end-forces;
  • element span extremes (|N|max, |V|max, M⁺, M⁻);
  • modal tables with frequency, period, effective mass per mode and the running cumulative mass (ΣX%, ΣY%).

docs.title: Exports
docs.text:
• Write Report… (Ctrl+Shift+W) — a PDF, Word, or Excel report; pick the format and the content (tables, drawings, result views per case).
  • Write Tables to Excel… (Ctrl+Shift+T) — one-click workbook of the model and result tables (Displacements, Reactions, Constraint forces, Element forces, Span extremes, Reaction sums, Modal). The Constraint-forces sheet appears only when the model has constraints.

See Exporting.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
A Scene is a named, saved subset of the model — a chosen set of nodes, elements (bars, triangles, quads) and geometry objects. While a scene is active, the canvas behaves as if only those members exist: rendering, hit-testing, window selection, viewport-fit, and the loads/diagrams/ reactions overlays are all confined to the scene.

Scenes are saved inside the .x2d file, and each remembers its own zoom.

docs.title: Switching scenes
docs.text: Use the Scene menu or the Scene dropdown in the tool bar. Full model shows everything; selecting a scene confines the view to its members and restores that scene's saved zoom.

docs.title: Creating and editing
docs.text:
From the Scene menu:

  • New scene from selection… — select nodes/elements, then create a named scene from them.
  • Add selection to scene ▸ — add the current selection to a chosen scene. This is typically done from Full model, where you can freely select objects outside any scene.
  • Remove selection from scene — drop the current selection from the active scene.
  • Update scene to selection — replace the active scene's members with the current selection.
  • Rename scene… / Delete scene.

docs.title: Behaviour with edits
docs.text:
• New geometry created while a scene is active (add node/element, paste) joins the active scene so it stays visible.
  • Deleting geometry removes it from all scenes automatically; undo/redo keep scenes consistent with the model.

docs.title: Scripting with the engine
docs.text:
The calculation engine, xdfem2d, is a Python library that needs no interface: it builds a model, solves it and gives back numbers. Everything the application does with a model can be done from a script, and a model written by a script can be opened in the application (and the other way round: the application exports its models as scripts).

pip install xdfem2d

The engine needs Python 3.12 or newer, and uses numpy, scipy and eurocodepy. It is distributed under the LGPLv3.

docs.title: A first script
docs.text:
A simply supported beam of 5 m with 10 kN/m:

from xdfem2d import Structure2D

s = Structure2D(domain='plane')
s.add_material('C30', elastic_modulus=30e6, unit_weight=25.0)
s.add_section('S1', material_name='C30', b=0.3, h=0.6)
s.add_node('N1', 0.0, 0.0)
s.add_node('N2', 5.0, 0.0)
s.add_bar_element('E1', node_i='N1', node_j='N2', section_name='S1')
s.add_support('PIN', ux=True, uy=True)
s.add_support('ROLLER', uy=True)
s.assign_support('N1', 'PIN')
s.assign_support('N2', 'ROLLER')
s.add_load_case('LC1', self_weight_factor=0.0)
s.add_distributed_load('E1', 'LC1', fye=-10.0, fyd=-10.0)   # 10 kN/m downward
r = s.calculate()
print(r['reactions']['LC1']['N1'])                          # [Rx, Ry, Mz]: Ry = 25 kN
s.save('beam.x2d')                                          # opens in the application

The same model with the shortcuts (create_*), which have sensible defaults and fewer arguments:

s = Structure2D(domain='plane')
n = s.create_node_list([0, 0, 5, 0])
sec = s.create_rc_section('B30x60', 0.30, 0.60)
s.create_bar_element(sec, n[0], n[1])
s.pin(n[0]); s.roller(n[1])
s.create_uniform_load(s.bar_elements[0], 'LC1', 10.0)    # 10 kN/m downward
r = s.calculate()

The reference for every call is in the three pages of the Python API: building a model, loads and analysis and results and design, and the complete list of calls with their full signatures. Each call also has a docstring: help(Structure2D.add_section). The recipes, short and with one task each, are the Recipes.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
These apply to every call of the API.

  • Units are metres, kN, kN·m and kN/m². Mass is in tonnes. Angles are in degrees where an angle is named.
  • A model has a domain, fixed for its life: plane (frames and walls: ux, uy, θz) or plate (slabs and grillages: w, θx, θy). The three degrees of freedom of a node keep the same positions in both, only their meaning changes. In a plate model the aliases fz, mx, my (loads), w, tx, ty (supports) and kz, ktx, kty (springs) fill the same slots as fx, fy, mz, ux, uy, tz and kx, ky, kt. See Domains.
  • Signs. A load takes a positive value in the direction of the axis, so gravity is negative.
  • create_* and add_*. Most things can be built two ways. A create_* shortcut takes a magnitude or a name, has sensible defaults, and where it makes sense gets or creates (two calls for the same concrete class give one material). Prefer it. The add_* call it forwards to spells every field out: use it when a shortcut cannot say what you need (a load in a local frame with both components, a trapezoidal axial load). Each page of the API lists the shortcuts and the fundamental calls of a topic together.
  • Ids. A create_* call gives an id when you do not: "1", "2" for nodes, "B1" for bars, "T1" and "Q1" for triangles and quads, "LC1" for load cases, "AC1" for analysis cases. Element ids are unique across kinds. Where a call takes a node, a section or an element, it accepts the object another call returned or its id as text.
  • Geometry object, surface object and region all mean an item of geometry_objects (a rectangle, a polygon, a segment, …), discretised into bars, triangles or quads when the model is solved. The canonical name is geometry object.
  • Errors. A call that cannot do what it says raises, and changes nothing. A model that cannot be analysed is reported by check_references(), domain_problems() and xdfem2d.workflows.validate_for_analysis(struc). The removal calls (delete_*) are forgiving: removing what is not there does nothing.

docs.title: Names and aliases
docs.text:
Every name below still works as it always has, and none is deprecated: they are permanent aliases.

Still works Canonical name add_rc_section create_rc_section same signature add_steel_section create_steel_section same signature add_panel, create_panel create_polygon same signature add_geo_line add_geo_segment add_geo_polyline add_geo_multisegment add_geo_surface add_geo_polygon the keyword tri_section_name= section_name= on add_geo_rectangle and add_geo_polygon; the stored attribute and the file keep the old name the keywords element_id=, delta_t_uniform=, delta_t_gradient= bar_id=, dt_uniform=, dt_gradient= on add_temperature_load

The add_* calls of the fundamental layer (add_material, add_section, add_node, add_bar_element, add_tri_element, add_quad_element, and every other add_* of loads, supports and cases) are not aliases: the create_* shortcuts forward to them.

Six calls were renamed outright, with no alias: add_bar_load, add_bar_point_load, add_node_load, add_pressure, add_self_weight and add_temperature are now create_uniform_load (for the first and the fourth), create_bar_point_load, create_node_load, create_self_weight and create_temperature.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The examples/ folder of the repository has runnable scripts, each checked against a closed-form solution where one exists: example.py (a simply supported beam), example-slab.py, example-slab-mitc3.py, example-slab-quad.py, example-grillage.py and example-grillage-cantilever.py for plate models, example-cuts.py for section cuts and example-sequences.x2d for a construction sequence.

docs.title: From the application
docs.text:
• File ▸ Export… with the file type Python script writes the open model as a commented script that rebuilds it. See Exporting.
  • The Script editor (File ▸ Script editor…) runs a script against the open model.
  • The files the engine reads and writes, .x2d and .json, are described on File Formats and JSON data structure.
  • The Assistant, the Agent and the MCP server drive the same model through a short command language, without a script.

docs.title: Supports, springs and constraints
docs.text: Three ways to restrain a model, the same in mechanism in both domains. What differs is what the degrees of freedom mean: ux, uy, θz in a plane model, w, θx, θy in a plate model. Each section below says it for both.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text:
Supports restrain node degrees of freedom — ux, uy, θz in a plane model, w, θx, θy in a plate model (see Domains). Each restraint combination has a canonical name, so the same boundary condition is called the same thing whether it was drawn or written by script, and the canvas draws an expressive glyph per family. The name depends on the domain:

Restraints Plane name Plate name all three FIXED CLAMPED two translations / w only PIN SIMPLE one only ROLLER-X / ROLLER-Y SYM-X / SYM-Y translation + one rotation GUIDED-X / GUIDED-Y CLAMP-X / CLAMP-Y rotation(s), free to move BLOCK BLOCK

The symbols drawn for each family, and the quick presets of the support dialog, are described for each domain in Plane models and Plate models.

Assign supports on the Supports sub-tab or via the node editor. The on-canvas legend names each colour with its canonical family (the -X/-Y variants share one entry). With Colour by on Sections or Materials in the Display panel, a second key — the sections or materials in use — is drawn lower right.

docs.title: Springs
docs.text:
• Node springs — a stiffness per degree of freedom at a node.
  • Element springs — a Winkler elastic foundation along an element, per unit length.
  • Area springs (plate only) — a Winkler foundation under a slab, kz per unit area (a slab on grade). See Plate models.
Plane Plate Node spring Kx, Ky (translation), Kt (rotation) kz (transverse), ktx, kty (rotations) Element spring Kx, Ky, in global or local axes only the transverse (w) stiffness acts Unilateral mode the translational components the transverse component

A structure may be supported by springs alone (no classic supports), as long as the springs restrain enough degrees of freedom to prevent rigid-body motion.

docs.title: Unilateral (tension-/compression-only) springs
docs.text:
Each translational component of a node or element spring (in a plate model, the transverse one) has a behaviour mode:

Mode Acts when… Typical use both (default) always — resists in both directions ordinary elastic spring compression the spring is compressed (node moves in the −axis direction) soil under a footing, gap/contact support tension the spring is stretched (node moves in the +axis direction) tie / anchor that only pulls

Set the mode per component (Kx/Ky for global axes, axial/transverse for an element spring in local axes) in the spring dialog, the node/element editor, or the bulk-edit dialog. Rotational stiffness Kt is always bilateral.

Only NonLinear cases honour the mode

Tension-/compression-only behaviour is applied only by a NonLinear analysis case. In Linear (and every other) case the spring acts bilaterally, exactly as before. So model the unilateral effect by running a NonLinear case.

Sign convention: for a node spring the component direction is the global axis (or, for an element spring in local axes, the element's axial / transverse direction). "tension" is active when the displacement projected on that direction is positive; "compression" when it is negative. Element-spring activation is evaluated per end-node, consistent with the lumped foundation model.

Modelling a footing on soil (uplift)

Give the base nodes/elements compression-only springs and remove any rigid vertical supports at those nodes (a rigid support in parallel with a spring fixes the DOF and makes the spring inert). Keep a minimal horizontal restraint to prevent rigid-body motion, then solve with a NonLinear case: the springs that go into tension deactivate and that part of the footing lifts.

docs.title: Constraints (multi-point)
docs.text:
Supports and springs act on one degree of freedom at a time. A constraint instead couples several DOFs — of different nodes — through a linear equation. Three kinds are available, all built from the same underlying form Σ cᵢ·dofᵢ = value:

Kind What it does Rigid link A master node and one or more slave nodes move as one rigid body: each slave follows the master's two translations and rotation (ux_s = ux_m − Δy·θ_m, uy_s = uy_m + Δx·θ_m, θ_s = θ_m). Use it for rigid offsets and eccentric connections. Equal DOF A set of nodes shares the same value of one or more components (ux, uy, θz) — e.g. tying several nodes to the same horizontal displacement. Equation (advanced) The raw linear form: a list of (node, component, coefficient) terms and a right-hand-side value.

In a plate model the three degrees of freedom of a node are w, θx, θy. Equal DOF and Equation act on them the same way. A rigid link does not: its equations are the kinematics of a rigid body in the plane (ux, uy, θz), so use it in plane models.

Create constraints on the Constraints sub-tab (Geometry), or from Structure ▸ Constraints ▸ Add constraint (also under Structure ▸ Nodes). The Add constraint tool lets you click the nodes to tie on the canvas — each picked node is highlighted — and finishes when you double-click the last node, which opens the editor pre-filled with those nodes. Press Esc to leave the mode. The dialog previews the resulting equation(s) before you save, and gives a default name per kind (Rigid1, Equal1, Constraint1, …).

How constraints are imposed (penalty)

Constraints are enforced by penalty: each equation adds a very stiff term to the stiffness matrix. This is robust and works across all analysis types (Linear, NonLinear, P-Delta, Modal, Spectrum), but it is approximate — results satisfy the constraint to about 1 part in 10⁶, with a tiny residual reaction. An exact master–slave formulation is planned for a future version.

The model check flags common mistakes: a constraint referencing a missing node, a rigid link whose master is also a slave, two rigid links forming a cycle, a tied DOF that a support already restrains, and a constraint on θz at a node with no rotational DOF (CST-only).

See Results ▸ Constraint forces for the force each constraint transmits.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: A field is a named spatial expression — a formula in x and y — that can drive a value which varies across the model instead of a single constant. The main use is a Winkler foundation modulus that changes along a member: assign a field as an element spring's stiffness and the value is evaluated at each generated bar's midpoint. Define fields in Structure ▸ Fields, and preview one over the model with the Fields view mode.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
File → New from Template… (Ctrl+T) generates a ready-made model. Pick a Category and then a Type, set the geometry parameters and the common material/section properties, and watch the live preview update as you type; click OK to draw the structure onto the canvas.

The dialog is organised into three titled, consistently indented boxes — Geometry, Material and Section — followed by the live preview. Each box adjusts its height to the fields the current type needs.

The dialog opens with the settings of its last use (accepted with OK) in the current session; they are not kept after closing the application. The Mesh element of walls and slabs starts as Quadrilateral.

docs.title: Available templates
docs.text:
Templates are grouped into six families, in this order: Beams & Frames, Slabs, Walls, Trusses, Grillages, Arches. Beams & Frames, Walls, Trusses and Arches build plane models; Slabs and Grillages build plate models (out-of-plane bending — see Plate models).

Beams & Frames

Type Parameters Description Continuous beam spans, span length, left / intermediate / right support Multi-span beam with an independent support condition at each position Portal span, height Single-bay, single-storey, fixed bases Rectangular bays, floors, bay width, floor height Multi-bay, multi-storey, fixed bases

The continuous beam replaces the old single-span beam types: pick the support at the left end, the intermediate supports and the right end — each Free, Pin (canonical PIN) or Fixed (canonical FIXED). The intermediate combo is disabled for a single span. The span length accepts a single value (uniform spans) or a comma-separated list such as 6, 5, 4 for variable spans; a list overrides the number of spans.

Both bay width and floor height (frames) accept a single value or a comma-separated list (e.g. 5, 4, 6 widths, 4, 3, 3 heights) for variable spacing; a list overrides the corresponding bays / floors count. In parametric-object mode the rectangular frame emits one object per column (spanning the full height) and one object per floor beam (spanning the full length), welded to the joint nodes.

Trusses

Trusses use the same shaped bar section as beams and frames (not just an area).

Type Parameters Description King post panels, span, depth King-post truss; an odd panel count inverts the diagonals so it differs from the next even count Warren panels, span, depth Triangulated, no verticals (symmetric for any panel count) Howe panels, span, depth Verticals + diagonals sloping to centre; even panels only (odd would be asymmetric) Pratt panels, span, depth Verticals + diagonals (tension under gravity); even panels only Long (X-braced) panels, span, depth Howe + Pratt superimposed — a full X of diagonals in every panel (statically indeterminate); symmetric for any panel count Town lattice span, depth, diagonal pitch, lattice span k Dense crossing lattice: diagonals jump k panels, spaced by the pitch (rounded to fit the span), joined only at the chords, with end posts

For Howe and Pratt the panel spinbox steps in twos (a single diagonal per panel cannot be mirror-symmetric with an odd count). Warren and Long are symmetric for any count; King post keeps the full range and inverts its diagonals for an odd panel count. The Town lattice density is set by the diagonal pitch (target chord-node spacing, rounded so a whole number of panels fits the span) and the lattice span k (how many panels each diagonal jumps).

Arches

Type Parameters Description Parabolic (two-hinged) segments, span, rise Two-hinged parabolic arch

Walls

Type Parameters Description Wall panel width, height, mesh X/Y Rectangular plane-stress panel meshed in triangles, fixed along its base Deep beam width (span), height (depth), mesh X/Y Plane-stress panel supported at its two bottom corners (pin + roller) Wall + Frame bays, floors, bay width, floor height, wall width, wall mesh X, wall side Rectangular frame with a full-height shear wall at one end

Wall + Frame combines a rectangular frame with a plane-stress wall on the chosen wall side (Left / Right). The wall spans the full frame height and is meshed in modules aligned with the floor levels, so its interface nodes coincide with — and share — the frame's floor joints (the wall connects to the frame at every floor). It uses a single (concrete) material and a combined section giving both the frame bar dimensions (b, h) and the wall thickness / formulation. Bay width and floor height accept lists for variable spacing. Both frame bases and the wall base are fixed.

Every wall (and every slab) offers a Mesh element choice — Triangle or Quadrilateral — and an Element formulation whose options follow that choice: membrane triangles ES-FEM / Allman / CST or quads QM6 / Q4 for walls; plate triangles MITC3 / DKT or quads MITC4 / DKT4 for slabs.

Slabs (plate domain)

Type Parameters Description Rectangular slab Lx, Ly, mesh element/formulation, thickness, per-edge support Rectangular slab with an independent condition on each edge — Free, Pin (SIMPLE) or Fixed (CLAMPED), using the canonical plate support names Rib-stiffened Lx, Ly, mesh element/formulation, slab t, rib b/h Slab with edge beams (grillage ribs), resting on the corners Flat slab on columns bay Lx, Ly (value or list), column bays X/Y, max element size, thickness Slab carried only on a grid of columns (point W supports), no edge beams. Lx/Ly are the bay span — a single value (uniform bays) or a list like 6, 4, 6 for variable bays; columns land exactly on every bay line and each bay is meshed to the given max element size On grade (Winkler) Lx, Ly, mesh element/formulation, thickness, kz Slab on an elastic foundation (subgrade kz), the springs alone carry it Circular sector rmin, rmax, θ, max element size, thickness, per-edge support Circular slab sector with an independent condition on each edge — outer arc, inner arc and the two radial sides — each Free / Pin (SIMPLE) / Fixed (CLAMPED). rmin = 0 gives a solid sector (no inner arc), θ = 360 a full disc (no radial sides). The curved boundary is faceted and filled with a quality unstructured mesh at the given max element size

Grillages (plate domain — beam grids)

Type Parameters Description Beam grid Lx, Ly, bays X/Y, beam b/h Orthogonal grillage, simply supported on the perimeter Bridge deck span L, width W, girders, transverse stations, girder b/h, transverse b/h Longitudinal girders tied by transverse diaphragms, simply supported at the two abutments

A slab section is a thickness plus the chosen plate element (Triangle MITC3/DKT or Quadrilateral MITC4/DKT4); a grillage beam reuses the shaped bar section and gains a torsion constant J. All plate templates seed a self-weight load case; the slabs also carry a uniform area pressure pz.

docs.title: Material and Section
docs.text:
Below the Geometry box are two more, laid out in two columns each:

  • Material — pick a type (Concrete / Steel / Timber) and a grade (C25/30, S275, C24…), shown side by side. The preset sets E, γ and ν; fine-tune them later in the material editor.
  • Section — adapts to the family and material:
    • for beams, frames, arches and trusses, the bar section depends on the material type. Concrete and Timber show only b and h (with sensible defaults — concrete 0.30 × 0.50 m, timber 0.12 × 0.36 m). Steel shows only a rolled I-profile dropdown (HEA/HEB/HEM/IPE, IPE100 by default) whose dimensions define the section;
    • thickness t, the Mesh element (Triangle / Quadrilateral, default Quadrilateral) and the matching Element formulation for walls and slabs. The Circular sector is always meshed with triangles, so its mesh element is fixed, but its formulation (MITC3 / DKT) can be chosen;
    • a combined section (frame b/h + wall thickness / formulation) for Wall + Frame.

docs.title: Parametric objects (auto-meshed)
docs.text: For Beams & Frames, Arches, Walls and Slabs, a checkbox Create as parametric objects (auto-meshed) (checked by default for Slabs and Walls) makes the template emit geometry objects — lines / a polyline for the bar families, rectangles for walls (one per floor module in Wall + Frame), a rectangle/polygon for slabs — instead of explicit nodes and elements. The objects discretise into elements at solve time, so the model stays parametric and easy to re-mesh or edit. The wall's mesh divisions then set the target element size. Trusses have no single-object form and keep the explicit output.

docs.title: What every template includes
docs.text:
• A self-weight load case named SW with self-weight multiplier 1.0.
  • A Linear analysis case, also named SW, that applies it with factor 1.0.

So a template is ready to Run (F5) immediately and show its self-weight response. Add further load cases, analysis cases, and combinations as needed — see Loads and Analysis.
