docs.title: Variants & Construction Sequences
docs.text: Two related features study a structure under parallel scenarios and under a staged construction sequence. They share the support sets and the scenes, and each has its own side panel, opened from the Analysis menu: Support Sets…, Variants… and Construction Sequences…. (Variants and sequences also open from buttons in the toolbar.)

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
Variant Construction sequence What it is A parallel scenario: the same geometry with a subset of active elements and/or another set of supports A chain of phases in time: each phase adds and removes things How it is solved From scratch, independently of the others Incrementally: each phase inherits the locked-in forces of the previous ones State between them None A member built later does not attract load that was already resisted before it existed Use it to Compare alternatives, or one structure with different supports or loads Study how forces build up while a structure is built, propped and struck

Combining the results of variants with the same geometry is exact. Combining variants with different active geometry is only a comparison (a "what-if"): the mechanically correct way to treat added geometry is a construction sequence.

docs.title: Support sets
docs.text:
A support set is a named, reusable collection of node restraints, for example provisional supports used by a variant or by a construction phase. Define them in Analysis ▸ Support Sets…: a list of sets and, for the selected one, an editor of its nodes and the degrees of freedom each restrains (UX, UY, TZ in a plane model, W, θx, θy in a plate model). Nodes can be picked on the canvas or loaded from the selection.

A set replaces the base supports when it is applied: it lists all the supported nodes of that scenario, and a node that is not listed is free. A set can also carry springs, and those replace the base springs the same way.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
A variant is a what-if overlay on the working model: the same shared geometry, with a chosen subset of active elements and an optional support set. The base model is never changed; each variant is resolved into a derived structure only when it is solved.

Open Analysis ▸ Variants…. The panel lists the variants (New, Rename, Delete) and, for the selected one:

  • a Description;
  • the Support set to apply, with an Edit button that opens the Support Sets panel;
  • All elements: the variant keeps the full geometry and follows any change of the base model automatically. With it off, the Active elements list says which elements the variant has: Use selection and Remove selection take them from what is selected on the canvas. Selecting a variant draws its active elements in red;
  • Seed from the base model: on a new variant, copy all the loads, load cases, analysis cases and combinations of the base, so the variant has an action model of its own. Off, it starts clean. A variant that has none inherits the base model's.

Save variant stores the changes. Sync with base reconciles the variant with the current base model and shows what changed (a sync also runs when you select a variant or press Run). Export as .x2d… writes the variant's model as a file of its own.

Once variants exist, a variant selector appears in the toolbar (the base model and each variant). Picking one shows its model and results in the normal editors and views. To edit a variant's own loads, save it and then switch to it in the selector.

Variant combinations… opens a window that combines the results of several variants with the same arithmetic as a load combination: a list of variant × case × factor terms and an operation (LinearSum, Envelope, AbsSum or SRSS).

docs.title: Construction sequences
docs.text:
A construction sequence is an ordered chain of phases. Each phase adds and removes elements, supports and load cases, and the analysis is incremental: locked-in internal forces from earlier phases are carried forward, so a member built later does not attract load that was already resisted before it existed. Open Analysis ▸ Construction Sequences….

The panel lists the sequences (New, Rename, Delete) and, for the selected one, its Name, the stages of its elements and its phases.

docs.title: Stages and scenes
docs.text:
The elements of a phase come in groups, of two kinds:

  • Construction stages. Every bar has a stage number. Select elements, set the Stage and press Assign to to give them that stage. View all stages colours every element by its stage, with a legend.
  • Scenes. Named canvas selections (the Scene menu), used as groups of elements.

docs.title: Phases and their operations
docs.text:
The Phases table lists the phases in construction order, with an indicative Time (days) (the age of the phase; nothing reads it yet) and a Name. Selecting a phase previews it on the canvas. Add…, Edit… (or a double-click on the name), Remove, Duplicate, Up and Down manage them, and Save sequence stores the changes.

A phase is a list of operations, replayed from the top on top of the previous phase. Each is one row of the phase's Operations table, with these columns:

Column What it is Action Add or Remove. What Elements (a whole group), Supports (a whole support set, restraints and springs) or Loads (a whole load case). From, Group For elements: whether the group is a Stage or a Scene, and which one. There is no way to pick individual elements: an operation stays a statement such as "add stage 2". Release For supports: when removing one, redistribute its accumulated reaction onto the rest of the structure (see below). Factor For loads: a multiplier on the case in this phase, for example 0.5 for half a live load during an intermediate stage. Note Free text.

A stage group is read again from the elements' stage number each time the phase is replayed, so re-tagging elements later updates the phases that use it. A scene group is a snapshot of the scene's elements at the moment the operation was written; editing the phase offers to refresh it.

docs.title: Running a sequence
docs.text:
Sequences appear in the analysis cases drop-down in the toolbar, next to the normal cases. Select a sequence and press Run (F5) as usual. Each phase is solved incrementally and its results are stored. A phase selector in the toolbar then navigates phase by phase, for displacements, internal forces and reactions.

For displacements, the Cumulative Δu box (shown with the deformed and displacement views) chooses between the increment of the selected phase (Δu) and the running total up to and including it. It does not change what is solved, but the choice is kept with the sequence: it survives saving, opening and the Python export.

docs.title: Supports and release
docs.text:
A phase can apply a support set to install provisional supports such as props or shores. When a later phase removes that support set, the accumulated reaction is converted into an equivalent load on the rest of the structure, so the redistribution is captured. Clear Release on the operation to drop the reaction without redistributing it.

The same holds for a removed bar: its locked-in end forces are released onto the remaining structure. Removing a triangle or quad (a wall or a slab element), or a geometry object, does not redistribute what it carried: only its carried state is dropped, so the rest of the structure under-reports until that is added. Plan a sequence so that surfaces are built and not removed.

For a wall or slab the initial state of the surface elements is carried within one sequence; it always starts from zero at the first phase.

docs.title: Sequences in the analysis flow
docs.text:
Each sequence appears as an analysis case of type Sequence in the Analysis Cases panel, read-only. So:

  • sequences appear in the view drop-down with the normal cases and combinations (order: analysis cases, then sequences, then combinations);
  • the Analysis Cases panel has a Status column (solved / pending) for every case, sequences included;
  • sequences, and the variants, are written by the Python script export, so running the exported script rebuilds the model with all its phases and operations.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Short recipes for writing a model in code, in the order a model is built: each page is a task, divided by what it handles, and each of those by what you do with it: add, edit, remove. They use the shortcut calls (create_*, see Scripting with the engine) of a model, and every example on them is run by the test suite. The Assistant reads them too, when it builds a model.

  1. Materials and sections: concrete, steel and timber materials; bar and area sections; another section or material for what exists.
  2. Nodes and bars: nodes, bars, hinges at a bar end, ids.
  3. Slabs and walls: regions with create_polygon; their edges; their loads.
  4. Supports: pin, roller and fixed supports, on nodes and on edges.
  5. Springs: node springs, one-sided springs, plate springs.
  6. Loads: load cases; loads on nodes, bars and regions; self weight; temperature; settlement of a support.
  7. Analysis cases and combinations: linear, non-linear, mass, modal, spectrum; combinations and their types.

Two rules for every recipe. Read the id of what already exists (geometry tool) and write it as text: 'N2', 'B1'; do not guess an id. And a call that edits something that is not there raises an error and changes nothing.

docs.title: Analysis cases and combinations
docs.text:
Two different things, with two different lists of types:

  • An analysis case is one way of analysing the model. Its type (analysis_type) is one of 'Linear', 'NonLinear', 'Mass', 'Modal', 'Spectrum', 'GeometricNonlinear', 'Sequence'.
  • A load combination adds up results. Its type (combo_type) is one of 'LinearSum', 'Envelope', 'AbsSum', 'SRSS', 'NonLinearCombo'.

'LinearSum' and 'Envelope' are combination types: they are never an analysis_type.

docs.title: Analysis case: add a linear case from load cases
docs.text:
create_load_case already makes a linear analysis case with the same name. To combine several load cases with factors:

model.create_analysis_case('ULS', 'Linear', {'G': 1.35, 'Q': 1.5})

docs.title: Analysis case: add a non-linear case
docs.text:
Same coefficients, another type:

model.create_analysis_case('NL1', 'NonLinear', {'G': 1.0, 'W': 1.0})

docs.title: Analysis case: add a mass case, then a modal case, then a spectrum case
docs.text:
They chain: the modal case uses a mass case, and the spectrum case uses a modal case and a response spectrum.

model.create_analysis_case('MASS', 'Mass', {'G': 1.0, 'Q': 0.5})   # masses from G + 0.5 Q
model.create_analysis_case('MODAL', 'Modal', num_modes=8, modal_case_id='MASS')
model.create_analysis_case('SEISMIC-Y', 'Spectrum', modal_case_id='MODAL',
                           spectrum_id='EC8-A', direction='Y')      # direction 'X', 'Y' or 'XY'

The spectrum spectrum_id names must exist already (add_spectral_function).

docs.title: Analysis case: edit
docs.text:
Change an analysis case: rename it.

model.rename_analysis_case('ULS', 'ULS-1')

To change its factors, remove it and create it again with the new ones.

docs.title: Analysis case: remove
docs.text:
Delete an analysis case:

model.remove_analysis_case('NL1')

docs.title: Combination: add
docs.text:
model.create_load_combination('SLS-ALL', {'G': 1.0, 'Q': 1.0, 'W': 1.0})   # sum, the default type
model.create_load_combination('ENV1', {'G': 1.0, 'Q': 1.0, 'W': 1.0}, combo_type='Envelope')

The keys are case ids as text, or the case objects. "1.35 G + 1.5 Q" is {'G': 1.35, 'Q': 1.5}.

docs.title: Combination: add one around a non-linear case
docs.text:
'NonLinearCombo' wraps a single non-linear analysis case; it does not add:

model.create_analysis_case('NL2', 'NonLinear', {'W': 1.0})
model.create_load_combination('NLC1', {'NL2': 1.0}, combo_type='NonLinearCombo')

docs.title: Combination: edit
docs.text:
Change a combination: rename it.

model.rename_load_combination('SLS-ALL', 'SLS')

To change its factors, remove it and create it again.

docs.title: Combination: remove
docs.text:
Delete a combination:

model.remove_load_combination('ENV1')

docs.title: Analysis case: common mistakes
docs.text:
• create_analysis_case('X', 'LinearSum', ...) or 'Envelope' as an analysis type: those are combination types, use create_load_combination.
  • A load case or analysis case that does not exist yet: create it first.
  • A modal case without its mass case, or a spectrum case without its modal case.

docs.title: Loads
docs.text:
Every load belongs to a load case. Create the case, then put loads in it. Magnitudes are positive numbers; the direction gives the sign. The bar, node, region and case can each be given as the object a create_* call returned or as its id as text ('B1', 'N2', 'G'): the objects only exist in the reply that made them, the ids always do.

The same calls add a load to a model that already has some: nothing that is there changes. A load on a bar that is already loaded in that case adds to it.

Load Call Unit uniform, on a bar create_uniform_load(bar, case, value, 'down') kN/m trapezoidal, on a bar create_bar_distributed_load(bar, case, q_i=, q_j=) kN/m point load along a bar create_bar_point_load(bar, case, p, at=0.5) kN, at is the fraction of the span point load on a node create_node_load(node, case, p, 'down') kN pressure on a slab or wall region create_uniform_load(region, case, value, 'down') kN/m² self weight load_case option or create_self_weight(factor, case) temperature create_temperature(bar, uniform=, gradient=, load_case=) degrees settlement of a support create_support_settlement(node, case, uy=) m

There is no call to edit a load in place: to change one, delete it and create it again (delete_load). The headings below are one type of load each, with Add, Edit and Remove.

docs.title: Load case: add
docs.text:
A case has an id and, optionally, a type: 'permanent' (the default), 'live', 'wind', 'seismic' or 'temperature':

model.create_load_case('HLOAD', action_type='wind')
model.create_load_case('SW', self_weight_factor=1.0)      # a case that carries the self weight

A linear analysis case with the same name is created with it.

docs.title: Load case: edit
docs.text:
Change a load case: rename it.

model.rename_load_case('G', 'Permanent')

docs.title: Load case: remove
docs.text:
Delete a load case (with the loads in it):

model.remove_load_case('Q')

docs.title: Node load: add
docs.text:
model.create_node_load('N2', 'G', 20, 'down')                 # 20 kN
model.create_node_load('N2', 'G', 5, 'right')                 # 'left' / 'right' are horizontal

docs.title: Node load: edit
docs.text:
Change a nodal load: remove it and create it again with the changed value.

model.delete_load('N2', 'G')                                  # what N2 carries in case G
model.create_node_load('N2', 'G', 25, 'down')                 # the new value

docs.title: Node load: remove
docs.text:
Delete the loads on a node:

model.delete_load('N2', 'G')          # one case; '' (or no case) for every case

docs.title: Line load: add a uniform load
docs.text:
model.create_load_case('G')                         # permanent actions
model.create_uniform_load('B1', 'G', 10, 'down')    # 10 kN/m on bar B1, gravity

direction is 'down' or 'up' for gravity, and 'perp' or 'axial' for the bar's own axes. The bar is its id as text ('B1'), or the object create_bar_element returned when it is made in the same reply; a list loads several bars (['B1', 'B2']).

docs.title: Line load: add a load over part of a span
docs.text:
A line load covers a whole bar. For "10 kN/m over the second half" put a node where the load stops, so that the loaded part is a bar of its own, and load that bar only:

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(1.5, 0.0)       # where the load starts
n3 = model.create_node(3.0, 0.0)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)
second = model.create_bar_element(sec, n2, n3)
model.fix(n1)
model.create_load_case('Q')
model.create_uniform_load(second, 'Q', 10, 'down')    # the first half stays unloaded

docs.title: Line load: add a triangular or trapezoidal load
docs.text:
create_bar_distributed_load(bar, case, q_i=..., q_j=...) gives the value at each end of the bar, in kN/m. "Zero at the left end and 20 kN/m at the right end" is:

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.25, h=0.5)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(5.0, 0.0)
bar = model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)       # from n1 (left) to n2 (right)
model.pin(n1)
model.roller(n2, free='x')
model.create_load_case('Q')
model.create_bar_distributed_load(bar, 'Q', q_i=0, q_j=20, direction='down')

q_i is at the bar's first node, q_j at its second: the order of the nodes in create_bar_element decides which end is which.

docs.title: Line load: add a point load along a bar
docs.text:
model.create_bar_point_load('B1', 'G', 15, at=0.5, direction='down')  # at mid-span

A load in the middle of a bar is applied there; no extra node is needed. at is the fraction of the span from the bar's first node, so a load 2 m from the left support of a 7 m beam is at=2/7.

docs.title: Line load: edit
docs.text:
Change the value of a load on a bar: remove it and create it again.

model.delete_load('B1', 'G')                        # the loads on B1 in case G
model.create_uniform_load('B1', 'G', 15, 'down')    # the new value

docs.title: Line load: remove
docs.text:
Delete the loads on a bar:

model.delete_load('B1', 'G')          # the loads on B1 in case G ('' for every case)

docs.title: Area load: add
docs.text:
The region is the object create_polygon made (or its id):

model.create_load_case('Q')
model.create_uniform_load('L1', 'Q', 5, 'down')         # 5 kN/m²
model.create_edge_load('L1', 'top', 'Q', 8)             # kN/m along one edge

Edge names are as in Edges of a region in Slabs and walls.

docs.title: Area load: edit
docs.text:
Change the pressure on a region: remove it and create it again.

model.delete_load('L1', 'Q')
model.create_uniform_load('L1', 'Q', 6, 'down')

docs.title: Area load: remove
docs.text:
Delete the loads on a region:

model.delete_load('L1', 'Q')          # the region's loads in case Q

docs.title: Self weight: add
docs.text:
Part of the case itself:

model.create_load_case('SW', self_weight_factor=1.0)    # full self weight

or on an existing case: model.create_self_weight(1.0, 'SW').

docs.title: Self weight: edit
docs.text:
Change the self-weight factor of a case:

model.create_self_weight(0.5, 'SW')                     # half of it

docs.title: Self weight: remove
docs.text:
Take the self weight out of a case:

model.create_self_weight(0.0, 'SW')                     # none

docs.title: Temperature: add
docs.text:
A temperature action goes in a load case of its own. uniform is the change in degrees; gradient is the difference through the depth:

sec = model.create_steel_section('S1', 'IPE300', 'S275')
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(8.0, 0.0)
bar = model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)
model.fix([n1, n2])
model.create_load_case('T', action_type='temperature')
model.create_temperature(bar, uniform=30, load_case='T')    # a rise of 30 degrees

A list of bars takes the same temperature. With both ends fixed the bar cannot expand and takes an axial force instead.

docs.title: Temperature: edit
docs.text:
Change a temperature action: delete it and create it again with the changed value.

model.create_load_case('T', action_type='temperature')
model.delete_temperature('B2', 'T')
model.create_temperature('B2', uniform=20, load_case='T')

docs.title: Temperature: remove
docs.text:
Delete the temperature loads on a bar:

model.delete_temperature('B2', 'T')   # '' for every case

docs.title: Settlement: add
docs.text:
A settlement is an imposed displacement of a supported node, in a load case of its own. The sign is the axis: uy negative is downwards, ux positive is to the right. "The middle support settles 10 mm" is uy=-0.01 (metres):

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.6)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(6.0, 0.0)
n3 = model.create_node(12.0, 0.0)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n2, n3)
model.pin(n1)
model.roller([n2, n3], free='x')
model.create_load_case('SETTLE')                           # a case of its own
model.create_support_settlement(n2, 'SETTLE', uy=-0.01)    # 10 mm down at the middle support

docs.title: Settlement: edit
docs.text:
Change a settlement: set its displacement again.

for s in model.support_settlements:
    if s.node_id == 'N2':
        s.uy = -0.02                                       # now 20 mm

docs.title: Settlement: remove
docs.text:
Delete the settlement of a support:

model.support_settlements = [s for s in model.support_settlements if s.node_id != 'N2']

docs.title: Loads: combine several cases
docs.text:
Each case is loaded on its own; they are combined when the analysis is defined:

model.create_load_case('G')
model.create_load_case('Q')
model.create_uniform_load('B1', 'G', 10, 'down')
model.create_uniform_load('B1', 'Q', 5, 'down')
model.create_analysis_case('ULS', 'Linear', {'G': 1.35, 'Q': 1.5})     # 1.35 G + 1.5 Q

The keys are the case ids as text, or the load case objects create_load_case returned ({g: 1.35, q: 1.5}); both work.

create_load_case already makes a linear analysis case of the same name, so a single case needs nothing more. create_analysis_case(id, 'Linear', {case: factor}) combines several. create_load_combination('C1', {'G': 1.35, 'Q': 1.5}) is for the combinations used in the design checks. See Analysis cases and combinations.

docs.title: Loads: common mistakes
docs.text:
• A load on a case that does not exist: create it with create_load_case first.
  • A negative magnitude with 'down': it points up. Use 'up' instead.
  • A load on a bar that has not been created yet: the bar comes first.
  • A load on a bar id you did not see: bar ids follow the order of creation, so in a frame whose columns come first B1 is a column (see Ids in Nodes and bars).

docs.title: Materials and sections
docs.text: A material is not a section. A section is a material plus a cross-section (b x h, or a profile); bars use sections. There is no set_section() call: create the new section first, then point the element at it. Pointing a bar at a section name that was never created leaves it without a section.

docs.title: Material: add
docs.text:
To create only a material (for example "create the steel material S355"):

model.create_steel_material('S355')     # steel grade
model.create_rc_material('C25/30')      # concrete class
model.create_timber_material('C24')     # timber class

Each returns the material and is shared if it already exists. A material alone changes nothing in the model until a section uses it. Do not make up a section (or give a section the name of a grade) when the request is for a material.

docs.title: Material: edit (change the material)
docs.text:
Make a material, then change what the section points to; every bar using that section follows:

mat = model.create_rc_material('C25/30')        # concrete class, shared
model.sections['S1'].material_name = mat.name

For steel or timber use create_steel_material('S355') or create_timber_material('C24'). To change only the name: model.rename_material('C25/30', 'Concrete').

docs.title: Material: remove
docs.text:
Delete a material:

model.remove_material('C25/30')

It is refused while a section still uses the material.

docs.title: Section: add
docs.text:
The section makes its material too:

model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5, concrete='C30/37')    # b x h in metres
model.create_steel_section('S2', 'IPE300', grade='S355')          # a profile
model.create_timber_bar_section('S3', 0.1, 0.2, timber='C24')

Materials are shared: asking for the same concrete class twice does not duplicate it. The section must exist before the bar that uses it.

docs.title: Section: edit (change the section)
docs.text:
Change the section of an existing bar (give it another section): create the new one, then point the bar at it.

# 1. create the new section (it makes its material too)
model.create_rc_section('S2', b=0.3, h=0.6, concrete='C25/30')

# 2. point the existing bar at it
model.bar_elements_by_id['B1'].section_name = 'S2'

Several bars:

model.create_rc_section('S2', b=0.3, h=0.6, concrete='C25/30')
for bar_id in ('B1', 'B2', 'B3'):
    model.bar_elements_by_id[bar_id].section_name = 'S2'

A steel profile instead:

model.create_steel_section('S3', 'IPE300', grade='S355')
model.bar_elements_by_id['B1'].section_name = 'S3'

To rename a section (the bars that use it follow): model.rename_section('S1', 'Beam').

docs.title: Section: remove
docs.text:
Delete a section:

model.remove_section('S1')

It is refused while a bar still uses the section.

docs.title: Area section: add and edit
docs.text:
An area section is created with its material, then the elements are pointed at it.

model.create_area_section('A2', 'C25/30', thickness=0.25)
model.tri_elements_by_id['T1'].section_name = 'A2'
model.quad_elements_by_id['Q1'].section_name = 'A2'

To change only the material of an area section, as for bars: model.tri_sections['A1'].material_name = mat.name (and quad_sections).

The section of a slab or a wall made with create_polygon comes with the region: see Slabs and walls.

docs.title: Ids
docs.text: Ids are text ('B1', 'T1', 'Q1'). Read them with the geometry tool before changing anything; do not invent them.

docs.title: Nodes and bars
docs.text:
The order that always works: a section, the nodes, the bar that joins them, the supports. Keep what each create_* call returns and pass that on; do not look up what you just made. A call that takes a node or a bar accepts either the object or its id as text: model.pin(n1) and model.pin('N1') are the same.

  • In the same reply, use the objects the create_* calls returned.
  • In a later reply those variables no longer exist: use the id as text ('N1', 'B1'), read with the geometry tool. Do not guess an id: see Id below.

docs.title: Node: add
docs.text:
Create a new node with create_node. A node is (x, y) in metres; y is up. The call returns the node:

n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(7.0, 0.0)                         # 7 m to the right
row = [model.create_node(x, 0.0) for x in (0.0, 5.0, 10.0)]

docs.title: Node: edit
docs.text:
Move a node, or rename it. A node's coordinates are plain attributes; the bars on it follow:

model.nodes['N2'].x = 6.0
model.nodes['N2'].y = 1.5

To rename it (the bars that use it follow): model.rename_node('N2', 'A').

docs.title: Node: remove
docs.text:
Delete a node with remove_node:

model.remove_node('N3')       # a node, and everything hanging on it:
                              # its supports, loads and the bars that use it

Remove a bar first if the nodes should stay. Removing a node removes the bars attached to it.

docs.title: Bar: add a bar (a 7 m beam)
docs.text:
Create a new bar between two nodes, with a section:

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)    # section (it makes its material)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(7.0, 0.0)
bar = model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)           # section first, then the two nodes
model.pin(n1)                                         # supports: see the Supports tutorial
model.roller(n2, free='x')

The section must exist before the bar: create_bar_element('Sec', ...) with no section called Sec leaves the bar without one. Create it first (create_rc_section, create_steel_section), or read the names that exist with the geometry tool.

sec = model.create_steel_section('S2', 'IPE300', grade='S355')

docs.title: Bar: add a continuous beam
docs.text:
sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)
nodes = [model.create_node(x, 0.0) for x in (0.0, 5.0, 10.0, 15.0)]
for a, b in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
    model.create_bar_element(sec, a, b)
model.pin(nodes[0])
model.roller(nodes[1:], free='x')

pin, fix and roller take a node or a list of nodes.

docs.title: Bar: add a portal frame
docs.text:
sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)
a = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
b = model.create_node(0.0, 3.5)       # y is up
c = model.create_node(6.0, 3.5)
d = model.create_node(6.0, 0.0)
for i, j in ((a, b), (b, c), (c, d)):
    model.create_bar_element(sec, i, j)
model.fix([a, d])

docs.title: Bar: add a standard structure in one call
docs.text: For a beam, frame, truss, wall or slab of a standard kind, model.create_from_template(kind, **params) builds geometry and supports together; see the Templates page. Use the calls above for anything else, or to add to what is already there.

docs.title: Bar: edit
docs.text:
Change a bar: rename it, give it another section or material (see Materials and sections), or move its end nodes (see Node: edit). Do not index the model's dictionaries with numbers: model.nodes and model.bar_elements_by_id are dictionaries keyed by the id as text, not lists. model.nodes[0] is a KeyError.

# wrong: model.create_bar_element('S1', model.nodes[0], model.nodes[1])
# right: use the objects create_node returned, or the ids as text
bar = model.create_bar_element('S1', 'N1', 'N2')

To rename a bar: model.rename_bar_element('B1', 'Beam1'). To give it another section or material, see Sections: edit in Materials and sections.

docs.title: Bar: remove
docs.text:
Delete a bar with remove_element:

model.remove_element('B1')            # a bar; its nodes stay

docs.title: Hinge: add
docs.text:
A hinge is a property of the bar's end, not a support: hinge_i releases the moment at the bar's first node, hinge_j at its second. Use it for "a hinge at the start of the second span" or for a Gerber beam. Do not confuse it with model.pin(n), which is a support.

When the bar is created:

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(5.0, 0.0)
n3 = model.create_node(10.0, 0.0)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n2, n3, hinge_i=True)   # hinge at n2, on the second bar
model.pin([n1, n2, n3])

On a bar that already exists. Read the bar's nodes first (geometry tool) to know which end is which:

model.bar_elements_by_id['B2'].hinge_i = True     # releases the moment where B2 starts (N2)

Put the hinge on one of the two bars that meet at the node, not on both.

docs.title: Hinge: edit
docs.text:
To change which end of the bar has the hinge:

model.bar_elements_by_id['B2'].hinge_i = False
model.bar_elements_by_id['B2'].hinge_j = True

docs.title: Hinge: remove
docs.text:
Delete a hinge by setting the flag back:

model.bar_elements_by_id['B2'].hinge_i = False    # back to a rigid joint

docs.title: Id: bar and node ids are numbered in the order they are created
docs.text:
create_bar_element without id gives B1, B2, ... in the order of the calls, so in a frame whose columns are made first B1 is a column. Do not write an id you did not see. Keep the object the call returned, or give the bar an id of your own:

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(0.0, 4.0)
n3 = model.create_node(6.0, 4.0)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)                    # B1, a column
beam = model.create_bar_element(sec, n2, n3, id='BEAM')  # the one that will be loaded
model.create_load_case('G')
model.create_uniform_load(beam, 'G', 10, 'down')

If the request says "the bar", "that node" or "the support at N2", find the id with the geometry tool first. A wrong id raises an error and changes nothing.

docs.title: Slabs and walls
docs.text: A slab, a wall or a panel is one region: model.create_polygon(outline, thickness, material, id). The section and the mesh come with it; there is no section call to make first.

docs.title: Region: add a rectangle
docs.text:
An outline of two opposite corners, [x0, y0, x1, y1], is a rectangle:

model.create_polygon([0, 0, 4, 3], thickness=0.15, material='C30/37', id='S1')   # 4 m by 3 m

A slab 5 m by 6 m at (5, 1) is [5, 1, 10, 7]. The id is optional (Panel1, Panel2, ...); give one to refer to the region later.

docs.title: Region: add any polygon
docs.text:
Three or more (x, y) points:

model.create_polygon([(0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4), (3, 6), (0, 4)], thickness=0.2, id='S2')

A regular shape is not written out by hand: its corners are computed from the size that was asked. For a hexagon in a circle of diameter D, the radius is R = D / 2 and the corners are at R from the centre, every 60 degrees. math is already there: do not import it. The example is for a circle of 4 m, not for yours: put the diameter of the request in D.

D = 4.0                      # the diameter of the circle in the request
R = D / 2
corners = [(round(R * math.cos(math.radians(60 * k)), 3),
            round(R * math.sin(math.radians(60 * k)), 3)) for k in range(6)]
model.create_polygon(corners, thickness=0.18, material='C25/30', id='S3')

For a polygon of n sides use 360 / n instead of 60 and range(n). Never copy the numbers of an example into a request of another size.

docs.title: Region: add a standard slab or wall in one call
docs.text: For a rectangular slab or wall of the standard kinds, model.create_from_template('slab', Lx=6, Ly=6, thickness=0.22, ...) builds the region, the supports and the pressure together (see the Templates page).

docs.title: Region: edit
docs.text:
Change the thickness of a region. The thickness lives in the region's section, which has the region's id plus _sec. It is kept for triangles and for quads, so change both:

for sections in (model.tri_sections, model.quad_sections):
    sections['S1_sec'].thickness = 0.30

docs.title: Region: remove
docs.text:
Delete a region:

model.delete_area('S1')       # the region, with its supports and loads

docs.title: Edge: add supports
docs.text:
An edge is addressed by its index (0, 1, 2, ... in the order of the outline), by a side name ('bottom', 'right', 'top', 'left', on a rectangle), or 'all':

model.support_edge('S1', 'all', kind='pin')        # simply supported all round
model.support_edge('S1', 1, 'pin')                 # only edge 1
model.support_edge('S1', 3, 'pin')                 # and edge 3
model.support_edge('S1', 'bottom', 'fix')          # clamped along the bottom

kind is 'pin', 'fix', 'roller-x', 'roller-y', 'symm-x', 'symm-y' ('pin' is a simple support in a slab). If the user gives an edge number, use that number as the index. You do not need to mesh the region or look up any node first.

docs.title: Edge: edit
docs.text:
Change the support of an edge: support it again with the other kind:

model.support_edge('S1', 'bottom', 'pin')          # was 'fix'

docs.title: Edge: remove
docs.text:
Delete the support of an edge (free it):

model.free_edge('S1', 1)                           # edge 1 is free again

docs.title: Region load: add
docs.text:
model.create_load_case('Q')
model.create_uniform_load('S1', 'Q', 5, 'down')        # pressure, kN/m2
model.create_edge_load('S1', 'top', 'Q', 8)            # kN/m along one edge

See Loads, area loads, to change or remove them.

docs.title: Springs
docs.text: There is no create_spring. A spring on a node is model.add_node_spring. Stiffnesses are in kN/m (kNm/rad for kt). A node has one spring: a second call replaces it.

docs.title: Spring: add
docs.text:
model.add_node_spring('N2', kx=500.0)                    # 500 kN/m along x
model.add_node_spring('N2', kx=500.0, ky=200.0)          # and 200 kN/m along y
model.add_node_spring('N2', kt=1500.0)                   # rotational, kNm/rad

docs.title: Spring: add compression-only or tension-only
docs.text:
mode_x and mode_y are 'both' (the default), 'tension' or 'compression':

model.add_node_spring('N2', kx=500.0, mode_x='compression')   # acts only in compression

A one-sided spring only behaves so in a NonLinear analysis case; a linear case treats it as a two-sided spring. So a compression-only spring usually comes with a non-linear case:

model.create_load_case('SW')
model.create_analysis_case('NL1', 'NonLinear', {'SW': 1.0})

docs.title: Spring: add in a plate model (slabs, grillages)
docs.text:
Use kz (kN/m, vertical) and ktx, kty (kNm/rad):

model.add_node_spring('N2', kz=800.0)

docs.title: Spring: edit
docs.text:
Change the stiffness of a spring. The new call replaces the spring of the node:

model.add_node_spring('N2', kx=800.0)                    # was 500

docs.title: Spring: remove
docs.text:
Delete the spring of a node:

model.remove_node_spring('N2')

There are springs on elements and areas too (add_element_spring, add_area_spring) for a bar or a slab resting on an elastic foundation; model.delete_spring(target) removes the spring of a node, an element or an area.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text: How to hold a structure. Every call takes a node, or a list of nodes (the objects create_node returned, or ids as text such as 'N1'). Without a support the structure is a mechanism and cannot be solved.

docs.title: Support: add a pin, a roller or a fixed support (which call for which)
docs.text:
Add, or create, a support at a node with one call. Portuguese terms in brackets, as users write them.

Support Call Restrains Pin (hinged; apoio duplo, apoio fixo, articulado) model.pin(n) ux, uy. Rotation is free Roller (apoio simples, apoio móvel) model.roller(n, free='x') uy only; the node can slide in x Fixed (encastramento, apoio encastrado) model.fix(n) ux, uy and the rotation

A pin is not a fixed support: pin leaves the rotation free, fix restrains it. A pinned support is not a hinge in a bar: for that see Hinges in Nodes and bars.

docs.title: Support: add a simply supported beam (pin + roller)
docs.text:
Add a pin at one end and a roller at the other:

sec = model.create_rc_section('S1', b=0.3, h=0.5)
n1 = model.create_node(0.0, 0.0)
n2 = model.create_node(5.0, 0.0)
model.create_bar_element(sec, n1, n2)
model.pin(n1)                  # pin at one end
model.roller(n2, free='x')     # roller at the other, free to slide in x

free='y' makes the roller slide in y instead (it restrains ux).

docs.title: Support: add a cantilever (fix)
docs.text:
Add a fixed support (encastramento) at a node, the built-in end of a cantilever, with fix:

model.fix('N1')                # the other end stays free

docs.title: Support: add to several nodes at once
docs.text: model.pin(['N1', 'N2', 'N3'])

docs.title: Support: add in a plate model (slabs, grillages)
docs.text: There is no roller in a plate model. pin restrains the vertical displacement w only, fix restrains w and both rotations, symm(n, axis='x') is a symmetry support, and create_support(n, w=True, tx=True, ty=False) sets each degree of freedom.

docs.title: Support: add any other combination
docs.text: model.create_support(n, ux=True, uy=True, tz=False) restrains exactly the degrees of freedom set to True.

docs.title: Support: edit (replace one)
docs.text:
Change the support of a node, for example from a pin to a fixed support. A node has one support: the new call replaces the old one.

model.fix('N1')                # was a pin

docs.title: Support: remove
docs.text:
Delete the support of a node:

model.delete_support('N1')            # only the support of a node

docs.title: Supports on an edge of a region
docs.text: For a wall or slab region, address the edge by index or by name instead of looking up nodes: model.support_edge('W1', 'bottom', kind='pin'). Kinds: 'pin', 'fix', 'roller-x', 'roller-y', 'symm-x', 'symm-y'. To add, change or free an edge, see Edges in Slabs and walls.
